chapters.title: Chapter 951
paragraphs: *Whoosh...*
The sudden downpour sent everything into a flurry of activity.
Birds folded their wings and hurried into the grass. Beasts that had been prowling for food settled inside caves far from human footsteps.
Anything to keep warm beneath the heavy rain that fell without pause.
But the animals that inhabited this vast stretch of grassland would soon realize something: for once, the rain they had never welcomed had saved them from an unseen danger.
*Rumble. Rrrumble.*
A sudden vibration.
The earth shook. No—it felt as though the entire grassland was trembling.
Hidden in their shelters, the animals instinctively bristled. With the senses they had been born with—their noses, their ears, their eyes—they detected what was coming.
Beyond the rain, so dense they could barely see an inch ahead, countless riders crossed their land.
*Splash! Thududududu!*
Mud sprayed in every direction. Hooves trampled through puddles of standing water as the horses charged forcefully onward.
At the head of the enormous, seemingly endless column, two men stood out.
“It doesn’t look like it’s going to let up.”
The lean man muttered as he gazed at the sky, then turned to the hulking man riding beside him.
“Temur.”
At the sudden call, Temur flinched.
“Y-yes?”
“We should pick up the pace. If we delay, the whole area will turn into a quagmire.”
“Yes. I suppose so.”
Temur nodded, his voice hoarse. The lean man frowned.
“And?”
“Hm?”
“Is that all?”
“Oh.”
Temur blinked, then realized his mistake. He beckoned, and dozens of cavalrymen armed with bows and lances came galloping over. They bowed their heads.
“What is it, Khan Temur?”
“Tell every commander of a thousand under me: no rest until the rain stops. We move at full speed.”
Temur did his best to sound stern. With a sidelong glance at the lean man, he added, “Anyone who neglects this order will be severely punished in my name and that of Khan Chinggen here.”
“Yes, sir!”
The cavalrymen saluted and scattered in every direction.
Only then did the furrow between Chinggen’s brows ease.
“Good. That’s how it should be. Well done.”
Temur swallowed dryly and nodded.
“Thanks for the praise.”
“Now it’s time for you to do your part as a khan. I can’t stand beside you and give you every little piece of advice forever, can I? Right, my proud brother?”
*Tap.*
Chinggen patted his armor. Temur gave a start.
“You must be cold. Are you all right?”
“...Of course. Nothing’s wrong.”
“No. I know what’s in your heart better than anyone, brother.”
Chinggen let out a quiet sigh, then suddenly clenched his teeth.
“Those filthy, despicable bastards. Every one I capture, I’ll tear to pieces and throw to the eagles.”
Chinggen’s voice rang through the rain. The nomads racing silently around them, their eyes fixed ahead, flashed killing intent in their eyes beneath their helmets.
Everyone on the grasslands knew of the massacre that had taken place that day.
Temur and Chinggen.
The two young khans had seized the eastern grasslands in a single stroke, bringing peace and prosperity. Each had brought a hundred trusted retainers to their meeting.
Neither had dreamed that the ger filled with laughter would soon be stained with blood.
“Who could have known those damned Han Chinese were plotting something so terrible?”
The uninvited guests, several hundred strong, had been Han Chinese from the Central Plains—people known as Murim martial artists.
They had burst in at the height of the feast and swung their weapons at anyone in reach.
By the grace of heaven, the two khans had survived. But after a fierce battle, most of their retainers lay in pools of blood.
“My dear brother. If Tengri hadn’t watched over us, the eastern grasslands would have been torn apart in an instant and fallen into the hands of those Han Chinese.”
Chinggen gripped his reins until his knuckles turned white.
“It’s obvious what they were after. They must have judged that we’d become a threat, with each of us commanding a powerful force. At last, they’ve shown the ambition they’d kept hidden.”
At the cold look in Chinggen’s eyes, Temur answered in a voice rough as iron.
“I—I think so too.”
“It wasn’t just us. Everyone on this land was being used by them from the very beginning. Those despicable bastards were planning to seize the entire grassland all along.”
The nomads listening to Chinggen’s seething voice nodded as one.
He was right. The Han Chinese had always been like that.
Since time immemorial, they had called the nomads barbarians, scorned them, and considered them worth less than beasts.
Even after their great ancestors had trampled the Central Plains beneath countless hooves and built a vast empire, that had not changed.
No—their contempt had become hatred.
All because a mere band of barbarians had sullied the history of the continent.
But human beings were creatures of forgetfulness.
As the years passed and their ancestors’ achievements faded from memory, the nomads began to want something new.
Peace instead of conquest.
Gold and silver instead of horse manure.
Perhaps that was why everyone had welcomed Temur and Chinggen with open arms when the two promising young men of the Golden Clan joined forces with the Han Chinese.
“It was my mistake.”
Chinggen lamented as the rain poured down on him.
“I should have thought more deeply about what kind of people they were and why they’d agreed to work with us. Noble warriors of the grasslands died because their leader was ignorant and foolish.”
At the sight of his grief and regret, everyone lowered their heads.
Then a calm, powerful voice spoke.
“If you correct that mistake, the warriors of the grasslands will be welcomed into Tengri’s embrace.”
Chinggen’s eyes widened at the sight of a middle-aged man with the distinctive braided hairstyle of the nomads.
“Why is Khan Jamukha here? You should be in the rear...”
“Greetings, Khan Jamukha!”
Cries rose all around them, beginning with Chinggen.
The middle-aged man, Jamukha, swept his gaze over the riders. There was a force in his eyes that none of them could resist.
“It was dull staying in the rear. I thought this old man might be of some help, so I came to see.”
His sideburns were as black as night, and his imposing build was sturdier than that of a young man in his prime.
But that was only how he looked. Jamukha was well over eighty years old.

He was the greatest warrior on the grasslands, another khan who had ruled the western grasslands for many years. He had joined the army with more than twenty thousand tribespeople, and in practice, he led this immense force.
“Old man? Who would dare think that of you? Isn’t that right, Temur?”
Temur gazed at Jamukha with trembling eyes, then hurriedly nodded.
“Y-yes.”
“Khan Jamukha is our elder in the Golden Clan, a great warrior and a khan. We’re grateful that you entrusted us with the vanguard.”
Chinggen raised his voice so everyone around them could hear.
“Those foolish Han Chinese probably never knew how strong Khan Jamukha was—not even as they were dying.”
Chinggen needn’t have said a word. The eyes fixed on Jamukha were already full of admiration and reverence.
Jamukha, the greatest warrior on the grasslands.
According to the story, several hundred Han Chinese had attacked him before they attacked Temur and Chinggen.
He had only a dozen or so personal guards with him.
But the outcome had been staggering.
Jamukha had proved his prowess beyond doubt.
With a mere handful of guards—barely a match for the enemy numbers—he had fought a battle against the Han Chinese that was little short of a massacre.
In the end, the Han Chinese plot against the western grasslands had failed. Enraged, Jamukha had led his tribes toward the Central Plains.
Just as he was doing now.
“It was nothing. My men were simply skilled.”
Jamukha answered calmly and jerked his chin over his shoulder. His personal guards, clad in dark armor, galloped after him with expressionless faces.
They were the elite warriors created by the great conqueror who had laid the foundations of the nomadic empire in the distant past.
Known as the *Keshik*, they still followed Jamukha as remnants of the Golden Clan.
Each was as strong as a warrior who represented an entire tribe.
And there were a thousand of them.
The grassland army numbered tens of thousands. Its confidence in victory was not based on hope alone.
“From here on, some of my personal guards will take the vanguard.”
“The Keshik...?”
“Yes. Is there a problem?”
Chinggen fell silent for a moment at Jamukha’s unexpected words, then shook his head.
“Of course not. We would have asked you ourselves. Isn’t that right, Temur?”
“...That’s right. I agree.”
The strongest warriors would lead the charge.
It was a natural decision, and everyone accepted it.
Everyone but one person.
*Are you sure that’s wise?*
At the sudden Sound Transmission in his ear, Jamukha’s lips moved.
*Didn’t you just say you would have asked me yourself?*
*That was...*
*I won’t change my mind. We’ll put those children in the vanguard and cross the border in the shortest time possible.*
*There could be a trap. The place is crawling with fodder to take arrows for us. Why waste precious forces?*
*What trap? Fire King and Jin Taekyung, who won’t reach Shanxi Province for several days? Or those insignificant Shanxi fools?*
Jamukha answered bluntly and stared straight at the source of the Sound Transmission.
*Keep that idiot beside you under control. I’m beginning to regret not killing him back then.*
*I told you we should have kept the smarter one alive instead.*
Chinggen—or someone wearing his face—let out a chuckle too faint for anyone to notice and ran a hand over his features.
*He was impressive in his own way. Even while his men were dying all around him, he tried to negotiate.*
He remembered it clearly.
Beside Temur, who had yielded to the overwhelming difference in strength and even wet himself, Chinggen had stood firm and told them to name what they wanted.
*Compared to that dead man, this idiot...*
*I kept him alive because he’s an idiot. Someone who’s surrendered deep in his heart is that much easier to handle.*
*I’ll grant you that. Thanks to his cooperation, far more barbarians gathered than I expected.*
His amused gaze swept across the vast army filling the grasslands.
Only a little more than a day’s travel remained.
When the rain stopped, they would cross the grasslands and go over the walls.

chapters.title: Chapter 952
paragraphs: The Double Ninth Festival was one of the continent’s biggest holidays.
It came when swallows flew south to warmer lands and snakes and frogs burrowed underground to prepare for winter.
At this time of year, people climbed mountains, drank chrysanthemum wine, recited poetry, and enjoyed the scenery.
Commoners who lived from one day’s wages to the next did it. So did high officials who wanted for nothing, and martial artists who lived in the turbulent martial world.
“Do you remember?”
A voice sounded suddenly behind him.
The young man gazing at the field of bright yellow chrysanthemums showed no surprise. He had known who was there for some time.
“Remember what?”
Jin Mukyung asked without taking his eyes off the flowers. A familiar presence came to stand beside him.
“Five years ago, when the three of us climbed the hill behind the house and spent the Double Ninth Festival together. We had such a wonderful time.”
“...You mean the Double Ninth Festival ten years ago?”
Jin Wikyung looked hurt at his younger brother’s doubtful response.
“Goodness. You don’t even remember anymore?”
“I remember. I asked because your version sounds quite different from mine.”
“Different?”
“Taekyung, that reckless fool, got completely drunk and caused a scene. It wasn’t exactly a pleasant time.”
Jin Wikyung tilted his head.
“Really? You looked like you were enjoying yourself when you beat him with your scabbard.”
“I wasn’t smiling. I was disciplining my own flesh and blood to set him on the right path.”
“Then why were you grinning from ear to ear?”
Jin Mukyung fell silent.
Come to think of it, perhaps he had been smiling.
His youngest brother was always causing trouble, and their eldest brother doted on him. When an excuse to punish Taekyung finally presented itself, how could Mukyung not smile?
Of course, that was long ago. Only a small fragment of the day remained in his memory.

“The youngest bawled like the sky had fallen, and you didn’t touch your food. You just started training. You went off into the woods, away from everyone, and swung your sword until sunset. I can still picture you as clearly as if it were yesterday.”
“I don’t remember that, but I’m sure I did.”
Jin Mukyung’s reply was matter-of-fact.
Training was a matter of course for him. He had held a sword since childhood and practiced wherever he was, whenever he could.
Five years ago, the last time the three brothers of the Jin Family of Taiyuan had spent the Double Ninth Festival together, Mukyung had already reached the Peak realm, though he was barely twenty.
“I still remember the day you left home.”
“Ah.”
Jin Mukyung smacked his lips. He remembered Wikyung coming to see him off with a swollen face, as though he had spent the previous night crying.
“Do you... do you really have to go?”
“Yes. I really do.”
“Even if your older brother begs you to stay?”
“Not a chance.”
“What’s so special about Heaven’s Gate Temple that you’d abandon your family and go all the way to a distant land?”
“Even disciples of the great sects wait years to get into that Heaven’s Gate Temple you’re dismissing.”
“All right. If that’s what you want, I’ll escort you to Henan myself.”
“...You’re serious?”
“There’s something I need to tell the Hall Master in person.”
“What on earth would you tell him?”
“Just a few important precautions he absolutely needs to know. Some foods you hate, your habits... Mukyung! Where are you going, Mukyung!”
He had run. With every last bit of strength he had.
It was the first time in his life he had put so much effort into his movement technique.
Jin Mukyung had only wanted to grow stronger at Heaven’s Gate Temple. He’d never had the slightest intention of earning the distinction of being its shortest-lived expelled cadet.
“I still remember your back as you left, covering your eyes with your sleeve to hide your sobs.”
Jin Mukyung quietly closed his mouth.
Some truths were more beautiful left untold. That he had raised his sleeve to shield his eyes from the dust, for instance. Or that he had run to escape his overzealous brother.
Before he knew it, a quiet laugh escaped him.
“Why are you laughing?”
“It’s nothing. Just...”
Jin Mukyung managed to stop laughing and turned his head.
There was the face he remembered from about two years ago, when he had left once more to enter seclusion with no end in sight. Wikyung had watched him go with worry in his eyes.
Just as he was looking at him now.
“I laughed because I’m glad to see you. You haven’t changed at all, older brother.”
“Mukyung, you...”
“I’m glad everything is still the same.”
He had spent a little over two years in pitch-black darkness.
He had kept hunger at bay with bitter, astringent fasting pills and quenched his thirst with dew and rainwater collected in the training hall deep inside the cave.
And whenever he swung his sword until he collapsed from exhaustion, sprawled on the cold ground, a thought would come to him.
*Where was this place? Who was he?*
*If he ever left that darkness, what would be waiting for him?*
“Part of me was afraid, too. Afraid that the world I knew, the people I knew, would have changed beyond recognition.”
He had been half right and half wrong.
Everything around him had changed. The people he knew had not.
Surely that included his troublemaking youngest brother, wherever he was now.
“The day that brat left the family, he came to see me and said something.”
Mukyung had turned their conversation over in his mind thousands of times. No, tens of thousands. Taekyung’s voice, unusually calm that day, still lingered in his ears.
“See you later.”
It had not been a simple farewell.
The Star-Array Grand Banquet.
Taekyung had challenged him to meet there, among the countless stars from the Nine Provinces and Eight Wastes and the Four Seas and Five Lakes, and test their skills alongside Cheongpung.
As brothers born of the same mother. As martial artists.
After Taekyung left, Mukyung had stood staring at the empty space he had occupied and murmured the answer he had failed to give him.
*Yeah. See you later. I promise.*
But that promise had never been kept.
In that place, where he could not even feel time passing, Jin Mukyung swung his sword without rest. He slashed, stabbed, and tore through what lay beyond the pitch-black darkness.
Whenever he opened his eyes to something new, another wall rose before him.
He had to get over it. Break through it.
With the unkept promise tucked away in a corner of his heart, Jin Mukyung pressed on.
Until he found a faint light in the darkness.
Until that light grew as clear as the sun.
At last, he came back into the world.
He left behind the darkness that had enveloped him for two years and emerged into a world filled with another kind.
“Hyung.”
Jin Mukyung called softly and looked his own flesh and blood straight in the eyes.
There was light in his gaze, and a directness that made it impossible to lie to him.
“Now tell me what I must do.”
“No. Give me an order, as the Lesser Family Head of the Jin Family of Taiyuan.”
For a moment, Jin Wikyung’s eyes trembled.
“You knew...?”
Jin Mukyung nodded.
The Jin Family of Taiyuan now stood at the head of Shanxi Murim. With the Family Head missing, Jin Wikyung led them all as its Alliance Leader.
Shanxi Province was already at war.

Li Feng, a lay disciple of Huashan and Shanxi Province’s Assistant Military Commissioner, had mobilized every force at the Shanxi Provincial Office to evacuate the people in the north. Some five thousand martial artists had gathered in the central region.
Every moment mattered.
Wikyung had not come looking for him solely to reunite with the brother who had emerged from seclusion after two years.
“Just as you know me well, hyung, I know you.”
“This will be a dangerous mission.”
“I don’t mind.”
Jin Mukyung went on calmly.
“I learned martial arts because I loved the sword. But I wanted to grow stronger for our family.”
Only great strength could restore a fallen martial family.
His sword had carried more than a passion for martial arts all these years.
“Jin Mukyung, Second Young Master of the Jin Family of Taiyuan. I will devote myself to carrying out the Lesser Family Head’s orders.”
His younger brother cupped his hands in a salute, his voice unwavering. Jin Wikyung slowly closed his eyes.

After a brief hesitation, he opened them again. He was no longer speaking as Mukyung’s older brother, but as the Alliance Leader of Shanxi Murim and the Lesser Family Head of the Jin Family of Taiyuan.
“From this moment on, you are neither the Second Young Master of the Jin Family of Taiyuan nor the Lesser Family Head’s younger brother.”
He released the breath he had been holding.
Then Wikyung looked calmly at his brother—no, his retainer—and continued.
“I command Jin Mukyung, Commander of the Heaven Shaking Squad.”
Jin Mukyung, the Heaven Shaking Sword.
About five years ago, a young prodigy from the frontier had reached the Peak realm at barely twenty and earned a new epithet. His only older brother had named a fighting force after it.
He had hoped Mukyung would one day return to this place.
And with the wish that, just like the two characters in Heaven Shaking, his name would one day resound beyond the world and reach the heavens.
“The enemy vanguard that invaded the north has split off some of its troops and is taking a detour to avoid Jeongyang. Take two hundred men from the Heaven Shaking Squad and blunt their vanguard.”
Jin Mukyung smiled.
“As you command.”
The next day.
The vast steppe army entered the north without resistance. What awaited it was not chrysanthemums but dark-red blood covering the mountain slopes—and one terrified survivor of its vanguard.
“K-Khan...”
Jamukha stared silently at the man trembling like a leaf.

He knew at once that the thousand-man vanguard sent into Shanxi Province half a day ahead of the main force had been wiped out. The lone surviving fool had been sent back with a warning for the invaders.

sentences.text: The Double Ninth Festival was one of the continent’s biggest holidays.
It came when swallows flew south to warmer lands and snakes and frogs burrowed underground to prepare for winter.
At this time of year, people climbed mountains, drank chrysanthemum wine, recited poetry, and enjoyed the scenery.
Commoners who lived from one day’s wages to the next did it.
So did high officials who wanted for nothing, and martial artists who lived in the turbulent martial world.
“Do you remember?”
A voice sounded suddenly behind him.
The young man gazing at the field of bright yellow chrysanthemums showed no surprise.
He had known who was there for some time.
“Remember what?”
Jin Mukyung asked without taking his eyes off the flowers.
A familiar presence came to stand beside him.
“Five years ago, when the three of us climbed the hill behind the house and spent the Double Ninth Festival together.
We had such a wonderful time.”
“...You mean the Double Ninth Festival ten years ago?”
Jin Wikyung looked hurt at his younger brother’s doubtful response.
“Goodness.
You don’t even remember anymore?”
“I remember.
I asked because your version sounds quite different from mine.”
“Different?”
“Taekyung, that reckless fool, got completely drunk and caused a scene.
It wasn’t exactly a pleasant time.”
Jin Wikyung tilted his head.
“Really?
You looked like you were enjoying yourself when you beat him with your scabbard.”
“I wasn’t smiling.
I was disciplining my own flesh and blood to set him on the right path.”
“Then why were you grinning from ear to ear?”
Jin Mukyung fell silent.
Come to think of it, perhaps he had been smiling.
His youngest brother was always causing trouble, and their eldest brother doted on him.
When an excuse to punish Taekyung finally presented itself, how could Mukyung not smile?
Of course, that was long ago.
Only a small fragment of the day remained in his memory.
“The youngest bawled like the sky had fallen, and you didn’t touch your food.
You just started training.
You went off into the woods, away from everyone, and swung your sword until sunset.
I can still picture you as clearly as if it were yesterday.”
“I don’t remember that, but I’m sure I did.”
Jin Mukyung’s reply was matter-of-fact.
Training was a matter of course for him.
He had held a sword since childhood and practiced wherever he was, whenever he could.
Five years ago, the last time the three brothers of the Jin Family of Taiyuan had spent the Double Ninth Festival together, Mukyung had already reached the Peak realm, though he was barely twenty.
“I still remember the day you left home.”
“Ah.”
Jin Mukyung smacked his lips.
He remembered Wikyung coming to see him off with a swollen face, as though he had spent the previous night crying.
“Do you... do you really have to go?”
“Yes.
I really do.”
“Even if your older brother begs you to stay?”
“Not a chance.”
“What’s so special about Heaven’s Gate Temple that you’d abandon your family and go all the way to a distant land?”
“Even disciples of the great sects wait years to get into that Heaven’s Gate Temple you’re dismissing.”
“All right.
If that’s what you want, I’ll escort you to Henan myself.”
“...You’re serious?”
“There’s something I need to tell the Hall Master in person.”
“What on earth would you tell him?”
“Just a few important precautions he absolutely needs to know.
Some foods you hate, your habits...
Mukyung!
Where are you going, Mukyung!”
He had run.
With every last bit of strength he had.
It was the first time in his life he had put so much effort into his movement technique.
Jin Mukyung had only wanted to grow stronger at Heaven’s Gate Temple.
He’d never had the slightest intention of earning the distinction of being its shortest-lived expelled cadet.
“I still remember your back as you left, covering your eyes with your sleeve to hide your sobs.”
Jin Mukyung quietly closed his mouth.
Some truths were more beautiful left untold.
That he had raised his sleeve to shield his eyes from the dust, for instance.
Or that he had run to escape his overzealous brother.
Before he knew it, a quiet laugh escaped him.
“Why are you laughing?”
“It’s nothing.
Just...”
Jin Mukyung managed to stop laughing and turned his head.
There was the face he remembered from about two years ago, when he had left once more to enter seclusion with no end in sight.
Wikyung had watched him go with worry in his eyes.
Just as he was looking at him now.
“I laughed because I’m glad to see you.
You haven’t changed at all, older brother.”
“Mukyung, you...”
“I’m glad everything is still the same.”
He had spent a little over two years in pitch-black darkness.
He had kept hunger at bay with bitter, astringent fasting pills and quenched his thirst with dew and rainwater collected in the training hall deep inside the cave.
And whenever he swung his sword until he collapsed from exhaustion, sprawled on the cold ground, a thought would come to him.
*Where was this place?
Who was he?*
*If he ever left that darkness, what would be waiting for him?*
“Part of me was afraid, too.
Afraid that the world I knew, the people I knew, would have changed beyond recognition.”
He had been half right and half wrong.
Everything around him had changed.
The people he knew had not.
Surely that included his troublemaking youngest brother, wherever he was now.
“The day that brat left the family, he came to see me and said something.”
Mukyung had turned their conversation over in his mind thousands of times.
No, tens of thousands.
Taekyung’s voice, unusually calm that day, still lingered in his ears.
“See you later.”
It had not been a simple farewell.
The Star-Array Grand Banquet.
Taekyung had challenged him to meet there, among the countless stars from the Nine Provinces and Eight Wastes and the Four Seas and Five Lakes, and test their skills alongside Cheongpung.
As brothers born of the same mother.
As martial artists.
After Taekyung left, Mukyung had stood staring at the empty space he had occupied and murmured the answer he had failed to give him.
*Yeah.
See you later.
I promise.*
But that promise had never been kept.
In that place, where he could not even feel time passing, Jin Mukyung swung his sword without rest.
He slashed, stabbed, and tore through what lay beyond the pitch-black darkness.
Whenever he opened his eyes to something new, another wall rose before him.
He had to get over it.
Break through it.
With the unkept promise tucked away in a corner of his heart, Jin Mukyung pressed on.
Until he found a faint light in the darkness.
Until that light grew as clear as the sun.
At last, he came back into the world.
He left behind the darkness that had enveloped him for two years and emerged into a world filled with another kind.
“Hyung.”
Jin Mukyung called softly and looked his own flesh and blood straight in the eyes.
There was light in his gaze, and a directness that made it impossible to lie to him.
“Now tell me what I must do.”
“No.
Give me an order, as the Lesser Family Head of the Jin Family of Taiyuan.”
For a moment, Jin Wikyung’s eyes trembled.
“You knew...?”
Jin Mukyung nodded.

Every moment mattered.
Wikyung had not come looking for him solely to reunite with the brother who had emerged from seclusion after two years.

“This will be a dangerous mission.”
“I don’t mind.”
Jin Mukyung went on calmly.
“I learned martial arts because I loved the sword.
But I wanted to grow stronger for our family.”
Only great strength could restore a fallen martial family.
His sword had carried more than a passion for martial arts all these years.

Jin Mukyung, the Heaven Shaking Sword.
About five years ago, a young prodigy from the frontier had reached the Peak realm at barely twenty and earned a new epithet.
His only older brother had named a fighting force after it.

And with the wish that, just like the two characters in Heaven Shaking, his name would one day resound beyond the world and reach the heavens.
“The enemy vanguard that invaded the north has split off some of its troops and is taking a detour to avoid Jeongyang.
Take two hundred men from the Heaven Shaking Squad and blunt their vanguard.”

The next day.

paragraphs: When dozens or hundreds of people fought tangled together, it was a battle.
But when the numbers grew to thousands, tens of thousands, it could no longer be called a battle.
It was war.
A war in which both sides threw everything they had into the fight.
And Jin Wikyung had no intention of staking everything he had on a single gamble.
“Jin Mukyung, Commander of the Heaven Shaking Squad, reporting to the Lesser Family Head.”
His voice was calm, though his whole body was soaked in blood.
Mukyung had left at noon and returned only around midnight. He looked like a blood demon.
So did his men, whose squad took its name from his epithet, the Heaven Shaking Sword.
But their proud strides and bright, fierce eyes were proof of the Jin Family of Taiyuan’s first victory.
“By your command, we broke the enemy’s vanguard and returned.”
Mukyung went on with his report.
Of the slightly more than two hundred men in the Heaven Shaking Squad, twenty-three had died and thirty-seven had suffered injuries, serious or minor.

Several of the senior leaders grew somber at the news. In a single battle, the Jin Family of Taiyuan had lost sixty men from an elite force it had devoted itself to raising alongside the Jin Dragon Squad. But the rest of Mukyung’s report swept even that brief sorrow away.
A thousand.
They had annihilated an enemy vanguard five times their number.
And among them had been a hundred of the enemy’s elite troops.
“Waaaah!”
Everyone who had been listening in tense silence cheered at once.
Their first victory against the enemy.
An overwhelming victory, beyond any dispute.
Yet even as excitement surged around him, Jin Wikyung kept his composure.
*This is only the beginning.*
He knew it.
War was like building a sandcastle. You had to scoop up sand and pile it on, again and again, before it was complete.
And even a sandcastle built with such care could collapse from a single hard kick.
*But if we build it solidly enough to withstand that kick, it’s another story.*
Fortunately, the Jin Family of Taiyuan’s preparations had been thorough despite the little time they’d had.
By now, the grassland army—likely crossing the Great Wall and passing through northern Shanxi Province—must have been bewildered.
First, by the news that its vanguard, which included its finest troops, had been wiped out.
And then by finding the north truly *empty*.
*You won’t find a thing to take there.*
It wasn’t only the people who had left the north.
Wikyung had withdrawn all the troops and commoners and ordered every field, though harvest was near, burned.
A scorched-earth strategy.

Against an army of tens of thousands, it was an excellent tactic. Even so, Wikyung had agonized over the decision dozens of times—until Assistant Military Commissioner Li Feng of Shanxi Province and several hundred others came to him of their own accord.
“We have several tens of thousands of seok of provisions in reserve. We can more than handle their food supply.”
With Zhu Bao and Hong Jin absent, Li Feng was effectively the highest-ranking official at the Shanxi Provincial Office. He promised his full cooperation.
“Just burn the whole damn lot.”
The people of the north who had been forced to leave their homes overnight—or rather, their village headmen—were already half blind with rage.
“Those damn bastards. They come raiding and raising hell all the time, and now they want to take what’s growing in our fields, too?”
“Everyone in our village has already agreed. If even one grain of rice gets into those barbarian bastards’ mouths, I’ll be torn to pieces.”
“I’d sooner feed rice to the cows and pigs. I won’t stand for those bastards eating it, even when I’m dead!”
“Shit. If anyone objects, step forward now. I don’t care who you are—open your mouth and I’ll take you for a barbarian, shave your head, and give you a queue.”
“Hey, Mr. Song! Why aren’t you saying anything? You got honey spread over your fields?”
Mr. Song, the village headman who had said nothing at all, earned everyone’s applause with a single suggestion.
“Don’t just set fires. Let’s poison the wells.”
“It’d be even better if we took a dump and pissed in the stream before we left.”
“What’s the shit and piss for?”
“It’ll dirty the water. You think those bastards will be fine after gulping down water mixed with shit and piss?”
“Good heavens! How did you come up with a plan like that...?”
“I tried it once. Drank about half a gallon. Thought I was going to die.”

Mr. Song, a farmer with the unusual distinction of having drunk sewage, became a hero overnight. As people shoved poisonous weeds into the wells and shat and pissed by the streams, they wondered why he hadn’t placed first in the civil service exams.
All while saying that the only good barbarian was a dead one—words that would have shocked someone if they’d heard them.
*The road here won’t be easy.*
Jin Wikyung smiled coldly.
Shanxi Province was undeniably a frontier.
It produced plenty of grain, but it was neither as developed as the Central Plains nor as strong militarily.
Yet that was why its people could unite all the more fiercely in a crisis.
Long years of raids by mounted bandits and nomads had instilled a stubborn resolve in the people of Shanxi. Now that resolve had caught fire.
*We will protect it. No matter what.*
Wikyung had already made up his mind.

He had gone without sleep or rest to devote himself to the preparations. He sent swift-footed subordinates to watch the north and organized small detachments to look for any enemy forces that might split off from the main army.
He had ordered traps and iron caltrops set along every detour except Jeongyang. Checking the progress of the work himself was part of that effort.
“How is the earthen fort coming along?”
“With the reinforcement work included, it should be finished within half a day at the latest.”
Eight Spring Gorge.
At the far end of the vase-shaped gorge, which had swallowed countless lives from the Great Faction War to the present day, stood five towers where none had stood before.
Built of mud, wood, and stone, each rose three *jang* high. Each had a level platform large enough to hold a little over two hundred people.
Two hundred archers, to be exact.
“Taking the heights above the gorge isn’t enough. These forts are essential to victory. Please do everything you can to make sure they don’t collapse.”
“Of course, sir.”
The old carpenter answered in a folksy drawl.
Even as the two spoke, countless people around them went about their assigned tasks.
They came from all walks of life.
Martial artists in uniforms bearing the names of their sects hauled weapons and heavy materials without pause. Government troops in official uniforms moved at their officers’ commands.
But Wikyung’s gaze settled on another group, people dressed in all sorts of clothes with no affiliation to mark them, working just as hard.
“Pull on three!”
“One, twooo!”
“Hyaah!”
Men covered in dust kept up the grueling labor, sweat pouring off them.
“Where should we put these arrows?”
“Oil! Bring the oil over here!”
Women carried supplies for the battle and prepared simple food.
Looking at the thousands of commoners, Wikyung felt a tightness in his chest.
*I told them to flee as far away as they could.*
He had warned them sincerely, again and again. He had tried to persuade them.
This wasn’t merely a dispute among martial artists.
It was a brutal war that would claim countless lives, and they, with no strength to defend themselves, would suffer the most.
But they had made up their minds and refused to leave.
They had even come to help here, on a battlefield that would soon be swept by bloodshed.
Like the old carpenter standing before him.
“Looks like our Lesser Family Head has a lot on his mind.”
The old carpenter, who had been glancing sideways at Jin Wikyung, chuckled.
He had passed seventy several years ago. When he laughed, air whistled through the gaps between the few teeth he had left.
“Don’t you worry about it. This old man and all those folks out there came prepared.”
“But still... how could I not worry?”
“Goodness, please don’t speak so formally to me. I may be an old man without much time left, but I’m not shameless enough to expect honorifics from the Lesser Family Head.”
The old carpenter hurriedly waved his hands. Warmth shone in his pale gray eyes as he looked at Wikyung.
“Even a beast that can’t speak will repay a kindness someday. How could people turn their backs at a time like this?”
“What do you mean...?”

“When I was young and full of life, you’d have thought the country was falling apart. The Demonic Cult, or demons, or whatever those wretches were, stirred up trouble everywhere. Then came years of famine.”
It had happened long ago, before Jin Wikyung was born.
But the old carpenter remembered it clearly: boiling leather to eat and stripping bark from trees to chew.
Everyone was starving. There was no one they could ask for help, and no one able to give it.
If a group of men hadn’t come to their village one day under the blazing sun, he and his family would have starved to death before long.
“Is this Hong Family Village?”
“Y-yes, it is. What brings you here...?”
“Phew. Thank goodness we found the right place.”
What was the point of tilling fields that yielded not a single grain?
They had abandoned the barren land long before, gone into the mountains, and become slash-and-burn farmers.
So at first, they had thought the newcomers were bandits.
Or men sent by someone powerful to squeeze the last drops from people who had neither an iron coin nor a handful of grain left.
Why else would anyone come this deep into the mountains?
But instead of drawing the swords at their waists, the men set down the loads on their backs.
They were huge sacks.
Dozens of them, filled to the brim with grain and meat—the kind of sight they could barely remember ever seeing.
“W-what in the world is this...?”
“Get in line. We’ll hand it out in order.”
It felt like a dream.

It still felt like one when everyone in the village lined up as the men instructed, and when he watched his wife and children, who had lain weak and helpless for days, eat until their bellies were full to bursting.
Only after staring at that unbelievable sight and swallowing a mouthful of warm meat broth did he realize it was real.
So he cried.
No—everyone cried.
They wept aloud even as they chewed and swallowed the food in their mouths.
Because they wanted to live. Because they wanted to know they were alive.
“If they hadn’t helped us that day, this old man and my family would have starved to death there.”
The old carpenter looked at Wikyung with tears in his eyes. Unlike back then, he had a broad smile on his face.
“But those good people tried to leave without a word. So I grabbed one of them by the leg and hung on.”
He couldn’t read, not even the writing on their clothes.
So he’d clung on stubbornly, asking where they were from and begging them to tell him their three-character names.
After a long struggle, he got the answer he wanted.
“From that day on, I vowed that if the Jin Family of Taiyuan ever needed me, I would give this worthless life of mine.”
“And I’m not the only one. Every person here has received help from the Jin Family of Taiyuan, large or small.”
Some of those who had received that kindness had left. Others had stayed.
And those who stayed were ready to lay down their lives.
To protect the land where their fathers and mothers had lived, where they themselves had lived.
For the Jin Family of Taiyuan, who had reached out to them when they lay exhausted, waiting to die.
That was the Jin Family of Taiyuan’s true strength. It was what had sustained a distinguished family through three hundred years of rises and falls.
*Ah.*
Wikyung felt an ache deep in his chest.
Perhaps he was the one who had underestimated the Jin Family of Taiyuan—and Shanxi Province—most of all.
He turned away to hide his reddened eyes.
*Thududududu!*
Hooves pounded fiercely, their sound clear even from far away.
A fine horse raced across the gorge as though something were chasing it. Hanging from the horse was a martial artist of the Jin Family of Taiyuan, dead with his eyes wide open.
The air froze in an instant. Jin Wikyung shouted as if spitting blood.
“Everyone, prepare for battle!”
They were here.

Each had a level platform large enough to hold a little over two hundred people.
Two hundred archers, to be exact.
“Taking the heights above the gorge isn’t enough.
These forts are essential to victory.
Please do everything you can to make sure they don’t collapse.”
“Of course, sir.”
The old carpenter answered in a folksy drawl.
Even as the two spoke, countless people around them went about their assigned tasks.
They came from all walks of life.
Martial artists in uniforms bearing the names of their sects hauled weapons and heavy materials without pause.
Government troops in official uniforms moved at their officers’ commands.
But Wikyung’s gaze settled on another group, people dressed in all sorts of clothes with no affiliation to mark them, working just as hard.
“Pull on three!”
“One, twooo!”
“Hyaah!”
Men covered in dust kept up the grueling labor, sweat pouring off them.
“Where should we put these arrows?”
“Oil!
Bring the oil over here!”
Women carried supplies for the battle and prepared simple food.
Looking at the thousands of commoners, Wikyung felt a tightness in his chest.
*I told them to flee as far away as they could.*
He had warned them sincerely, again and again.
He had tried to persuade them.
This wasn’t merely a dispute among martial artists.
It was a brutal war that would claim countless lives, and they, with no strength to defend themselves, would suffer the most.
But they had made up their minds and refused to leave.
They had even come to help here, on a battlefield that would soon be swept by bloodshed.
Like the old carpenter standing before him.
“Looks like our Lesser Family Head has a lot on his mind.”
The old carpenter, who had been glancing sideways at Jin Wikyung, chuckled.
He had passed seventy several years ago.
When he laughed, air whistled through the gaps between the few teeth he had left.
“Don’t you worry about it.
This old man and all those folks out there came prepared.”
“But still... how could I not worry?”
“Goodness, please don’t speak so formally to me.
I may be an old man without much time left, but I’m not shameless enough to expect honorifics from the Lesser Family Head.”
The old carpenter hurriedly waved his hands.
Warmth shone in his pale gray eyes as he looked at Wikyung.
“Even a beast that can’t speak will repay a kindness someday.
How could people turn their backs at a time like this?”
“What do you mean...?”
“When I was young and full of life, you’d have thought the country was falling apart.
The Demonic Cult, or demons, or whatever those wretches were, stirred up trouble everywhere.
Then came years of famine.”
It had happened long ago, before Jin Wikyung was born.
But the old carpenter remembered it clearly: boiling leather to eat and stripping bark from trees to chew.
Everyone was starving.
There was no one they could ask for help, and no one able to give it.
If a group of men hadn’t come to their village one day under the blazing sun, he and his family would have starved to death before long.
“Is this Hong Family Village?”
“Y-yes, it is.
What brings you here...?”
“Phew.
Thank goodness we found the right place.”
What was the point of tilling fields that yielded not a single grain?
They had abandoned the barren land long before, gone into the mountains, and become slash-and-burn farmers.
So at first, they had thought the newcomers were bandits.
Or men sent by someone powerful to squeeze the last drops from people who had neither an iron coin nor a handful of grain left.
Why else would anyone come this deep into the mountains?
But instead of drawing the swords at their waists, the men set down the loads on their backs.
They were huge sacks.
Dozens of them, filled to the brim with grain and meat—the kind of sight they could barely remember ever seeing.
“W-what in the world is this...?”
“Get in line.
We’ll hand it out in order.”
It felt like a dream.

It still felt like one when everyone in the village lined up as the men instructed, and when he watched his wife and children, who had lain weak and helpless for days, eat until their bellies were full to bursting.
Only after staring at that unbelievable sight and swallowing a mouthful of warm meat broth did he realize it was real.
So he cried.
No—everyone cried.
They wept aloud even as they chewed and swallowed the food in their mouths.
Because they wanted to live.
Because they wanted to know they were alive.
“If they hadn’t helped us that day, this old man and my family would have starved to death there.”
The old carpenter looked at Wikyung with tears in his eyes.
Unlike back then, he had a broad smile on his face.
“But those good people tried to leave without a word.
So I grabbed one of them by the leg and hung on.”
He couldn’t read, not even the writing on their clothes.
So he’d clung on stubbornly, asking where they were from and begging them to tell him their three-character names.
After a long struggle, he got the answer he wanted.
“From that day on, I vowed that if the Jin Family of Taiyuan ever needed me, I would give this worthless life of mine.”
“And I’m not the only one.
Every person here has received help from the Jin Family of Taiyuan, large or small.”
Some of those who had received that kindness had left.
Others had stayed.
And those who stayed were ready to lay down their lives.
To protect the land where their fathers and mothers had lived, where they themselves had lived.
For the Jin Family of Taiyuan, who had reached out to them when they lay exhausted, waiting to die.
That was the Jin Family of Taiyuan’s true strength.
It was what had sustained a distinguished family through three hundred years of rises and falls.
*Ah.*
Wikyung felt an ache deep in his chest.
Perhaps he was the one who had underestimated the Jin Family of Taiyuan—and Shanxi Province—most of all.
He turned away to hide his reddened eyes.
*Thududududu!*
Hooves pounded fiercely, their sound clear even from far away.
A fine horse raced across the gorge as though something were chasing it.
Hanging from the horse was a martial artist of the Jin Family of Taiyuan, dead with his eyes wide open.
The air froze in an instant.
Jin Wikyung shouted as if spitting blood.
“Everyone, prepare for battle!”
They were here.

chapters.title: Chapter 954
paragraphs: When the sun sank toward the western mountains and darkness settled over the land, the quiet world carried sounds on the wind that no one could hear by day.
The cries of insects. Leaves brushing against one another.
And, from hundreds of *jang* away, something like a shout from someone whose voice carried internal energy.
“I don’t know who that bastard is, but he’s got a set of lungs on him. Don’t you think?”
At the low voice that pierced his ears, Temur swallowed nervously.
In his trembling eyes was the reflection of a man smiling beneath the faint moonlight.
Chinggen.
His blood relative, who had grown up alongside him since a childhood now hazy in his memory.
They hadn’t been born to the same parents, but Chinggen was a cousin closer than any brother, and a sworn brother bound to him by the anda oath.
And... a dead man. Someone who no longer belonged to this world.
*This is no time to laugh and chatter, Temur.*
The memory flashed before Temur’s eyes: Chinggen speaking to him with a worried look, just before an unusually cold steppe wind pushed open the entrance to the ger.
*Brother, I’m sorry. You were right.*
Temur lowered his head in misery.
Why hadn’t he listened to Chinggen?
Even before that day—the day of a tragedy that made him shudder just to remember it—Chinggen had sent word through messengers several times.
Something was wrong on the grasslands.
Something unknown seemed to be starting beyond their reach.
But Temur had let the warnings go in one ear and out the other. He’d filled his ger with rare treasures brought along the trade routes, then feasted on meat and liquor with his men.
He’d never dreamed what would come of it.
“What’s got you so lost in thought this time, brother?”
The Chinggen of his memory vanished. Temur jerked his head up like a man startled awake and answered in a trembling voice.
To the man who had killed Chinggen—and had now become Chinggen.
“Nothing. It’s nothing.”
“Goodness. You must be nervous before the battle. Is that why you didn’t hear me?”
“What do you mean...?”
“That shout just now. Don’t you recognize the voice?”
Only then did Temur understand. He answered quickly.
“Y-yes. The Lesser Family Head of the Jin Family of Taiyuan. It has to be him.”
“Ah, I see. I thought I’d heard that voice before.”

Of course, the man was lying to keep anyone nearby from growing suspicious. Temur might be simple, but the meticulous Chinggen would never have forgotten someone important whom he’d met several times.
“Jin Wikyung... So that’s who it is.”
Chinggen smacked his lips in satisfaction and glanced over his shoulder. At the look he gave him, Jamukha, riding with his customary calm, nodded slightly.
*The Lesser Family Head of the Jin Family of Taiyuan has more than a loud voice. He has nerve, too.*
Their Sound Transmission passed discreetly through the darkness. A faint smile touched Jamukha’s lips.
*If he’d meant to flee from the start, he wouldn’t have gone to the trouble of pulling that stunt.*
*It was quite a stunt. It cost us more than we expected.*
Chinggen frowned and spat phlegm from his swaying saddle.
The Great Wall, which a cruel emperor had built across a full ten thousand *li* after unifying the continent long ago, hardly deserved to be called a wall.
Yet the north, which should have been unoccupied, was littered with obstacles everywhere.
*Losing the vanguard was one thing. I didn’t expect them to turn the whole place into such a filthy shitshow.*
A shitshow. Chinggen couldn’t think of a better word for it.

Northern Shanxi Province, which they had reached through wind and rain, had been devastated. Paddies and fields that should have been nearing harvest were ruined. Wells and streams were fouled with poison and filth. Even the houses had been reduced to ashes.
*Those lunatics. They burned down the places they’d been living in until recently, then left.*
At Chinggen’s Sound Transmission, Jamukha’s lips moved, his expression still calm.
*Do you know Emperor Gaozu of Han?*
*I’ve heard of him. Liu Bang, from the story of Xiang Yu and Liu Bang?*
*Yes. Even the eventual victor was once driven back by Xiang Yu and had to leave for Hanzhong. On the advice of his strategist Zhang Liang, he burned the plank roads behind him.*
*He cut off his own way back.*
*But he returned to the Central Plains, defeated Xiang Yu, and became ruler of all under Heaven. This land is their plank road. As long as its people survive, they can always rebuild it.*
One person alone was an individual. Ten made a group.
But gather a hundred or a thousand, and villages and cities arose.
People were what mattered.

Though everything in the north had been destroyed, those who burned their own homes must have made a vow as they left. They would return and reclaim this land. Just as their ancestors had done long ago, they would begin again amid the ruins, even with nothing left.
*Of course, it’s all a vain hope.*
Jamukha smiled faintly.
Xiang Yu had been arrogant and foolish. Despite possessing the martial might and forces to look down on all under Heaven, he had ultimately lost to Liu Bang.
Jamukha was different.
For decades, he had strengthened his hold on the western grasslands and built up his forces, waiting for that person to call him.
And at last...
*The time has come.*

Jamukha gazed into the pitch-black darkness. There, where even the moonlight was dimmed by dark clouds, he could almost see the enemy holding their spears and swords upright, struggling to master their trembling hearts.
“Can you feel it? Their fear.”
His low voice rang through the darkness. Charged with internal energy, it reached every ear clearly, and his eyes shone fiercely.
“Our enemies have spent their lives hiding behind tall walls. They’re no different from cows and pigs—softened by peace, doing nothing but eating!”
What of the grasslands?
Their people had been born of grass and earth. They had endured the cold north wind in gers, not behind walls, and ridden through snowy fields to hunt wild beasts.
To the nomads, death came cheap. Plunder and killing were taken for granted.
“They don’t know where we came from! They don’t know what great conquerors our ancestors were!”
His forceful voice pressed down upon the night air.
It was as if the sound of their ancestors’ hooves, trampling across lands covered in frost and ice and crossing the dreadful, scorching desert, were faintly echoing in everyone’s ears.

“Keep your eyes sharp as you draw your bows! Thrust your spears like a tiger’s claws! Cut through their flesh with crescent sabers like an eagle’s talons, then trample them beneath your horses’ hooves!”
A light slowly kindled in the nomads’ slack eyes.

They had marched without rest for more than half a month, through traps laid on every side. Thousands had lost horses they treasured as much as their own lives to poisoned iron caltrops. Thousands more had collapsed after drinking fouled water.
And that wasn’t all.
With the houses burned down, they’d had to sleep outdoors beneath the night dew and fill their bellies with tough jerky made while sitting in the saddle, all to keep up their speed.
It didn’t matter.
Thousands of men and horses had fallen, but tens of thousands remained. If they crushed an enemy less than half their number—if they won this battle—it would all be over.
Beyond the gorge, shrouded in darkness, more than weak enemies awaited them.
Wealth. Honor. A new age.
“My beloved brothers, remember our ancestors! Remember the grasslands in all their former glory!”
Jamukha cried out like a king of the beasts that ruled the grasslands. Like one of the great conquerors of old, who had ridden out from their gers and shaken the continent with thunderous hoofbeats.
Then he fixed his eyes on the gorge, now only a hundred or so *jang* ahead, and spoke in a low, clear voice.
“Now, it’s time to conquer.”
At that moment—
*Clang-clang-clang-clang!*
A wave of steel swallowed the darkness. Gently curved crescent sabers, sharp lances, and arrows nocked to bowstrings in a flash gleamed on every side.
“Waaaaah!”
A roar shattered the deep night and seemed to shake heaven and earth.
*Thududududu!*
Dozens became hundreds. Hundreds became thousands. At last, tens of thousands swept toward the gorge like the wind.

They cried out in strange voices that chilled anyone who heard them, their hair streaming behind them like horses’ tails with every jolt of the ride. They drove forward with all their might to avenge a tragedy stained by lies and claim the glory their ancestors had once won.
*Rrrrummmble!*
Beyond the gorge, the people waiting there felt the fierce vibration through their bodies, as if an earthquake had struck.
“So it comes to this, after all.”
Jin Wikyung murmured, then looked down at his hand. It was clenched around his sword hilt, and it had begun to tremble.
Why?
Was he afraid of the enemy bearing down on them with such overwhelming momentum?
No.
He feared the countless allies who would die here. He feared that he would not be able to protect them all.
*That’s why... we have to win.*
He had taken every measure he could. There was no undoing any of it, and no retreating now.
*Do everything within your power, then leave the rest to Heaven.*
The old saying came to him suddenly. So did someone who hated it more than anyone—someone who wasn’t here.
*No. If you’re just going to leave it to Heaven in the end, why go through all that hell? You’ve got to make Heaven change its mind, even if you have to raise all kinds of hell to do it.*
Yes, that was exactly what the guy would have said.
At the sound of that voice, so vivid in his ears, Jin Wikyung let out a quiet laugh before he knew it.
Then, the next moment, he realized his hand had stopped trembling.
“Wipeng.”
At the low call that cut through the thunder of approaching hooves, his longtime loyal retainer answered.
“Your orders, my lord.”
Tens of thousands of men and horses would be upon them in moments. Ragged breaths sounded all around.
Every eye turned to Jin Wikyung, their commander-in-chief. Then he said the last thing anyone expected.
“I think we should spend next year’s Double Ninth Festival on Mount Heng.”
“All of us together. We’ll drink chrysanthemum wine, make music, and enjoy ourselves.”
“M-my lord.”
“Why? Don’t you like the sound of it?”
Wipeng and the others stared at Wikyung’s faint smile. Then, as if by agreement, they smiled just like him, holding back the emotion rising in their chests.
*Next year’s Double Ninth Festival. All of us together.*
Those few words stirred something deep within them.
As they smiled, their fear faded. When they laughed aloud, the stiffness left their bodies. The darkness surrounding them no longer felt so ominous.
*Step.*
A footfall sounded with startling clarity. Someone stepped out in front of them and spoke.
“Next year’s Double Ninth Festival sounds rather enjoyable.”
Jin Mukyung was smiling.
Amid the vibration and shouts that had swallowed the gorge.
In the darkness that had been his only friend for the past two years.
And in the next moment—
*Thudududu—whoosh!*
He turned toward the dozens of men and horses bursting from the pitch-black darkness, as though a curtain had been drawn aside.
*Shing!*
A dazzling flash rose from his waist and cleaved through the faint moonlight.

chapters.title: Chapter 955
paragraphs: Tap.
Something cold touched me, and my eyes flew open.
My body moved on instinct, too.
*Whoosh!*
My fist cut through empty air.
As my vision snapped back into focus, the Bow Saint—watching me from the tree across from us—spoke with a calm expression.
“Looks like you had a nightmare.”
*Ah.*
Only then did I realize I’d been asleep—so deeply that I hadn’t even noticed myself drifting off.
And, just as the Bow Saint had said, everything I’d seen and experienced in it had been the worst of the worst.
“How long was I asleep?”
I asked as I tried to steady my ragged breathing. The Bow Saint dropped lightly from the branch and answered.
“Let’s see. About one *shichen*.”
“One *shichen*...”
“Sleep a little longer. At least until daybreak.”
Dawn was still dim.
Above us, the morning dew that had woken me was slowly rolling down a leaf, and now and then the only sound in the deserted mountain woods was the chirping of insects.
“Old—no, where’s Master?”
“Hunting. We’ve had nothing but jerky and water for more than seven days and nights. It’s the least he can do. And...”
The Bow Saint tossed a dry twig onto the dying campfire.
“You needn’t worry about what to call him. I’ve already guessed the general situation. You two are surprisingly sentimental for such rough-looking men.”
“How did you—”
“If you have the energy to ask about every little thing, come warm yourself by the fire.”
After a moment’s hesitation, I got up and started walking.
Not toward the campfire, but toward the still-dark woods.
“Where are you going?”
“I’ll go on ahead, slowly. When Old Master gets back, we can—”
“You really are a stubborn brat.”
The Bow Saint clicked her tongue and reached out.
*Fwish!*
Finger Qi shot toward me with a sound like tearing wind and grazed the back of my neck. Its chilling whistle drove away every trace of sleepiness.
“...What are you doing?”
“A beating is the best medicine for a disobedient child. Sit by the fire while I’m still asking nicely. Or lie down and go back to sleep.”
I’d forgotten. The woman who looked barely thirty was still a Murim martial artist, and force came more naturally to her than words.
And the Three Saints were, among other things, a top-tier corporation—no, a nationwide gang.
I glared at her in silence, then said, “I have to go.”
“Of course you do.”
“I mean right now.”
“And I mean a little later.”
“So that’s how you’re going to play it?”
“If I do, what will you do about it?”
She answered calmly, poking at the fire.
“I was like you once. I struggled with everything I had to save even one person. I risked my life to shave off a few moments.”
“Not anymore?”
“Who knows.”
There was something hollow in her answer.
She watched the fire slowly come back to life, lost in thought as though remembering long ago. Then she spoke.
“I’ve learned one small thing.”
“What’s that?”
“That my impatience was driving me further into danger.”

“I gave every moment my best, but the results still fell short. There wasn’t even time to sit back and enjoy a meal or a cup of tea. I had to kill people and watch others die. Even after I discovered the inner demon that had taken root deep in my heart, that didn’t change.”
The eyes she fixed on the campfire glowed red, like the flames of the wars she had witnessed so many times long ago.
“I don’t like the word ‘fate.’ If everything happens as it was always going to, no matter how hard we struggle, then what does our struggle mean? But...”
*Crackle. Fwoosh.*
The fire swelled as it came back to life. Beyond the drifting sparks, the Bow Saint looked at me, her gaze deep and steady.
“If something can’t be stopped even by someone who’s run without rest for seven whole days and nights... Then yes. That, surely, is fate.”
I gritted my teeth.
And I felt my body, drenched in exhaustion like a waterlogged cotton rag.
I knew she was right.
To me, *fate* was the shittiest word in the world. Even so, there were times when I had no choice but to admit it existed.
I was only human, after all. Not an all-knowing, all-powerful god.
“I had a dream. A nightmare.”
The cracked voice that came from my mouth sounded like someone else’s. My back had been damp from the moment I woke—not with morning dew, but with cold sweat.
“When I finally got there... everyone was dead. Every last one of them. Not a single exception.”
“Is that so?”
My voice trembled. The Bow Saint’s remained calm.
“You must have been terribly sad.”
I shook my head.
It wasn’t sadness. It was despair—despair that seemed to punch through the earth and plunge deep beneath it.
Even now that I was awake, I could still see them before me, all of them horribly dead.
“That’s why I have to go. Before it’s too late. As soon as possible.”
At first, I’d thought this was just a game. Nothing more than data made by bespectacled developers in black turtlenecks or plaid shirts.
But before long, I’d learned the truth. This was another world, and the people in it were individuals with feelings and wills of their own.
So I’d opened my heart to them.

To the Lesser Family Head of the Jin Family of Taiyuan, who firmly believed I was his own flesh and blood. To the young gate guard who’d picked a fight with me the moment we met, looking at me like he couldn’t stand the sight of me.
And to the deranged old man who’d wandered the world searching for the Disciple who remained his final regret and lingering attachment.
The sincerity they’d shown me had gathered in my heart until it overflowed.
Another friend and comrade. A Master and family.
When I closed my eyes, the faces and names of everyone I’d met rose out of the darkness.
That was why I had to run, even if it meant wringing every last bit of strength from this tired, impatient body.
*Just as I have for the past seven days and nights.*
I’d given it everything I had.

I’d crossed rugged mountains that even seasoned hunters avoided. Rather than waste time waiting for a boat, I’d burned through an enormous amount of internal energy to cross a river using Rising on Duckweed, Crossing Water.
That was how I’d made it here. To this place.
*Only about two days to Taiyuan now.*

I might already have overtaken the imperial messengers or the messenger eagles. I’d abandoned even the fine horse the Son of Heaven had given me, seeking the fastest route and running day and night without rest.
But those two short days were also enough time for the nightmare I’d had today to become reality.
*I can’t let that happen.*
I curled my hand into a tight fist. My nails dug into my flesh, and I felt hot blood well up.
The Bow Saint had been watching me in silence. Just then, she spoke.
“Strange.”
“What do you mean...?”
“You treasure them beyond measure, yet you don’t trust them at all.”
“Sometimes you need to trust them. They aren’t as weak as you think, or so easily uprooted.”
My whole body stiffened. For a moment I was at a loss for words, and then the Bow Saint’s voice continued in my ear.

“Of course, you can do a great deal. You could shatter a boulder weighing ten thousand *geun* with one hand, and split a river with the other. But what if it were a mountain instead of a boulder? An ocean instead of a river? Would you just quietly bear it alone, like Yu Gong long ago?”
Yu Gong. The foolish old man who had tried to bring down a vast mountain by digging out its earth and carrying away its stones.
In the end, the Jade Emperor was moved by his devotion and helped him achieve his goal. Yu Gong hadn’t done it through his own strength and effort alone.
“What if the countless people who heard Yu Gong’s story hadn’t laughed at him for being a fool, but had joined forces to help him?”
I didn’t answer, but I thought to myself:
With their help, the old man would have achieved his goal in the end. Not through the Jade Emperor, but through the people who believed in him and followed him.
Through all of them.
*Ah.*
Something stirred in a corner of my heart. I looked down at my hands, smudged with dirt here and there.
As the Bow Saint had said, I had tremendous power. I could crush a huge boulder with a single punch, or split a small river for a short while with one palm.
But even that wasn’t nearly enough to move a mountain or an ocean.
The same was true of the disaster looming over Shanxi Province. To clear away the dark clouds filling the sky, I needed everyone’s help.
“Let me ask you something.”
Her gaze was calm, yet somehow warm. She looked at me like a grandmother gently chiding her young grandson.
“Which do you believe in—Heaven or people?”
Instead of answering, I looked east, where light was slowly spreading.
Then I spoke.
“Do you happen to know what the Jade Emperor looks like?”
“What?”
“I’m a suspicious sort. I can’t really put my faith in someone I haven’t seen with my own eyes.”
The Bow Saint blinked at my unexpected answer. Then she caught my meaning and let out a quiet laugh.
“The Daoists would be horrified if they heard you.”
“That’s all right. The man behind me may not be the Jade Emperor, but he’s at least Yama.”
*Shff.*
A deliberately loud footstep.
I turned and saw Yama himself—no, Jeok Cheongang—standing there with a frown.
*Thump.*
Jeok Cheongang set down a large deer, who knew where he’d caught it, and spoke.
“You cheeky brat. I leave for a moment, and you call me Yama?”
His tone was gruff and his brow deeply furrowed. But the corner of his mouth was twitching—a sure sign he was hiding a smile.
He’d plainly heard my conversation with the Bow Saint. Pretending otherwise, he asked, “Enough. Spare me the excuses. How about some meat for a change?”
Meat, when every second mattered.
I glanced toward the thick woods to the north, then answered with a faint smile.
“Sounds good.”
I wasn’t Yu Gong. I was Jin Taekyung.
And now, I trusted them. All of them.
*Don’t die. Not a single one of you.*
I spoke the words in my heart, where none of them could hear, and sat down by the campfire.
My first proper rest in seven days and nights.
I had to save all the strength I could for the two days still ahead.

paragraphs: Eight Spring Gorge was a little over a hundred *jang* long.
A natural gateway enclosed by cliffs some thirty *jang* high.

It was barely wide enough for thirty grown men to stand shoulder to shoulder—the worst possible place to attack. Yet there was a reason two great battles for the fate of Shanxi Province had been fought in this jar-shaped gorge.
“Break through! Trample them and keep going!”
“Brothers of the Great Steppe! Once we cross this godforsaken gorge, Shanxi Province will be ours!”
Eight Spring Gorge was the most important strategic passage in Shanxi.
It offered the quickest route through the rugged northern mountains and was the last gateway to the plains of central Shanxi.

If they took this place, positioned on the border between north and central Shanxi, nothing would remain to stop tens of thousands of cavalry charging side by side, shaking the earth beneath their hooves.
And even if something did stand in their way, they could simply trample it.
Sand and gravel could not hold back a wave.
That was precisely why the defenders had to stop the invaders before them, whatever it took.
“Hold the line! Don’t give up a single step!”
“Proud people of Shanxi! Defend your homeland from these merciless barbarians!”
“Raaaaaah!”
Screams of defiance pierced the darkness and echoed through the gorge.
Amid the dense rain of arrows the two armies loosed at each other, a single streak of light moved with graceful ease, seemingly untouched by the chaos around it.
*Whoosh!*
Space split apart.
The dozen or so mounted warriors charging forward with the steppe nomads’ distinctive cries suddenly felt a wind.
Not one that merely brushed past them, but a cold wind that swept through the depths of their bodies.
Their eyes widened. Their vision wavered.
And then—
*Shhk.*
Eternal darkness. Light would never reach them again.
*Fwoosh!*
Fountains of blood surged into the air. The things that had once been people and horses were severed into pieces and flung in every direction.
They hurtled onward with all the speed of their charge—
toward the enemies they had chosen as their first targets, whom they would never reach alive.
*Crunch!*
Even the lightest man and horse had weighed hundreds of *geun* in life, and some nearly a thousand.
Jin Mukyung calmly looked down at the enormous chunks of flesh, caked in dirt and blood, that had carved deep furrows as they slid to his feet.
More precisely, he looked at their impossibly clean cut surfaces—and the sword in his grasp.
*It really is sharp. Unbelievably so.*
Admiration flickered in Jin Mukyung’s eyes as he gazed at the blade, which radiated a cold, keen aura even in the dark.
Only two days earlier, he had seen what the new sword could do in battle against a thousand enemies. Yet it still astonished him.
He was a swordsman with an appetite for fine blades, after all.
*I wondered what was going on when he suddenly handed me a sword I’d never seen before. If I’d refused it, I’d have regretted it for the rest of my life.*
To a martial artist, a cherished weapon was his closest friend and family.
But just before Jin Mukyung’s first campaign, as he was polishing his beloved sword, a sturdy old man came to see him. He dropped a long bundle of cloth in front of him and said:
“Get rid of that one. Use this from today on. I forged it for you well in advance, Second Young Master.”
At first, Mukyung had thought the old man was out of his mind.
He wanted him to discard the sword he had used for over ten years? The fine blade his older brother Jin Wikyung had practically torn a pillar out of the Jin Family of Taiyuan to pay for?
But then a sword appeared between the folds of cloth. When its pure-white blade finally emerged naked from its scabbard, Jin Mukyung understood.
The mad old man before him was an extraordinary artisan, unlike any he had ever seen.
One with more than enough skill to forge a divine weapon.
“You’ve got a good eye, judging by your face. That’s a relief. You look worthy of being its owner, at least.”
“What on earth is this...?”

“Can’t you tell? One of the finest things this old man has ever made. I worked myself to the bone on it in my old age. I forged it from something that can rival Ten-Thousand-Year Cold Iron, so take good care of it.”
The old man had left without hesitation after saying that. Jin Mukyung remained absorbed in his new sword for a long while, until one of the family retainers finally told him who the old man was.
“Come to think of it, Second Young Master might not know. The Ironcraft Hall was newly established in our family while you were in secluded training.”
“The Ironcraft Hall? Then that old man was...”
“Yes. Hall Master Jang Taebo, head of the Ironcraft Hall. Before that, he served as Guild Leader of the Ironcraft Guild for over thirty years.”
Even Jin Mukyung, who had devoted himself to martial arts both at the Jin Family of Taiyuan and at Heaven’s Gate Temple, knew of the Ironcraft Guild.
It was home to some of the finest artisans in the world.
They had the skill and pride to refuse to sell a weapon to anyone they deemed unworthy, even for a fortune in gold.
The retainer didn’t know why Jang Taebo, who had reigned as the guild’s greatest artisan for decades, was now at the Jin Family of Taiyuan. But there was one thing he knew for certain.
“I believe he formed a connection with the Third Young Master. So, around the time you entered secluded training, he reversed his retirement and joined our family.”
“Taekyung? That guy?”
“Yes. And somehow, Hall Master Jang brought a great many artisans who’d belonged to the Ironcraft Guild along with him. It was probably because of his old ties to them.”
But there was something neither the retainer who’d given him that information nor Jin Mukyung, fresh out of secluded training, knew.
The artisans who had dropped everything and rushed to the Jin Family of Taiyuan had not done it out of loyalty.

What had drawn even the old Master Artisans who had left their forges before Jang Taebo back to work was the final gift of a great spiritual creature that had once swum in a deep river more than ten thousand *li* away.
The Water God Dragon.

The imugi had never obtained a dragon pearl and so had failed to become a dragon. In the end, Dark Heaven had corrupted it. But with a young man’s help, it had found eternal rest, leaving its sacred body behind.
An ingredient for working metal so rare that even a meteorite fallen from the heavens or Ten-Thousand-Year Cold Iron might pale in comparison—something no famous artisan could resist.
And, naturally, a considerable portion had secretly made its way to the Jin Family of Taiyuan.

Its flesh and blood, steeped in spiritual power over hundreds of years, had become elixirs in their own right. Its immensely strong bones had become weapons, while its thick, sturdy tendons and muscles had become parts of armor.
Before long, parts of the Water God Dragon had found their way throughout the Jin Family of Taiyuan.
Just as they were at this very moment.
*Whoosh!*
No matter how fine the net, it could not catch every minnow.

With their path blocked by Jin Mukyung alone, the steppe nomads had faltered at the sight of their comrades’ gruesome deaths. The arrows they loosed to keep the Jin forces at bay slipped between the government troops’ shields and struck a martial artist of the Jin Family of Taiyuan in the chest.
Or so it seemed for a moment.
*Thunk!*
Despite its powerful whistle through the air, the arrow bounced away feebly.
The martial artist, certain he had been dealt a mortal wound and about to scream, stared wide-eyed.
“Guh—huh?”
He blinked in confusion. Then he remembered the thin layer the Lesser Family Head had strictly ordered him to place over his chest beneath his martial uniform.
It was so light, with such a strange sheen, that he could not tell whether it was iron or leather.
The moment he remembered, he burst out laughing as though nothing had happened.
“You stupid barbarian bastards! Shooting like that, you couldn’t hit our family dog!”
The nomads, who had been ready to trample the weak Han Chinese, could only look at one another in dismay.
Their bows could pierce most leather armor with ease. Now they were useless.
It was only natural for unease to spread at the thought that one of the grasslands’ greatest weapons had been taken away from them.
But they soon learned that even a moment spent worrying was a luxury they could not afford.
“Now! Now’s the time!”
“Loose!”
The nomads, who by then filled the gorge, heard a forceful shout from high above—from the steep cliffs rising on either side.
Another layer of darkness fell over their heads.
*Shhhhhhh.*
A chill sound like the rush of waves filled the air. Countless arrows blotted out even the faint moonlight as they plunged down across the entire gorge.
“E-everyone, shields—!”
The cry, almost a scream, was swallowed before it could finish.
*Clang-clang-clang!*
Sparks sprang from arrowheads striking the rock walls.
In the slowed world, through that brief, hazy light born of friction, they could see countless men and horses collapsing, spattering blood.
*Whoosh—thud-thud-thud!*
By the time they heard the arrows tearing through the air, it was too late.
The steel rain drove straight down from thirty *jang* above with more force than the nomads’ composite bows could muster. It drenched the gorge in dark red blood and cries of pain.
“Raaaaagh!”
“Neigh!”
A vast tangle of screams filled the gorge, impossible to tell apart.

A nomad who had instinctively looked up rolled on the ground, clutching the arrow lodged in his eye. A steppe horse thrashed with all its might, heedless of its rider. And a lucky hundred-man commander who had saved himself with a tough leather shield breathed a sigh of relief.
Before he could finish that breath, he heard an ominous sound overhead.
*Rumble. Rrrrattle.*
*Thunder?*
No. He was wrong.
He soon saw the answer for himself.
“Ah.”
A hollow sigh escaped him.
*Thump.*
The shield, now bristling like a porcupine, slipped from the middle-aged commander’s weakened grasp. He paid it no mind.
He already knew that the shield that had saved his life could not stop the enormous things bearing down on him through the darkness.
*Rrrrrumble!*
Black spheres poured down the rock face out of the darkness, shaking the earth as they came.
The steel rain had scarcely stopped when the avalanche of rocks arrived. The hundred-man commander looked up at a sky where even moonlight could not reach him.
“...Tengri.”
*Ka-boom!*
No answer came.
His sky closed over him.
“Isn’t this dangerous?”
Chinggen scratched his chin as he asked. Jamukha answered without changing expression.
“How many did you send in?”
“Five or six hundred-man companies?”
Chinggen smacked his lips and added:
“Though they’re gone now.”
A mere half an hour.
That was all it had taken for more than five hundred troops to vanish.
And they hadn’t even had a proper chance to begin fighting.
Their enemies were proving more capable than expected.
“That man’s quite something.”
Jamukha knew whom Chinggen meant. He nodded quietly.
“He has the makings of a Sword Demon. Like you.”
“He must be the one who wiped out the vanguard, too.”
“So, you want him?”
“If I asked, would you give him to me?”
Chinggen’s eyes gleamed red.
