sentences.text: Eight Spring Gorge was a little over a hundred *jang* long.
A natural gateway enclosed by cliffs some thirty *jang* high.
It was barely wide enough for thirty grown men to stand shoulder to shoulder—the worst possible place to attack.
Yet there was a reason two great battles for the fate of Shanxi Province had been fought in this jar-shaped gorge.
“Break through!
Trample them and keep going!”
“Brothers of the Great Steppe!
Once we cross this godforsaken gorge, Shanxi Province will be ours!”
Eight Spring Gorge was the most important strategic passage in Shanxi.
It offered the quickest route through the rugged northern mountains and was the last gateway to the plains of central Shanxi.

If they took this place, positioned on the border between north and central Shanxi, nothing would remain to stop tens of thousands of cavalry charging side by side, shaking the earth beneath their hooves.
And even if something did stand in their way, they could simply trample it.
Sand and gravel could not hold back a wave.
That was precisely why the defenders had to stop the invaders before them, whatever it took.
“Hold the line!
Don’t give up a single step!”
“Proud people of Shanxi!
Defend your homeland from these merciless barbarians!”
“Raaaaaah!”
Screams of defiance pierced the darkness and echoed through the gorge.
Amid the dense rain of arrows the two armies loosed at each other, a single streak of light moved with graceful ease, seemingly untouched by the chaos around it.
*Whoosh!*
Space split apart.
The dozen or so mounted warriors charging forward with the steppe nomads’ distinctive cries suddenly felt a wind.
Not one that merely brushed past them, but a cold wind that swept through the depths of their bodies.
Their eyes widened.
Their vision wavered.
And then—
*Shhk.*
Eternal darkness.
Light would never reach them again.
*Fwoosh!*
Fountains of blood surged into the air.
The things that had once been people and horses were severed into pieces and flung in every direction.
They hurtled onward with all the speed of their charge—
toward the enemies they had chosen as their first targets, whom they would never reach alive.
*Crunch!*
Even the lightest man and horse had weighed hundreds of *geun* in life, and some nearly a thousand.
Jin Mukyung calmly looked down at the enormous chunks of flesh, caked in dirt and blood, that had carved deep furrows as they slid to his feet.
More precisely, he looked at their impossibly clean cut surfaces—and the sword in his grasp.
*It really is sharp.
Unbelievably so.*
Admiration flickered in Jin Mukyung’s eyes as he gazed at the blade, which radiated a cold, keen aura even in the dark.
Only two days earlier, he had seen what the new sword could do in battle against a thousand enemies.
Yet it still astonished him.
He was a swordsman with an appetite for fine blades, after all.
*I wondered what was going on when he suddenly handed me a sword I’d never seen before.
If I’d refused it, I’d have regretted it for the rest of my life.*
To a martial artist, a cherished weapon was his closest friend and family.
But just before Jin Mukyung’s first campaign, as he was polishing his beloved sword, a sturdy old man came to see him.
He dropped a long bundle of cloth in front of him and said:
“Get rid of that one.
Use this from today on.
I forged it for you well in advance, Second Young Master.”
At first, Mukyung had thought the old man was out of his mind.
He wanted him to discard the sword he had used for over ten years?
The fine blade his older brother Jin Wikyung had practically torn a pillar out of the Jin Family of Taiyuan to pay for?
But then a sword appeared between the folds of cloth.
When its pure-white blade finally emerged naked from its scabbard, Jin Mukyung understood.
The mad old man before him was an extraordinary artisan, unlike any he had ever seen.
One with more than enough skill to forge a divine weapon.
“You’ve got a good eye, judging by your face.
That’s a relief.
You look worthy of being its owner, at least.”
“What on earth is this...?”
“Can’t you tell?
One of the finest things this old man has ever made.
I worked myself to the bone on it in my old age.
I forged it from something that can rival Ten-Thousand-Year Cold Iron, so take good care of it.”
The old man had left without hesitation after saying that.
Jin Mukyung remained absorbed in his new sword for a long while, until one of the family retainers finally told him who the old man was.
“Come to think of it, Second Young Master might not know.
The Ironcraft Hall was newly established in our family while you were in secluded training.”
“The Ironcraft Hall?
Then that old man was...”
“Yes.
Hall Master Jang Taebo, head of the Ironcraft Hall.
Before that, he served as Guild Leader of the Ironcraft Guild for over thirty years.”
Even Jin Mukyung, who had devoted himself to martial arts both at the Jin Family of Taiyuan and at Heaven’s Gate Temple, knew of the Ironcraft Guild.
It was home to some of the finest artisans in the world.
They had the skill and pride to refuse to sell a weapon to anyone they deemed unworthy, even for a fortune in gold.
The retainer didn’t know why Jang Taebo, who had reigned as the guild’s greatest artisan for decades, was now at the Jin Family of Taiyuan.
But there was one thing he knew for certain.
“I believe he formed a connection with the Third Young Master.
So, around the time you entered secluded training, he reversed his retirement and joined our family.”
“Taekyung?
That guy?”
“Yes.
And somehow, Hall Master Jang brought a great many artisans who’d belonged to the Ironcraft Guild along with him.
It was probably because of his old ties to them.”
But there was something neither the retainer who’d given him that information nor Jin Mukyung, fresh out of secluded training, knew.
The artisans who had dropped everything and rushed to the Jin Family of Taiyuan had not done it out of loyalty.

What had drawn even the old Master Artisans who had left their forges before Jang Taebo back to work was the final gift of a great spiritual creature that had once swum in a deep river more than ten thousand *li* away.
The Water God Dragon.
The imugi had never obtained a dragon pearl and so had failed to become a dragon.
In the end, Dark Heaven had corrupted it.
But with a young man’s help, it had found eternal rest, leaving its sacred body behind.
An ingredient for working metal so rare that even a meteorite fallen from the heavens or Ten-Thousand-Year Cold Iron might pale in comparison—something no famous artisan could resist.
And, naturally, a considerable portion had secretly made its way to the Jin Family of Taiyuan.
Its flesh and blood, steeped in spiritual power over hundreds of years, had become elixirs in their own right.
Its immensely strong bones had become weapons, while its thick, sturdy tendons and muscles had become parts of armor.
Before long, parts of the Water God Dragon had found their way throughout the Jin Family of Taiyuan.
Just as they were at this very moment.
*Whoosh!*
No matter how fine the net, it could not catch every minnow.
With their path blocked by Jin Mukyung alone, the steppe nomads had faltered at the sight of their comrades’ gruesome deaths.
The arrows they loosed to keep the Jin forces at bay slipped between the government troops’ shields and struck a martial artist of the Jin Family of Taiyuan in the chest.
Or so it seemed for a moment.
*Thunk!*
Despite its powerful whistle through the air, the arrow bounced away feebly.
The martial artist, certain he had been dealt a mortal wound and about to scream, stared wide-eyed.
“Guh—huh?”
He blinked in confusion.
Then he remembered the thin layer the Lesser Family Head had strictly ordered him to place over his chest beneath his martial uniform.
It was so light, with such a strange sheen, that he could not tell whether it was iron or leather.
The moment he remembered, he burst out laughing as though nothing had happened.
“You stupid barbarian bastards!
Shooting like that, you couldn’t hit our family dog!”
The nomads, who had been ready to trample the weak Han Chinese, could only look at one another in dismay.
Their bows could pierce most leather armor with ease.
Now they were useless.
It was only natural for unease to spread at the thought that one of the grasslands’ greatest weapons had been taken away from them.
But they soon learned that even a moment spent worrying was a luxury they could not afford.
“Now!
Now’s the time!”
“Loose!”
The nomads, who by then filled the gorge, heard a forceful shout from high above—from the steep cliffs rising on either side.
Another layer of darkness fell over their heads.
*Shhhhhhh.*
A chill sound like the rush of waves filled the air.
Countless arrows blotted out even the faint moonlight as they plunged down across the entire gorge.
“E-everyone, shields—!”
The cry, almost a scream, was swallowed before it could finish.
*Clang-clang-clang!*
Sparks sprang from arrowheads striking the rock walls.
In the slowed world, through that brief, hazy light born of friction, they could see countless men and horses collapsing, spattering blood.
*Whoosh—thud-thud-thud!*
By the time they heard the arrows tearing through the air, it was too late.
The steel rain drove straight down from thirty *jang* above with more force than the nomads’ composite bows could muster.
It drenched the gorge in dark red blood and cries of pain.
“Raaaaagh!”
“Neigh!”
A vast tangle of screams filled the gorge, impossible to tell apart.
A nomad who had instinctively looked up rolled on the ground, clutching the arrow lodged in his eye.
A steppe horse thrashed with all its might, heedless of its rider.
And a lucky hundred-man commander who had saved himself with a tough leather shield breathed a sigh of relief.
Before he could finish that breath, he heard an ominous sound overhead.
*Rumble.
Rrrrattle.*
*Thunder?*
No.
He was wrong.
He soon saw the answer for himself.
“Ah.”
A hollow sigh escaped him.
*Thump.*
The shield, now bristling like a porcupine, slipped from the middle-aged commander’s weakened grasp.
He paid it no mind.
He already knew that the shield that had saved his life could not stop the enormous things bearing down on him through the darkness.
*Rrrrrumble!*
Black spheres poured down the rock face out of the darkness, shaking the earth as they came.
The steel rain had scarcely stopped when the avalanche of rocks arrived.
The hundred-man commander looked up at a sky where even moonlight could not reach him.
“...Tengri.”
*Ka-boom!*
No answer came.
His sky closed over him.
“Isn’t this dangerous?”
Chinggen scratched his chin as he asked.
Jamukha answered without changing expression.
“How many did you send in?”
“Five or six hundred-man companies?”
Chinggen smacked his lips and added:
“Though they’re gone now.”
A mere half an hour.
That was all it had taken for more than five hundred troops to vanish.
And they hadn’t even had a proper chance to begin fighting.
Their enemies were proving more capable than expected.
“That man’s quite something.”
Jamukha knew whom Chinggen meant.
He nodded quietly.
“He has the makings of a Sword Demon.
Like you.”
“He must be the one who wiped out the vanguard, too.”
“So, you want him?”
“If I asked, would you give him to me?”
Chinggen’s eyes gleamed red.
How many years had he spent in a ger reeking of horse manure?
Now, catching the scent of prey for the first time in ages, he could feel his blood boil.
Jamukha clicked his tongue softly.
“Still young, I see.
At your age, and you still haven’t broken that habit.”

“I’ll give it to you now.
No.”
“What a shame.”

There’s prey elsewhere.”
“You mean...”
“Take the cliffs.
They’re being a nuisance, so we should deal with them before any more time passes.”
“An excellent choice.”
Chinggen beamed.
Then he set off toward the prey waiting for him atop the high cliffs.

chapters.title: Chapter 957
paragraphs: The cliffs flanking Eight Spring Gorge were enormous walls in their own right.
How could they not be?
They stood more than thirty *jang* high.
Even the Great Wall, built long ago by a tyrant who unified the continent by squeezing the lifeblood out of his people, was barely three *jang* tall.
To go around the cliffs and reach this place, an army would have to spend days crossing rugged mountain ridges. To break through head-on, they would have to climb the rock face towering above them.
Of course, that wasn’t impossible.

It was generally accepted that even an experienced Mountain Herb Gatherer or hunter could climb the cliffs given enough preparation and time. The uneven rock offered plenty of handholds and footholds.
But that was a different story if the thousand archers stationed atop the cliffs on either side of the gorge had no intention of welcoming visitors.
As they did now.
“AAAAAAAH!”
The nomads surged toward the cliffs like a swarm of ants, their cries somewhere between screams and battle shouts.
At that very moment, the officers, their sharp eyes fixed on the scene in the darkness below, spoke as one.
“Everyone!”
“Loose!”
*Flap!*
A red flag, its color barely discernible in the dark, dropped like lightning. At once, a thousand taut bowstrings were set free.
*Thrum-thrum-thrum! Fwoooooosh!*
The sound of waves echoed through the deep mountains.
Arrows quivered as they cut through the faint moonlight, as if they knew what awaited them at the end of their brief journey.
*Clang! Thud-thud-thud!*
“Gaaah!”
“No! Holrogu!”
Bodies tumbled in every direction amid the screams.
But the man watching the gruesome scene from high atop the cliff looked grim.
*Even with every archer firing in a concentrated volley, we only got a hundred.*
A faint, clear light shone in his eyes—a sign that he had mastered high-level martial arts and could see through the darkness below.
*Their losses are smaller than expected. Even if they abandoned their horses beforehand and came prepared with shields, this is...*
There was only one answer.
After a moment’s thought, the man raised his baton. His adjutant, waiting with a tense expression, tied his superior’s order to an arrow and shot it toward the opposite cliff.
*Fwish.*
The arrow traced a smooth arc, but it was still an arrow. Yet as it came whistling in, someone caught it as easily as if it had flown straight into his hand.
*Tap.*
The old man caught the arrow without looking, untied the missive fastened to its shaft, and handed it to an officer nearby. The armored officer quickly scanned its contents.
“Well? What does it say?”
“He says that, judging by how sharply their casualties have fallen, the enemy must have sent in their elite troops.”
“That’s a headache, but... it might actually work in our favor.”
The old man stroked his snow-white beard.

These towering cliffs were the perfect defensive position. They were one of the main reasons Eight Spring Gorge had become a natural fortress—and why the defenders had won decisive victories in both great battles fought here.
The enemy elites sent to scale them were about to see a hellscape.
“And what else?”
“He asks our left wing to deal with the men climbing the cliffs. The right wing will keep the enemy trying to break through the gorge in check.”
“Asked? By age, I may be the presiding chair, but on a battlefield like this, I follow the general’s orders. Don’t I?”
The officer answered with an uncertain smile.
As far as he knew, the old man before him was an astonishing master with a great reputation in Murim, while the man on the opposite cliff was his superior by far.
As a mid-ranking officer caught between them, he had no ready answer.
All he could do was follow orders and offer a cautious suggestion.
“The Assistant Military Commissioner did ask...”
“Enough, enough. It means this old man has to step in, doesn’t it?”
The old man waved a hand, patted his lower back, and stood. Something dark and dull was already in his hand.
*Thump.*
At nearly a *jang* long, it was far too long to be a cane. And the sound it made against the rock was too heavy for wood.
*What in the world is that?*
Leaving the officer’s unspoken question behind, the old man walked in front of the archers, who were firing without pause, and plopped himself down.
He recalled his conversation with Jin Wikyung before the battle.
“Senior, I’ll need you to take charge of the cliffs.”
“I owe you a debt, so of course I’ll do as you ask... but this doesn’t sound like you. Wouldn’t I be far more useful down below?”
The old man’s objection was reasonable enough.

Of the fifteen thousand troops, a thousand carefully selected archers held the cliffs and rained arrows down from above. How many enemies could possibly make it up alive? What need was there for a powerful master?
But Jin Wikyung had answered without hesitation.
“You’re right. They’ll think the same thing.”
“They’ll climb the cliffs. They’ll have to.”
“You’re already certain of it.”
“Our allies on the ground will fight to the death with everything they have. It’s only a matter of time before the enemy targets the cliffs, and their very best troops will be among those they send.”
“And you want this old man to stop them?”
“If we can stop them from scaling the cliffs, we can deal them a major blow. If we hold that position to the end, we can level the scales, even though they’re tipped so heavily against us.”
Only then had the old man remembered something.
He had known the Lesser Family Head of the Jin Family of Taiyuan for less than a year, but in all that time, Jin Wikyung had always made the wise choice.
“Fine. I’ll land you a big fish in this battle, just as you want.”
“Don’t push yourself too hard. I know you’ve recovered completely, Senior, but you still need time to recuperate...”
“Don’t worry. I already owe the Jin Family of Taiyuan my life twice. This time, I’ll repay that debt in full.”
People of Murim did not forget gratitude and grudges.
The older they were, and the more Fame they had earned, the truer that became.
The old man was both old and renowned.
He had spent his entire life in his hometown, never joining a sect. Even after reaching the lofty realm of Supreme Peak, he had stayed there.
He’d meant to lay his bones in the place where he was born and raised.
Until the day he met a woman of extraordinary beauty and, soon afterward, lost his mind.
“At last... the time has come to repay my debt.”
The old man murmured in a low voice.
The Jin Family of Taiyuan was not the only one to whom he owed a debt. They had restored the mind that had been taken from him against his will and spent months treating his grievous injuries.
There was Dark Heaven, too.
He owed them a debt of vengeance, too.
No—he had to take revenge.
“Come on, then.”
The small-framed old man smiled faintly and gripped his beloved weapon. With a motion he had repeated countless times since childhood, he swung both arms with force.
*Whoom.*
His weapon—an impressive three *jang* long—whipped and bent as it scattered a dark, dull flash.
A silver-white line and hook extended from its tip, shooting toward the enemies climbing the cliff to escape the rain of arrows.
*Shwaaaaa! Shhk!*
White streaks tore through everything in their path.
Flesh and bone split like tofu. Dozens of severed limbs, armor and all, slid down the cliff.
Overwhelming power.
With both his martial prowess and the terrain in his favor, it seemed no enemy could evade the old man’s attack.
No—or so it seemed.
Then a red flash flickered through the dense silver net spread across the cliff.
*Shhk. Shhk!*
The whistle it made was fainter than the wind.
But the old man felt it clearly. The blow had severed part of the silver line that writhed like a living thing as it tore enemies apart.
And the power behind that red flash was in no way beneath his own.
*Force...!*
There was no doubt about it. Only power of the same kind could sever Heavenly Silkworm Thread imbued with Force in a single swing.
“How dare you!”
*Shwick!*
The old man roared, and his hand blurred.
His beloved weapon, imbued with strength and speed, thrashed like an imugi. The archers, sensing something was wrong, gritted their teeth and drew their bows.
“Concentrate your fire!”
“That one! The man in front is their leader! Fire together!”
*Thrum! Sh-sh-sh-shhk!*
*Thud-thud-thud!*
“Gah... urk!”
“Aaaah!”
Arrows whistled and men screamed without pause.
But nothing could stop the figure that had slipped through the mighty web of arrows covering the cliff.
*Clang!*
He batted away the old man’s next attack.
*Whoosh!*
He twisted his body, dodging dozens of arrows aimed at him from every direction as if performing an acrobatic feat.
*Tap.*
He stepped onto the steep cliff.
No—he blasted off it.
*Ka-boom! Fwoooooosh!*
He was running and flying at once.
Even a master of the Wall Lizard Technique could not have matched his speed. He charged onward in defiance of the laws that had governed the world since time immemorial.
And finally—
*Tap.*
The figure reached the edge of the distant cliff and faced the old man waiting for him.
Or, more precisely, with the silver flash whipping around at the old man’s fingertips.
*Whoom. Shwaaaaa!*
Space split apart.
Amid wind cut into dozens, then hundreds of pieces and the brilliant white glow of Force, the old man saw the figure’s face.
A gaunt build. Sharp eyes.
The man was unmistakably a nomad—and at that moment, he was smiling.
*Crack!*
A section of the cliff crumbled under the tremendous force.
But there was no sign that anyone had died.
As the archers on the cliff wavered, the old man clicked his tongue and suddenly spoke to the man standing upright on empty air.
“Who are you?”
The man answered.
“A hunter.”
“Then you’ve come to the wrong place.”
“That’s what I thought at first, too. But I changed my mind.”
The man—Chinggen—looked at the old man and licked his lips.
“You’re a little old, but you look pretty appetizing. Don’t you think?”
The old man snorted.
“Third Rate hunter. You don’t even know that the older you get, the tougher you are.”
“That’s fine. I’ve got strong teeth.”
Chinggen bared his teeth in a grin, then asked,
“So who are you?”
“A fisherman.”
The old man answered calmly, then added,
“I thought there were only minnows here. Catching an unexpected whopper has put me in a fine mood.”
“That fish looks too big for an old man like you to catch.”
“What can a brat like you do, no matter how hard you flop around? I’ll grab you by the tail and slam you down a couple of times. That’ll be the end of it.”
“Oh, yeah?”
The hunter smiled at the fisherman. At that moment, the sobriquet of someone who resembled the old fisherman before him circled in his mind.
A previous-generation master who had reached great heights, yet never left the riverbank—and wielded a strange weapon.
“We’ll soon see who succeeds in the hunt. Won’t we, Dongting Fisherman?”
The old man, Dongting Fisherman, raised his beloved black-wood fishing rod and answered,
“Indeed. What a catch.”
*Shwaaa!*
Two currents of wind collided head-on.

“At last... the time has come to repay my debt.”
The old man murmured in a low voice.
The Jin Family of Taiyuan was not the only one to whom he owed a debt.
They had restored the mind that had been taken from him against his will and spent months treating his grievous injuries.
There was Dark Heaven, too.
He owed them a debt of vengeance, too.
No—he had to take revenge.
“Come on, then.”
The small-framed old man smiled faintly and gripped his beloved weapon.
With a motion he had repeated countless times since childhood, he swung both arms with force.
*Whoom.*
His weapon—an impressive three *jang* long—whipped and bent as it scattered a dark, dull flash.
A silver-white line and hook extended from its tip, shooting toward the enemies climbing the cliff to escape the rain of arrows.
*Shwaaaaa!
Shhk!*
White streaks tore through everything in their path.
Flesh and bone split like tofu.
Dozens of severed limbs, armor and all, slid down the cliff.
Overwhelming power.
With both his martial prowess and the terrain in his favor, it seemed no enemy could evade the old man’s attack.
No—or so it seemed.
Then a red flash flickered through the dense silver net spread across the cliff.
*Shhk.
Shhk!*
The whistle it made was fainter than the wind.
But the old man felt it clearly.
The blow had severed part of the silver line that writhed like a living thing as it tore enemies apart.
And the power behind that red flash was in no way beneath his own.
*Force...!*
There was no doubt about it.
Only power of the same kind could sever Heavenly Silkworm Thread imbued with Force in a single swing.
“How dare you!”
*Shwick!*
The old man roared, and his hand blurred.
His beloved weapon, imbued with strength and speed, thrashed like an imugi.
The archers, sensing something was wrong, gritted their teeth and drew their bows.
“Concentrate your fire!”
“That one!
The man in front is their leader!
Fire together!”
*Thrum!
Sh-sh-sh-shhk!*
*Thud-thud-thud!*
“Gah... urk!”
“Aaaah!”
Arrows whistled and men screamed without pause.
But nothing could stop the figure that had slipped through the mighty web of arrows covering the cliff.
*Clang!*
He batted away the old man’s next attack.
*Whoosh!*
He twisted his body, dodging dozens of arrows aimed at him from every direction as if performing an acrobatic feat.
*Tap.*
He stepped onto the steep cliff.
No—he blasted off it.
*Ka-boom!
Fwoooooosh!*
He was running and flying at once.
Even a master of the Wall Lizard Technique could not have matched his speed.
He charged onward in defiance of the laws that had governed the world since time immemorial.
And finally—
*Tap.*
The figure reached the edge of the distant cliff and faced the old man waiting for him.
Or, more precisely, with the silver flash whipping around at the old man’s fingertips.
*Whoom.
Shwaaaaa!*
Space split apart.
Amid wind cut into dozens, then hundreds of pieces and the brilliant white glow of Force, the old man saw the figure’s face.
A gaunt build.
Sharp eyes.
The man was unmistakably a nomad—and at that moment, he was smiling.
*Crack!*
A section of the cliff crumbled under the tremendous force.
But there was no sign that anyone had died.
As the archers on the cliff wavered, the old man clicked his tongue and suddenly spoke to the man standing upright on empty air.
“Who are you?”
The man answered.
“A hunter.”
“Then you’ve come to the wrong place.”
“That’s what I thought at first, too.
But I changed my mind.”
The man—Chinggen—looked at the old man and licked his lips.
“You’re a little old, but you look pretty appetizing.
Don’t you think?”
The old man snorted.
“Third Rate hunter.
You don’t even know that the older you get, the tougher you are.”
“That’s fine.
I’ve got strong teeth.”
Chinggen bared his teeth in a grin, then asked,
“So who are you?”
“A fisherman.”
The old man answered calmly, then added,
“I thought there were only minnows here.
Catching an unexpected whopper has put me in a fine mood.”
“That fish looks too big for an old man like you to catch.”
“What can a brat like you do, no matter how hard you flop around?
I’ll grab you by the tail and slam you down a couple of times.
That’ll be the end of it.”
“Oh, yeah?”
The hunter smiled at the fisherman.
At that moment, the sobriquet of someone who resembled the old fisherman before him circled in his mind.
A previous-generation master who had reached great heights, yet never left the riverbank—and wielded a strange weapon.
“We’ll soon see who succeeds in the hunt.
Won’t we, Dongting Fisherman?”
The old man, Dongting Fisherman, raised his beloved black-wood fishing rod and answered,
“Indeed.
What a catch.”
*Shwaaa!*
Two currents of wind collided head-on.

chapters.title: Chapter 958
paragraphs: *Ka-boom!*
A faint tremor followed the explosion.
Jamukha stroked his beard as he watched a pale cloud of dust rise from the distant cliff, visible even in the darkness.
*Looks like they’ve started.*
Jamukha knew Chinggen—or, more precisely, the person wearing Chinggen’s face—well.
Cruel, savage, and strong.
No matter who he encountered up there, he would carry out his assigned task. And he would do it exceedingly well.
*Clang! Krrrunch!*
Flashes flickered without pause through the dust cloud, followed by more deafening crashes.
Below, the nomads had shed their armor and taken up hooks and daggers. As the archers’ fire slackened, they seized the opportunity and rapidly climbed the cliffs.
“Loose!”
*Fwish-fwish-fwish!*
Arrows continued to fly, accompanied by occasional shouts, but that was all.
The archers’ composure and accuracy had faltered. So had the dense crossfire pouring down from either side. None of it compared to what it had been moments before.
Of the thousand archers holding the two cliffs facing each other, half were already tied up by Chinggen. The other half had to keep the ground forces in check as they surged into the gorge once more.
A loosened net would eventually tear.
Jamukha intended to bring that moment a little closer.
“Mukal. Jerme.”
“Yes.”
“Give your orders, Khan.”
At Jamukha’s quiet summons, two men stepped forward.
Their clothing alone set them apart from the other nomads. Among the Keshik Jamukha had personally trained over many years, they were two of the most capable.
Following the example of the great conqueror who had once crossed the steppe and ruled the continent, Jamukha called them the Five Steeds and Five Hounds.
Five fine steeds and five loyal hounds.
The ten commanders of a hundred were outstanding leaders and fearsome warriors alike. For decades, they had served Jamukha faithfully.
Though only days ago, he had lost one of them in vain.
“There are cowards hiding up there, doing nothing but shooting arrows. What should we do?”
“We’ll break their bows, cut their throats, and return.”
“It’s close to the heavens. Tengri will be watching over us.”
The two commanders struck their studded armor with clenched fists, then turned away.
Jamukha watched them lead a hundred Keshik apiece up the cliffs, deflecting arrows as they climbed. Then he spoke again.
“Tiraun. Boorchu. Ongge.”
Three this time.
Jamukha pointed toward the gorge, where screams rang out without end.
“Your sworn brother’s killer is there.”
The corners of the three men’s eyes twitched.
It wasn’t simply that they remembered their sworn brother, who had left days ago at the head of the vanguard with a hundred Keshik under his command, only for his head to return without him.
It was their pride.
Their lord was telling them to join forces and avenge the sworn brother who had died before them.
“Khan. I’m more than enough for him on my own.”
“The same goes for me, Tiraun!”
“Please send me, Ongge!”
Jamukha watched the three commanders vie to step forward.
Their bulging temples and sharp, shining eyes showed that these masters had reached the far edge of the Peak realm.
But Jamukha was both their lord and their teacher. He knew them better than anyone.
A few days ago, his subordinate’s severed head had returned instead of news of victory. Jamukha had seen the wound on its neck, leaving him no choice but to make this decision.
*He’s no pushover.*
Send one man, and he would never return. Send two, and only one would make it back. Send three, and they would surely return with the man’s head.
That was why their eagerness to fight could not sway him.
“Go.”
His voice was calm, but its chill was unmistakable.
This was an order. They could not refuse it.
Realizing there was no way to defy Jamukha, the three commanders bit their lips and turned away.
Then, like their comrades who had set off for the cliffs ahead of them, they led their Keshik forward at a run.
Hundreds of figures shot across the gorge, leaving their horses behind and vaulting over rocks and the bodies of fallen men and mounts.
Their first victims were not the Shanxi defenders, who continued to resist fiercely, but their own allies, backing away in fear.
“T-this isn’t right! This isn’t right!”
“Black Sheep Clan, withdraw at once! Fall back and regroup—!”
*Shhk!*
The old chieftain’s head flew into the air.
Several hundred members of his small tribe had joined the battle at the Great Steppe’s call to arms. Now, reduced to half their original number, the survivors stared wide-eyed.
“C-Chieftain!”
“How dare you!”
But dozens of spears and swords were already closing in from every direction.
*Fwoooosh! Thunk!*
“Guh—!”
With every flash of a blade, heads and limbs rolled across the ground.
The Keshik slaughtered a hundred or so tribespeople in moments with their lances and scimitars. The entire gorge froze at the sight.
So did someone watching from far away.
“W-what are you doing?!”
Temur’s voice shook as if the ground beneath him were quaking.
But the voice and gaze that answered him were drier than the steppe’s bitter wind.
“They disobeyed the Khan’s orders and ordered a retreat on their own. We simply carried out the summary execution.”
“B-but they’re under my command—”
“That’s right. They’re under your command, Khan Temur.”
Jamukha’s next words were too quiet for anyone else to hear.
“And you, the man who commands them, are standing right beside me.”
“Is there a problem? If you have any complaints, speak now.”
Under a pressure that seemed to grip his heart, Temur suddenly understood.
This was the limit the man before him had set for him.
Cross it even slightly, and he would not escape death either.
“N-no problem.”
“I can’t hear you very well. I must be getting old.”
“N-no problem.”
Only when Temur had forced out those words through his fear and humiliation did Jamukha nod.
“A wise choice. Military discipline must always be strict. Don’t you agree?”
Temur trembled instead of answering.
He had foreseen this when he begged for his life in front of Chinggen’s corpse, but he had tried to look away. Now that terrible future was unfolding before his eyes.
*Clang-clang-clang!*
*Raaaagh!*
From the cliffs. From the gorge.
Most of the ceaseless clashes of weapons and screams belonged to the tribespeople who had followed him into battle.

Yet as they died, those who had pledged loyalty and vengeance on the strength of a fabricated lie would never know that the two young Great Chieftains who had brought them a brief peace and prosperity had already betrayed them.
*No. I’m the only traitor. I’m the one who led them to their deaths.*
Temur clenched his teeth until they drew blood.
Chinggen had died with his courage intact. Temur had survived in shame.
He had fallen for the promise that if he cooperated fully, they would spare his life and let him keep his position as Khan.
No—that was just an excuse.
He had simply...
*Wanted to survive. No matter what it took.*
Yes. That was the only truth.
And this was the result.
Sending twenty thousand tribespeople who followed him and Chinggen ahead as arrow fodder, as human shields, to get through that dreadful gorge.
“Damn it.”
Jamukha’s brow furrowed at the mutter that slipped through Temur’s clenched teeth. Just then—
“Khan!”
A figure approached at a run, calling out urgently.
Jamukha recognized him as one of the Keshik who had headed into the gorge with the three commanders moments earlier. His gaze darkened.
More precisely, it darkened at the weapons in the man’s hands.
“These are...”
A lance, a scimitar, and a bow.
Even at a glance, the three weapons gave off a cutting edge far beyond that of anything the other nomads carried. They were familiar to Jamukha.
They had been specially made as gifts for the ten commanders of a hundred who had excelled above all others among the Keshik, his personal guard.
He didn’t need to ask what fate had befallen their owners.
“Did those boys go peacefully?”
The Keshik set down the weapons, now keepsakes, and bowed his head.
“They fought bravely as warriors. Surely they’ll be welcomed into Tengri’s embrace.”
“Yes. I see.”
Jamukha murmured softly.
Kill someone, and be killed by someone.
That was the inescapable fate of a warrior of the Great Steppe. The same fate awaited everyone else.
“What of the other losses?”
Everyone present understood what he meant.
Even now, dozens of nomads were bleeding and falling somewhere in the gorge, but their lives counted for nothing in his calculations.
Jamukha cared only about the losses among his personal guard.
“Though three commanders of a hundred have fallen, our overall casualties are small. Only around twenty are dead or wounded. The rest have withdrawn to the rear and await new orders.”
Three commanders had died, but their troops had suffered few losses. That could mean only one thing.
Remembering the commanders’ confidence that each of them was enough on his own, Jamukha let out a quiet laugh.
“They disobeyed my order.”
There was no doubt those three had fought a life-and-death duel.
One at a time.
Foolish as commanders, brave as warriors.
And one by one, they must have lost their lives to the young Sword Demon of the Jin Family of Taiyuan.
“Those pathetic fools.”
Jamukha silently looked down at the Keshik, who could only bow his head even lower rather than agree. Then, abruptly, he spoke.
“Order the Keshik still in the gorge to charge.”
“Khan. You mean—”
“The senior ten-man commanders will temporarily take the vacant posts of commanders of a hundred. Minimize our losses as much as possible and wear them down.”
There would be no more reinforcements.
Several other commanders of a hundred remained at Jamukha’s side, but Eight Spring Gorge was only the first hill they had to cross.
He had no intention of wasting more of his forces in this narrow gorge, or of trusting commanders who might do something foolish again.
He wanted a surer hand.
Not one of the fine steeds or loyal hounds that raced like the wind at the turn of his reins, but a vicious dog that served the same master he did.
*Ka-boom!*
Jamukha watched calmly as a tremendous roar shook heaven and earth. A streak of red light came hurtling toward the ground along with a section of the cliff.
*Fwoosh.*
The breeze felt cool as it brushed Jin Mukyung’s hair.
It was a freshness he could never have felt in the training hall deep inside the cave.
Like a reed swaying in the wind, he twisted his body smoothly.
*Shwaack!*
Five lances grazed his arms, legs, and waist as they passed.
Jin Mukyung reached out, and a gleaming white-silver blade slid along the steel shaft of a lance.
*Shhk!*
A cold slicing sound announced another death.
At the same moment, the strength and weight behind the shaft vanished.
Jin Mukyung seized the shafts that had crossed past him, grazing his body, and spun rapidly.
*Krrrunch!*
There were no screams. Only a thick mist of blood.
With the five lances as teeth and his own body as the turning axle, Jin Mukyung ground everything within a three-*jang* radius to pieces. When he stopped, there were no enemies left around him.
And he knew his martial prowess was not the only reason.
*Ka-boom! Rrrumble!*
The gorge shook.
Rocks large and small came pouring down amid a roar that seemed to split the sky. Among them, Jin Mukyung caught sight of a streak of red light bending like a living creature.
*Clang!*
A tremendous blow struck his sword.
As Jin Mukyung retreated, a dull ache running up to his wrist, an exuberant voice reached his ears.
“Now that’s a shame. If I’d gotten a little more used to it, I could’ve landed a whopper.”
Chinggen.
He tossed aside his black-wood fishing rod, soaked in dark red blood, and raised two swords, one long and one short. He smiled.
At his new prey.

chapters.title: Chapter 959
paragraphs: Everything in the world had its own color, and people were no exception.
Their eyes, their expressions, the distinctive qi surrounding them—all of it revealed who they were.
The moment Jin Mukyung saw the man before him, he knew instinctively what he was.
*A demon.*
The two syllables flashed through his mind.

There was no mistake. The eyes drunk on killing intent. The corners of his mouth lifted in a lazy smile. The scent of blood seeping from his entire body was so strong it stung Mukyung’s nose just to stand before him.
*What... is this bastard?*
Mukyung watched him, his gaze steady.
He could feel it in his skin. He understood it in his mind. This new enemy was nothing like an ordinary villain.

Even Pung Yang, the Red Wind Band Leader who had once raided the Mount Heng Sword Sect and inflicted a serious internal injury on Mukyung with his unexpected martial prowess, seemed like a mere mounted bandit beside this man.
A different breed. A different class.
In the lives he had taken, and in his martial prowess.
Chinggen looked back at Mukyung and grinned.
“Just as I thought. You’ve got good eyes.”
*Step. Whish!*
Chinggen took a light step, as though out for a stroll. Mukyung instantly sprang back and raised his sword at an angle.
“Your Qi Sense is useful, too.”
Chinggen nodded with satisfaction.
He had let only the faintest trace of killing intent slip, yet the young man had reacted without an instant’s hesitation.
Enemy though he was, Chinggen liked the young Sword Demon more than he had expected. It almost seemed a waste to treat him as mere prey.
“You’re as gloomy as an old man on his last legs, but you’re still just a brat... Who are you? Want to be my Disciple?”
No one had expected that. The battlefield, briefly stilled by Chinggen’s arrival, stirred with alarm.
More than anyone, the hundred or so nomads groaning amid the gaps in the collapsed rocks stared wide-eyed at their Great Chieftain, doubting their own eyes and ears.
They belonged to the western grasslands ruled by Temur and Chinggen. They knew both young Great Chieftains well, which made the offer all the harder to believe.

Chinggen had become Khan through strategy and leadership rather than personal martial prowess. Yet here he was, offering to take as a Disciple the man who, through extraordinary martial skill, had single-handedly slaughtered hundreds of their brothers from the grasslands.
“K-Khan!”
“What are you saying...?!”
Cries of shock rang out from every side.
The joy they’d felt at the arrival of Chinggen and the Keshik had vanished long ago.
Chinggen smacked his lips at the sight of the nomads staring at him with wide eyes, each nursing injuries of varying severity.
“Come to think of it, this is a strange time to make the offer, isn’t it? Especially with people watching.”
The short sword in his left hand blurred.
*Shk. Rrrrrumble!*
A cold slicing sound rang out. The pile of rocks, barely holding together, collapsed onto the nomads.
Their screams as they waited for rescue were swallowed by the roar, then disappeared completely.
“Useless things. Never any help, but they sure do run their mouths.”
“Now that no one’s watching, let’s get back to our conversation. Hmm?”
In the sudden silence, Mukyung fixed Chinggen with a steady gaze.
“So you’re Chinggen, you bastard?”
“Hey, now. Is that any way to address me?”
Chinggen clicked his tongue.
“You may be a brat, but that’s no way to speak to your Master. I ought to rip your tongue out.”
The swaggering manner. The ease of a man certain of his strength.
Mukyung had little trouble seeing that the man before him, wearing a nomad’s distinctive hairstyle, was hiding a great many secrets.
“You’ve disguised yourself. Where’s the real Chinggen?”
Chinggen thought for a moment.
“Who knows? Probably inside an eagle’s belly by now.”
“And the other one?”
“The other one? Oh, I left Temur alive. Had to keep one of them around to control the westerners.”
He answered without hesitation.
The Keshik controlled everything within several dozen *jang*. Jamukha had spent years raising them as his personal guard, and they would never betray their master.
Even the fiercest hunting dog did not bite its owner.
“Well, that should satisfy your curiosity. What do you say to my generous offer?”
Chinggen was looking at Mukyung with great anticipation when—
“Impossible.”
A low voice cut in. Chinggen frowned at the face he saw over Mukyung’s shoulder.
“Impossible? Why? No, first—who the hell are you?”
The uninvited guest answered calmly.
“How could a wolf serve under a mangy dog? He’s my little brother, whom I’ve cherished like my own son. As his older brother, I can’t let that happen.”
“Little brother? Older brother?”
Chinggen’s eyes widened slightly as he looked at Jin Wikyung. Then he let out a short laugh.
“The Jin brothers... This is a much bigger catch than I expected.”
*A big catch.*
Wikyung’s gaze grew heavy at those words. He remembered the old fisherman who had laughed heartily before the battle and promised to bring back a big catch.
“What happened to Senior?”
He had his suspicions, but he wanted to hear it from Chinggen himself.
What had become of the Dongting Fisherman, who had willingly risked his life for the Jin Family of Taiyuan? Of the owner of that dark fishing rod lying on the ground?
His worst fears were seldom wrong.
“Oh, that old man.”
Chinggen smiled faintly.
“He was a decent fisherman, but he wasn’t strong enough. Hooked something too big for him and snapped. Just like that rod.”
“Actually, ‘snapped’ isn’t enough. More like crushed to pieces. He was slammed more than thirty *jang* down.”
Wikyung swallowed a groan.
The black-wood fishing rod, soaked in dark red blood and cracked in several places, showed how fiercely the Dongting Fisherman had fought.
The old fisherman had often said that when he died, he wanted his remains scattered in a blue river. Today, he had laid his bones in this gray gorge instead.
He had given his life for the Jin Family of Taiyuan, repaying the life he owed them.
Now the Jin Family owed him a debt. Him, and everyone else who had died here.
“Give me your name and title.”
“What?”
“I need to know who you are, so I can speak with my head held high when we offer a memorial rite for the dead in the future.”
Wikyung met Chinggen’s eyes with a cold gaze.
“So we can say we personally tore apart and killed the bastard who dared invade Shanxi Province and harm you all.”
“No matter how rotten the world gets, isn’t that what people ought to do?”
Chinggen blinked his wide-open eyes, then suddenly burst into loud laughter.
“Ha! Hahahahaha!”
His laughter boomed through the gorge, pressing down on everything around it.
No—it was no longer mere sound.
*Vrrrrm. Rrrrattle!*
The air swelled. An immense pressure shook the ground and cliffs as though an earthquake had struck, drawing groans from all around.
“Urgh...!”
Was this what it felt like to be caught in a giant’s grasp?
The tremendous qi carried in Chinggen’s laughter made those nearby stagger. Some of the lower-level martial artists, whose internal energy was meager, went pale and coughed up blood.
“A Supreme Peak master...!”
The words slipped from someone’s lips like a groan. They gave voice to everyone’s shock.
And yet even that did not go far enough.
Just as mountain peaks differed in height, the man wearing Chinggen’s face could not be fully described by the words *Supreme Peak*.
*Sssssss.*
At that moment, the martial artists of Shanxi Province could hardly believe their eyes.
Fragments of broken rock were rising into the air as though suspended on invisible threads. There were a hundred or so of them.
Their jagged edges were hidden weapons in their own right, and the man standing tall at their center was nothing less than a monster.
A monster of endless change, wearing human skin.
*Crack. Crrrunch!*
Bone shifted and flesh compressed with sickening sounds. His appearance changed by the moment.
Everyone stared, stunned by the sight. Then three streaks of light flashed from somewhere.
*Shwaaa!*
The air split.
Three figures crossed the space like lightning, too fast for even the Keshik to react. As though they had planned it, all three struck at once.
*Whoom. Whish!*
A mighty punch and two swords blazed with brilliant light as they rushed toward Chinggen—
“How dare you!”
*KABOOM!*
With an enraged shout, an enormous surge of qi erupted like lava, driving everything around him away. A violent gale whipped through the gorge.
*Fwoooooosh!*
A thick cloud of pale dust rose, obscuring everything beyond arm’s reach.
The three attackers were thrown back three *jang* by the irresistible force. They exchanged deep, steady looks—when—
*Pop!*
A sharp crack cut through the air, and Chinggen appeared before them.
No. Not Chinggen. Someone none of them had ever seen.
*Thud.*
A heavy footstep.
The old man was as bulky as two or three ordinary men put together. He wiped the sweat from his brow with his sleeve and muttered, “Damn it. I just can’t get used to this.”
The man who had been called Chinggen moments ago felt his own face, restored after so long, then the flesh that seemed ready to burst from his body.
Old and ugly.
That alone was unpleasant enough. Being ambushed while enduring the painful reversal of his disguise technique and Bone-Shrinking Technique had made his mood far worse.
“You ungrateful little bastard...”
The old man glared at the rats who had dared to ambush him. His eyes were so narrow and buried in fat they seemed impossible to see.
He was furious—especially because Jin Mukyung, the first person in a long while to catch his interest, was among them.
“You dared ambush your Master? You’re expelled.”
At the old man’s declaration, Mukyung found himself wondering how his troublesome younger brother would have answered such nonsense if he were here.
Then he came up with a likely answer.
“Go suck a dog’s dick.”
“Oh. And you’re a pig bastard, too.”
The old man’s eyes reddened with rage. Reflected in them were the two men smiling on either side of Mukyung.
“And who are you two?”
The two men, one young and one old, answered readily.
“Ghost Sword Wipeng.”
“Tiger of Mount Heng, Cheol Mubaek.”
At the answers of the two Peak masters representing the Jin Family of Taiyuan and the Mount Heng Sword Sect, the old man licked his lips with a tongue surprisingly quick for his size.
“So, one of you’s about to die and become a ghost, and the other’s a dog from Mount Heng. Good to know.”
*Shing.*
Metal scraped coldly against metal. The old man crossed the two swords in his hands.
“When you reach the underworld, tell them the Demon Bird sent you.”
Those words were the signal.
The battlefield’s suspended moment ended, and the wick that had barely kept burning caught in a blood-red blaze.
*Waaaaaah!*
With a great roar that woke the deep night, two waves crashed into each other.

paragraphs: The time it takes to drink a cup of tea.
That was all the time that had passed, but the Demon Bird had to admit it: he had underestimated the prey before him. No—the people of Shanxi.
“Loose!”
*Fwish-fwish-fwish-fwish!*
The defenders had done more than hold the cliffs.

Five earthen forts stood near the entrance to the gorge. Their ramparts of earth and stone were still incomplete, but a considerable number of archers waited atop them. At a sharp command, a rain of arrows fell on the heads of the people surging together into a single mass.
More precisely, on the steppe forces streaming toward the gorge without pause.
*Fwoosh! Thud-thud-thud!*
“Aaagh!”
“M-my eye! My eye!”
Screams rose on every side, and blood sprayed into the air. Nomads struck in vital spots writhed where they fell.
Several volleys followed in quick succession, opening gaps in the densely packed formation. The people of Shanxi, led by the Jin Family of Taiyuan, drove into those gaps like awls.
“Attack!”
“Waaaaah!”
Those trying to break through and those trying to stop them.
The two waves of people surged toward each other. Where they met, there would be no white foam—only red blood.
*Clang! Krrrunch!*
*Thwack!*
Steel struck steel, throwing sparks.
A nomad’s lance pierced a government soldier through the chest. A martial artist of the Jin Family of Taiyuan leaped over the soldier’s collapsing body and cut the nomad’s throat.
*Shhk!*
“Ghk—cough!”
Screams and groans spilled from every direction. Everyone kept killing, and everyone kept dying.
On this battlefield, there was no trace of the mercy or compassion a human being ought to possess.
The strong devoured the weak. The weak could never survive here.
That was a battlefield. And at the center of this terrible slaughter, the Demon Bird felt a pleasure he had forgotten decades ago.
“Yes! More! More!”

He laughed aloud and swung his two swords, just as he had in the days when nothing could stand in his way. He remembered the great war called the Great Faction War, when he had taken his enemies’ lives and drunk their blood to his heart’s content.
*Shwaaa!*
The wind split. Force surged from the long and short swords, cleaving through the air toward the most delectable prey.
“Scatter!”
*Whoosh!*

It all happened at almost the same instant: Jin Mukyung, at the head of the line, shouted like a thunderclap; Cheol Mubaek, the Tiger of Mount Heng, and Wipeng, the Ghost Sword, twisted aside at his command; and—
*Shhk!*
The red Force barely missed them and swept away the unlucky men standing near its target.
*Fwoooosh!*
There were no screams. Only severed bodies and fountains of blood.
“Aah! Aaaaaah!”
Someone screamed in terror. It was the only clue to what had happened to the thirty or so government soldiers and martial artists.
In an instant, a single swing had taken dozens of lives.
No—erased them.
As though they had never existed. As though that had been their inevitable fate.
*So this is a Supreme Peak master...!*
A chill ran down Wipeng’s and Cheol Mubaek’s spines.
Peak and Supreme Peak. Only one character separated the names, but the wall between those realms was vast beyond measure.
If another Supreme Peak master hadn’t unexpectedly become a retainer of the Jin Family of Taiyuan about half a year earlier, they might have lost the will to fight just from seeing that attack.
*But even that Senior, as powerful as he was, fell to that monster.*
That was true even considering that the Dongting Fisherman had only recently recovered enough to leave his sickbed.

Wipeng and Cheol Mubaek had studied under him for months. They knew better than anyone how strong he was—and what a fortuitous encounter it had been to hear even a few words from a master of his caliber, much less spar with him so often.

The Dongting Fisherman had always been grateful to the Jin Family brothers for stopping him when he had run wild, then helping him recover. Through the goodwill he showed them, the Jin Family of Taiyuan had grown dramatically stronger.
And yet he was dead.
Killed by one man.
No—by a monster who hardly seemed human.
Now the monster who had chewed up and swallowed the old fisherman opened his jaws toward the new prey charging at him.
Even now.
*Whish.*
The air split with a faint sound. The instant a red flash flickered in the darkness, Wipeng and Cheol Mubaek twisted aside with all their strength.
*Pipip!*
Hot.
They had dodged the attack by a handspan, yet its pressure split the skin at the backs of their necks.
The sudden sting cleared their muddled thoughts.
*This is...*
Their eyes had widened for a moment. Now their gazes steadied.

That dodge had been no coincidence, no movement born of instinct alone. It was the result of everything they had gained from sparring with the Dongting Fisherman—their senses, their techniques, all of it.
And in half of those countless bouts, the two of them had fought together.
*We can do this.*
They needed only a glance to know what the other intended. Their gazes crossed for an instant, and both men blurred into motion.
*Fwap!*

They shot off to either side. They vaulted over friend and foe swinging blades at one another in the blood-soaked chaos, then raced along the steep rock face, throwing everything they had into evading the monster’s Force. It was faster and stronger than the Dongting Fisherman’s.
*Shhk! KABOOM!*

The solid cliff face, formed over what must have been hundreds of years, split like tofu. The tremendous energy that seeped into it tore everything around it to shreds, but Wipeng and Cheol Mubaek didn’t stop.
They couldn’t.

If they failed to bring down the enemy before them, everything would be over. And if they gave in to fear, or faltered at the wounds multiplying as they drew closer, how could they face the young man already ahead of them?
*Second Young Master.*
*Heaven Shaking Sword.*

They could see Jin Mukyung clearly, charging without hesitation through the ceaseless shower of Force. Flecks of blood scattered from him, but there was not the slightest tremor in his sturdy back or legs.

They found themselves wondering how he had spent those two years. How this other genius, briefly overshadowed by Jin Taekyung and Cheongpung, had lived in lightless darkness before finally emerging into the world.
And then they saw it.
*Hssss.*
Moonlight slid along the white blade.
No. It was a massive Sword Energy, shining brighter than either Wipeng’s or Cheol Mubaek’s.
*Whish.*
In a world that seemed to have slowed, the blue Sword Energy swept down at an angle and met the Demon Bird’s red Force.
*KABOOOOM!*
The explosion stopped everyone in their tracks for an instant and shook the gorge.
For someone at its center, it brought joy and astonishment as well.
*Rumble.*
“Ha! Hahahahaha!”
Beyond the fragments of rock scattering in every direction and the cloud of dust rising thick in the air, the Demon Bird laughed like a madman and thrust out his hand like a thunderbolt.
*Boom!*
Compressed air burst outward, clearing his view. Jin Mukyung stood at the far end of a deep furrow a full *jang* long. The Demon Bird bared his yellow teeth.
“Well, well! What a brazen little brat!”
Powerful killing intent mingled with delight. The two swords in his hands trembled—but not just because of what he was feeling.
*Tap.*
He already knew what had touched his heel.
A rock.

A fragment of stone that had been three steps behind him just moments ago, but now touched his heel. He felt its hardness and chill through his blood-soaked leather shoes, and that was the greatest reason for his smile.
“I can’t remember the last time someone made me step back.”
The rock had not moved toward him. He had retreated.
No—he had been forced back.
A brat not yet thirty had forced back an old monster whose life had been steeped in blood since the Great Faction War.
Though the distance of three steps and a *jang* was considerable, it meant nothing to the Demon Bird. He had seen it clearly.
Just before the two different streams of Sword Energy and Force met, the beautiful path traced by the brat’s fingertips.
That light, as blue as the sea.
“Ah. So that was it.”
*Squelch.*
The Demon Bird stepped forward slowly, his foot sinking into a pool of blood. Blood overflowed with his heavy step, a testament to his bulk.
“I thought it strange. Even while I fought that old Dongting Fisherman, why did your face keep coming to mind when I’d never seen it?”

A few days earlier, a messenger had brought news of the vanguard’s annihilation, along with the severed head of a Keshik commander of a hundred. In the cut, the Demon Bird had seen the Sword Demon’s handiwork.
“The moment I saw it, I was interested. The work was that perfect.”
Everything leaves a trace.
Beasts, people, martial arts.
Every death has its own cause, and that is especially true for a martial artist of Murim. Looking at the chillingly smooth cut, the Demon Bird had felt blood long gone cold begin to boil.
Was it because he had found traces of a divine art believed lost long ago?
Or because he had sensed the work of someone whose strength rivaled his own?
No.

“One Strike.”
He could watch it hundreds, thousands of times and find not one wasted movement.
Dazzling. Beautiful, even.
A perfect strike.
That single movement was what the young Sword Demon before him possessed.
He had not accumulated several *jiazi* of internal energy or mastered a divine art that could look down on the world.
It was colorless and odorless.
That was what made it more lethal than anything else.
Like the Formless Ultimate Poison, swallowing a life before its victim could react. Like an assassin approaching unseen in the dark to cut a man’s throat.
“Amazing. No—extraordinary.”
The Demon Bird’s admiration was genuine. As he looked at Jin Mukyung, regret and sorrow entered his eyes.
“Why? Why did I have to meet someone like you now?”
*Ptooey.*
Jin Mukyung spat out dark red, bloody phlegm and answered evenly.
“Even if I’d met you much earlier, there’s no way I’d have called a mangy pig like you my Master.”
Wipeng and Cheol Mubaek closed in alongside him, moving to surround the Demon Bird. The old man sighed regretfully.
*Why? Why now, of all times?*
If they had met a year—no, three years—later, their match might have made his whole body tremble with joy.
Only a half-collapsed wall stood before Jin Mukyung now.
That moment of joy would never come again.
Jin Mukyung wouldn’t survive this place today.
“What a shame. Truly.”
*Hssss.*
Blood-red light rose from the Demon Bird’s entire body.

sentences.text: The time it takes to drink a cup of tea.
That was all the time that had passed, but the Demon Bird had to admit it: he had underestimated the prey before him.
No—the people of Shanxi.
“Loose!”
*Fwish-fwish-fwish-fwish!*
The defenders had done more than hold the cliffs.
Five earthen forts stood near the entrance to the gorge.
Their ramparts of earth and stone were still incomplete, but a considerable number of archers waited atop them.
At a sharp command, a rain of arrows fell on the heads of the people surging together into a single mass.
More precisely, on the steppe forces streaming toward the gorge without pause.
*Fwoosh!
Thud-thud-thud!*
“Aaagh!”
“M-my eye!
My eye!”
Screams rose on every side, and blood sprayed into the air.
Nomads struck in vital spots writhed where they fell.
Several volleys followed in quick succession, opening gaps in the densely packed formation.
The people of Shanxi, led by the Jin Family of Taiyuan, drove into those gaps like awls.
“Attack!”
“Waaaaah!”
Those trying to break through and those trying to stop them.
The two waves of people surged toward each other.
Where they met, there would be no white foam—only red blood.
*Clang!
Krrrunch!*
*Thwack!*
Steel struck steel, throwing sparks.
A nomad’s lance pierced a government soldier through the chest.
A martial artist of the Jin Family of Taiyuan leaped over the soldier’s collapsing body and cut the nomad’s throat.
*Shhk!*
“Ghk—cough!”
Screams and groans spilled from every direction.
Everyone kept killing, and everyone kept dying.
On this battlefield, there was no trace of the mercy or compassion a human being ought to possess.
The strong devoured the weak.
The weak could never survive here.
That was a battlefield.
And at the center of this terrible slaughter, the Demon Bird felt a pleasure he had forgotten decades ago.
“Yes!
More!
More!”
He laughed aloud and swung his two swords, just as he had in the days when nothing could stand in his way.
He remembered the great war called the Great Faction War, when he had taken his enemies’ lives and drunk their blood to his heart’s content.
*Shwaaa!*
The wind split.
Force surged from the long and short swords, cleaving through the air toward the most delectable prey.
“Scatter!”
*Whoosh!*

It all happened at almost the same instant: Jin Mukyung, at the head of the line, shouted like a thunderclap; Cheol Mubaek, the Tiger of Mount Heng, and Wipeng, the Ghost Sword, twisted aside at his command; and—
*Shhk!*
The red Force barely missed them and swept away the unlucky men standing near its target.
*Fwoooosh!*
There were no screams.
Only severed bodies and fountains of blood.
“Aah!
Aaaaaah!”
Someone screamed in terror.
It was the only clue to what had happened to the thirty or so government soldiers and martial artists.
In an instant, a single swing had taken dozens of lives.
No—erased them.
As though they had never existed.
As though that had been their inevitable fate.
*So this is a Supreme Peak master...!*
A chill ran down Wipeng’s and Cheol Mubaek’s spines.
Peak and Supreme Peak.
Only one character separated the names, but the wall between those realms was vast beyond measure.
If another Supreme Peak master hadn’t unexpectedly become a retainer of the Jin Family of Taiyuan about half a year earlier, they might have lost the will to fight just from seeing that attack.
*But even that Senior, as powerful as he was, fell to that monster.*
That was true even considering that the Dongting Fisherman had only recently recovered enough to leave his sickbed.
Wipeng and Cheol Mubaek had studied under him for months.
They knew better than anyone how strong he was—and what a fortuitous encounter it had been to hear even a few words from a master of his caliber, much less spar with him so often.
The Dongting Fisherman had always been grateful to the Jin Family brothers for stopping him when he had run wild, then helping him recover.
Through the goodwill he showed them, the Jin Family of Taiyuan had grown dramatically stronger.
And yet he was dead.
Killed by one man.
No—by a monster who hardly seemed human.
Now the monster who had chewed up and swallowed the old fisherman opened his jaws toward the new prey charging at him.
Even now.
*Whish.*
The air split with a faint sound.
The instant a red flash flickered in the darkness, Wipeng and Cheol Mubaek twisted aside with all their strength.
*Pipip!*
Hot.
They had dodged the attack by a handspan, yet its pressure split the skin at the backs of their necks.
The sudden sting cleared their muddled thoughts.
*This is...*
Their eyes had widened for a moment.
Now their gazes steadied.
That dodge had been no coincidence, no movement born of instinct alone.
It was the result of everything they had gained from sparring with the Dongting Fisherman—their senses, their techniques, all of it.
And in half of those countless bouts, the two of them had fought together.
*We can do this.*
They needed only a glance to know what the other intended.
Their gazes crossed for an instant, and both men blurred into motion.
*Fwap!*
They shot off to either side.
They vaulted over friend and foe swinging blades at one another in the blood-soaked chaos, then raced along the steep rock face, throwing everything they had into evading the monster’s Force.
It was faster and stronger than the Dongting Fisherman’s.
*Shhk!
KABOOM!*
The solid cliff face, formed over what must have been hundreds of years, split like tofu.
The tremendous energy that seeped into it tore everything around it to shreds, but Wipeng and Cheol Mubaek didn’t stop.
They couldn’t.
If they failed to bring down the enemy before them, everything would be over.
And if they gave in to fear, or faltered at the wounds multiplying as they drew closer, how could they face the young man already ahead of them?
*Second Young Master.*
*Heaven Shaking Sword.*
They could see Jin Mukyung clearly, charging without hesitation through the ceaseless shower of Force.
Flecks of blood scattered from him, but there was not the slightest tremor in his sturdy back or legs.
They found themselves wondering how he had spent those two years.
How this other genius, briefly overshadowed by Jin Taekyung and Cheongpung, had lived in lightless darkness before finally emerging into the world.
And then they saw it.
*Hssss.*
Moonlight slid along the white blade.
No.
It was a massive Sword Energy, shining brighter than either Wipeng’s or Cheol Mubaek’s.
*Whish.*
In a world that seemed to have slowed, the blue Sword Energy swept down at an angle and met the Demon Bird’s red Force.
*KABOOOOM!*
The explosion stopped everyone in their tracks for an instant and shook the gorge.
For someone at its center, it brought joy and astonishment as well.
*Rumble.*
“Ha!
Hahahahaha!”

Compressed air burst outward, clearing his view.

What a brazen little brat!”
Powerful killing intent mingled with delight.

A rock.

The rock had not moved toward him.
He had retreated.
No—he had been forced back.

He had seen it clearly.

That light, as blue as the sea.

No.

chapters.title: Chapter 961
paragraphs: The moment he saw the faint blood-red glow rising through the darkness, the Tiger of Mount Heng, Cheol Mubaek, finally recognized the obese old man who had introduced himself as the Demon Bird.
“Blood Soul Fat Demon.”
The name escaped him like a groan. The Demon Bird’s face twisted.
“How does a brat like you know...?”
Cheol Mubaek would turn sixty in a few years, but even a veteran like him was little more than a green young pup in the Demon Bird’s eyes.
What bothered the old man most, though, was hearing that long-buried title again.
Blood Soul Fat Demon.
He had earned it by treating murder as a hunt. Even among the countless fiends, he had been unusually obsessed with death and blood. But the title carried mockery, too.
*Fat.*
That one word had always gotten under his skin, and the Demon Bird had never been one to resist his feelings or instincts.
“It’s been a long time since I heard that damned title. I’ve killed so many people for saying it that now, even when they recognize me, plenty pretend they don’t.”
He had killed the execution squads sent by the orthodox faction, the unorthodox rabble who bowed and scraped to curry favor with him, and even fiends he’d once been fairly close to.
The reason was simple.
They had called him by the title he couldn’t stand to hear.
Why else would he have named himself the Demon Bird, a title that didn’t suit his appearance in the slightest?
And now a green young pup with the unheard-of title Tiger of Mount Heng had dug up memories he’d put away.
*How dare you.*
Cheol Mubaek’s fate was all but sealed. The Demon Bird put his name at the top of the list of people he intended to kill, then spoke.
“A brat like you couldn’t possibly have met me before... Who was your master?”
*Crack.*
Cheol Mubaek clenched both fists.
“Fist Hero.”
“Fist Hero?”
The Demon Bird stopped in the middle of his unhurried approach.
He hadn’t expected much when he asked. He had spent his life killing, and once the count passed a thousand, he’d stopped keeping track. There was no reason to remember them all.
But Fist Hero’s title remained vivid in his memory. The man was one of the few who had survived a life-and-death duel with him.
“Well, isn’t this something. You’re Fist Hero’s Disciple? Wait—he raised a successor with that body?”
The Demon Bird forgot his anger and burst out laughing. Cheol Mubaek answered coldly.
“Don’t insult my master. He was a far greater man than you could ever be.”
“Of course he was. Even after his life as a fist fighter was over, he managed to raise a Disciple. I’ll give him credit for his grit. You should’ve seen his face when I cut off both his arms.”
“Now that I look again, this is quite a lavish feast. The young Sword Demon of the Jin Family of Taiyuan, and the successor of the Shura Annihilating Fist.”
As the Demon Bird surveyed them with satisfaction, Wipeng spat.
“Can’t see me?”
“Of course I can. I can already picture your corpse lying there in a moment.”
“You have to see how long or short it is before you can tell.”
“That’s the kind of bullshit weaklings say.”
*Thud.*
The old man’s heavy, wrinkled flesh rippled as he stepped forward. His sharp gaze seemed at odds with his massive frame as he sized up the three men.
“Well, then...”
*Whoosh.*
“Who should I kill first?”
In a single step, the Demon Bird closed a distance of several *jang*. The two swords in his hands swept through the air in arcs.
Like the blood-red claws of a bird.
*Whoooosh!*
*Shhk—KRRRUNCH!*
A gale howled.
Mighty pressure swallowed the air and tore at their skin. Dirt and shards of rock blasted outward with a roar.
—Second Young Master!
Wipeng’s Sound Transmission pierced Jin Mukyung’s ears.
Mukyung had been retreating again and again to avoid the Demon Bird’s Force. He jerked his head aside.
*Whoom.*
Two razor-sharp streams of wind skimmed past the back of his neck.
The two Keshik gripping crescent-shaped sabers clicked their tongues in disappointment. Mukyung had dodged their ambush as though he’d been expecting it.
That was the last anyone saw of them alive.
*Shhk!*
By the time the blood-red flash appeared, it was already over.
The Keshik fell quietly, never knowing how—or why—they had died.
Behind their collapsing, headless bodies stood someone who could have told them, radiating enormous killing intent.
“You dare try to steal my prey?”
*CRUNCH!*
Blood Soul Fat Demon. Or the Demon Bird.
The obese old man angrily trampled the fallen Keshik’s bodies, as though he’d completely forgotten the other prey rushing at him from behind.
Or as though they weren’t worth noticing.
“You bastard!”
The Tiger of Mount Heng, Cheol Mubaek, roared and threw a punch.
He was the Disciple of a great fist fighter who had lost both arms to a fiend long ago. He had become a protector of the Mount Heng Sword Sect to help a friend’s only daughter.
*Whoooooom—BANG!*
Compressed air exploded. Fist Energy shot from his spinning fist and engulfed his master’s killer.
Or at least, that was how it appeared for an instant.
*Fwoosh!*
A long sword, tinged red like its owner, sliced through the air.
The Fist Energy that had seemed ready to reduce anything in its path to ash faded and scattered. A sneer touched the Demon Bird’s lips.
“You’re certainly no match for your master. I’m not even sure that’s the Shura Annihilating Fist I knew.”
But the Demon Bird knew the truth.
Some two hundred years ago, the Shura Annihilating Fist had ranked among the ten greatest fist-and-foot arts in the world. Cheol Mubaek’s current realm wasn’t all that far from Fist Hero’s, either.
Neither the art nor its successor fell short. The Demon Bird had simply grown stronger.
“Come!”
He felt the blood in his body boil.
The two swords in his hands had never felt lighter. Every movement his prey made looked clear—and slow.
As though reading a future that had yet to happen, he raised his blade to meet a flash thrusting in at an angle.
*KABOOM!*
The impact was far too loud to have come from two swords simply clashing.
Wipeng groaned as the tremendous recoil sent him flying. The Demon Bird launched his massive body after him, certain of what would come next.
*One first.*
Water flowed from high to low. People grew old and died. Everything in the world had its destined course.
To the Demon Bird, Wipeng’s death was just as certain.
A Peak master who had reached an impressive realm for his age. An outstanding swordsman whose practical sword technique justified the title Ghost Sword.
But that was all Wipeng was.
With enough effort and luck, he might reach Supreme Peak in ten or fifteen years. That day would never come. Meeting the Demon Bird in this gorge was proof that Heaven had already abandoned him.
Those who had yet to cross the wall, and those who had.
That was the difference between Peak and Supreme Peak.
*Become a ghost. Live up to your title.*
Blood-red light flashed as the Demon Bird swung both swords.
The short sword in his left hand went for Cheol Mubaek, who was rushing to save his comrade. The long sword in his right went for Wipeng, who met it with all his strength.
But the clash unfolded in a way the Demon Bird hadn’t expected.
*CRUNCH—KRRRRANG!*
A substantial recoil traveled up both sword blades.
The Demon Bird’s eyes widened at the dazzling sparks blooming where three different streams of energy met.
*What?*
He was more shaken than he could have imagined.
Cheol Mubaek and Wipeng—those young pups who hadn’t crossed the wall, prey who should have been no more than a meal—had stopped his strike.
With nothing more than their paltry Fist Energy and Sword Energy, they were holding out against Sword Force he had unleashed with all his strength.
*How?*
The Demon Bird was a born killer and hunter. He knew better than anyone how far beneath him his prey stood, both in their enlightenment in martial arts and in the internal energy they held.
Yet the impossible was happening before his eyes.
A mere Peak master had met head-on the Force he’d swung with several *jiazi* of internal energy. It was something that couldn’t happen—and shouldn’t.
*Cough. Spurt.*
Blood mixed with bits of their innards poured from Cheol Mubaek’s and Wipeng’s split lips.
The Demon Bird stared, frozen in shock. The two men bared their bloodied teeth and smiled.
They could barely hold out against the blood-red Force. Cheol Mubaek’s snow-white gauntlet and Wipeng’s sword blade trembled beneath its overwhelming power.
Then the Demon Bird noticed the faint glow of their prized weapons, visible even through the thick blood, and remembered something he had briefly forgotten.
A Supreme Peak master’s Force could be resisted by something other than Force of the same kind.
*Ten-Thousand-Year Cold Iron...!*
The Demon Bird caught his breath.
How could he have known? In all his long life, even he had never obtained a divine weapon like these. Yet two Peak masters from remote Shanxi Province each held one.
Nor could he have guessed that the weapons he mistook for Ten-Thousand-Year Cold Iron were made from the bones of a spiritual creature that had guarded a river unseen for hundreds of years.
His moment of surprise gave someone who was still standing an opening.
*Hup!*
Wipeng wrung out every last bit of his strength and twisted his sword.
His wrist was already broken and his hand mangled, but he swallowed the blood rising from his severe Internal Injury and turned aside the energy bearing down on him.
*KRRRRUNCH!*
The long sword slid along the snow-white blade and drove into the ground.
Deep—driven by all the force behind it.
*Thud!*
Anger flared in the Demon Bird’s eyes as he recovered from his shock. At that very instant—
*CRUNCH!*
Cheol Mubaek grabbed the short sword that had been slowly forcing his gauntlet back. His hand closed around the Force shrouding its blade.
*Crack. Krrrunch.*
Something broke with a sickening sound, and unbearable pain followed.

The irresistible power crushed the flesh inside his gauntlet and splintered his bones. Without a divine weapon made from the Water God Dragon’s bones, both his hands would have vanished without a trace the moment they touched the Force.
But Cheol Mubaek did not let go.
The pain was too great even to groan. His organs twisted under the immense energy, yet he held on to the blade with all his strength.
He remembered the great master who had taught him long ago, even without his arms.
And he waited for someone to kill the bastard in his stead, to do what he, an unworthy Disciple, could not.
At last, that wish reached someone’s sword.
*Shwaash.*
A sound so faint it raised goose bumps.
A flash shot forward like a bolt of lightning and descended toward the Demon Bird.
