chapters.title: Chapter 981
paragraphs: Jin Mukyung didn’t know how much time had passed.
After his younger brother had told him everything, a long silence followed. In the end, there was only one thing Mukyung could say.
“I’m tired.”
And so he was left alone.
He forced his aching body upright, leaned against the bed, and stared blankly out the window.
In the first light spreading from the distant east, he watched his younger brother leave the pavilion with a subordinate. The words he’d heard a moment ago came back to him.
*Five thousand.*
Just two syllables. Far too short to hold the weight of thousands of lives. The number didn’t feel real.
But it was, without a doubt, reality.
*Over three thousand died. The rest suffered injuries, big and small, and many were left crippled.*
Of the fifteen thousand people of Shanxi who’d gathered at Eight Spring Gorge that day, a third had been killed or wounded.

Many of the casualties were government soldiers from the Shanxi Provincial Office, relatively weak in martial arts. But Mukyung knew they, too, were part of *us*—people who had put down roots and made their lives on this land.
*...A great victory.*
*Yeah. A great victory. One for the history books.*
More than five thousand casualties, yet in a single night they’d annihilated an army of well over thirty thousand.
They’d won an incredible victory against foreign enemies who outnumbered and overpowered them. It was no exaggeration to say they’d written a new page in the history of the Great Nation.
And yet, not a single person looked happy as they spoke of the great victory.
Those who took what belonged to others reveled in their victories. But those who fought to protect what was theirs mourned what they’d lost along the way.
The bodies and blood left behind by the dead were a burden the survivors alone had to bear.
*The Hebei Peng Family lost more than half its forces. Great Hero Peng, the Thunderbolt Saber King, still hasn’t regained consciousness.*
The great tiger of the Peng Family, which had held sway over Hebei for so long, had yet to wake from his grievous injuries.

No one could have anticipated that the North Heaven Demon Lord—someone he’d considered a friend—would betray him. And the martial arts he’d used in his sudden ambush were in no way inferior to those of the Thunderbolt Saber King.
*Even after we took down Jamukha and the North Heaven Demon Lord, things didn’t go smoothly. If we hadn’t subdued the nomads, we would probably have suffered much heavier losses.*
Despite having joined the battlefield some time before, the Murong Family’s forces had remained relatively intact until the fighting was nearly over.
If Jamukha had lived to see it, he would have realized the truth too late—and trembled.
Just as he’d used Temur to put the tribes of the eastern steppe in front as human shields, the North Heaven Demon Lord had used Jamukha to keep the Murong Family’s losses to a minimum.
The law of the strong preying on the weak applied everywhere.
*That’s when the final battle began.*
Sensing their end, the Murong Family fought with everything they had.

While their allies were dying all around them, they took the Temporary Strength Pill they’d held back until then and fought to open an escape route alongside the western steppe nomads who’d refused to abandon their cause even after Jamukha’s death.
Together, they numbered a staggering five thousand.

The people of Shanxi and the Hebei Peng Family were exhausted from the long battle, however high their spirits remained. Thousands of enemies, strengthened beyond their limits, scattered in every direction to avoid the three Supreme Peak masters. They tore through the weakened encirclement and fled.
No—they tried to flee.
Then, beyond the faint dawn light pushing through the darkness, came a roar that shook the whole world.
Three forces appeared beneath banners that should never have been here.
*We didn’t expect them either. They arrived much sooner than we thought.*
They said the scent of plum blossoms from Huashan filled the ridge in place of the Double Ninth Festival chrysanthemums, soaked in blood and stripped of their fragrance.

A force with a hundred Peak masters at its head charged beneath the Murim Alliance banner and swept through the enemy. Other new arrivals entered the narrow gorge, where quiet had fallen after the terrible fighting.
Their brilliant golden armor gleamed as they rode like the wind.
The world called them the Embroidered Uniform Guard.
*And that was the end of it.*
A dense fog of blood rolled over the gorge and engulfed the broad basin.

With the first light of dawn, reinforcements swept in from every direction and crushed the enemy. The Bow Saint and the Fire King dominated the battlefield, while Jin Taekyung drove his spearhead into the chest of Murong Wijin, Head Elder of the Murong Family, who had resisted until the very end.
The battle—the war—ended that day.
Its beginning and end marked by the Double Ninth Festival.
It left behind the joy of a great victory, and a sorrow heavier still.

Three full days had passed since then. Mukyung had finally regained consciousness, and his younger brother had told him everything that had happened. Now Taekyung was walking away, growing smaller beyond the window.
Before he left, he’d left behind an old book.
*He asked me to give it to you. No—to hyung.*
Remembering the last words Taekyung had tossed out on his way through the door, Mukyung blinked like someone only just waking from sleep.
A stifled groan escaped him.
His vision slowly clouded over. Taekyung was no longer in sight.
Only the four characters on the cover of the book resting on his knees remained clear.
Shura Annihilating Fist.
It was the last trace an old master had left in this world—and the legacy of his martial lineage, entrusted to the Sword Demon of the Jin Family of Taiyuan.
Another casualty of the battle three days ago. A man who had fought back-to-back with Mukyung but had not survived.
*Great Hero Cheol.*
Mukyung thought of Cheol Mubaek, the Tiger of Mount Heng.
Cheol had risked his life to buy him a moment against the formidable Demon Bird.

Mukyung remembered his last smile, blood staining his bared teeth. And he remembered Cheol’s voice from a day two years earlier, when the man had approached him as he was leaving the Mount Heng Sword Sect and spoken as though making a joke.
“I hear you’re crazy about martial arts.”
“Pardon?”
“So, I was wondering—are you interested in Seowol?”
“I’m sorry, what are you talking about all of a sudden...?”
“Exactly what I said. I don’t have much, so I can’t offer you gold or silver. But if the two of you got together, I’d gladly give you the Shura Annihilating Fist manual...”
“Uncle Cheol!”
“Goodness, you’ll burst my eardrums. You’ve only just become Sect Leader, and you’re already trying to boss me around?”
It was strange.
Mukyung had thought Cheol was someone whose path had merely crossed his own. Why, then, could he remember that hearty laugh so clearly?
Why did a heavy ache press against his chest?
*So that’s what this is.*
Only then did he recognize the emotions gripping him.
Sorrow. Anger. And...
Guilt over what he’d already lost.
*If I’d been stronger. If I’d been just a little stronger that day.*
He could have protected them. Saved more people.
But he hadn’t.
He’d fought with everything he had, swinging his sword without rest through a pitch-black darkness where a day felt like ten years. Still, he hadn’t been able to reach them.
*If it had been you instead of me—no, both of you—everything would have been different.*
Meeting Cheongpung had made him feel, for the first time, that there was a wall he could not cross.
Watching Jin Taekyung improve at an astonishing pace had rekindled a longing that had faded within him.

He’d been called a genius since the day he first picked up a sword. Only after seeing what those two were truly capable of had he understood: if his talent was a gift from Heaven, theirs was talent they’d taken from it.
*What do I... What do I have to do to reach you? To keep from losing anyone else?*
Emotions he couldn’t put into words swirled inside him.
He was staring out the window where his brother had disappeared when—
*Tap.*
A faint sound came from the crack around the firmly shut door.
Then a familiar voice reached him.
“Hey, Mujin. Remember that time?”
Mukyung’s eyes widened. He’d thought his brother had gone. An answer followed, so stiff it sounded unnatural.
“Um. W-Which time do you mean?”
“You know. When we formed that recon squad and were busting our asses.”
“Oh. Ah, yes. I remember.”

“Yeah, I saw a lot of things I wish I hadn’t back then. I just... at some point, I got so angry at how pathetic I was. Why was I only capable of this much? Why did people whose faces I’d gotten to know in passing have to die?”
“But you know what pissed me off the most?”
On the other side of the door, Taekyung leaned against it and went on as if talking to himself.
“No matter how hard I fucking try, I can’t get used to it. Nothing changes.”
Mukyung’s eyes trembled.
Forgetting even the pain, he clenched his fist as hard as he could and squeezed his eyes shut. Taekyung’s voice kept coming through the door.

“It’s always the same. I thought if I got stronger than I am now, I could stop bad things from happening. I thought once I could use Sword Energy and send out Force whenever I wanted, nothing as shitty as what happened back then would happen again...”
A low sigh slipped through the crack.
“But no. Every time, I still feel like shit. I was asking for too much.”
More. More. More.
The stronger a person became, the more they wanted. Their hopes grew grander, and their sense of responsibility swelled until it felt ready to burst.
Mukyung thought of himself as a boy, endlessly swinging a sword simply because he loved it.
Had that boy felt anything like the responsibility he felt now?
Back then, all he’d had was talent. He hadn’t even thought about restoring his family’s fortunes.
Taekyung’s voice reached him again.
“But I know this much. If we give up, it ends here.”
Taekyung no longer waited for an answer. Hyuk Mujin’s awkward attempts to play along had stopped, too.
The voice continued as though its words were meant for someone else.

“We just have to keep trying. Do the best we can with what we can do right now. If you despair and give up because nothing changes, that’s when hell really begins. Because later, you realize that all the effort you put in meant fewer people were taken from you.”
“So just keep doing what you’ve been doing. Keep at it, like you always have.”
The bitterness in Taekyung’s voice slowly faded. A brief silence fell.
Then something whistled fiercely through the air.
*Whoosh—thwack!*
“Ow! Why’d you hit me?”
“Answer me, you bastard. When someone’s talking, you’re supposed to give them something back. Don’t make it awkward.”
“Seriously? You’re not even talking to me anyw—Mmph! Mmph!”
At the muffled sounds and the scrape of something being dragged away, Mukyung smiled faintly.
Then, in a voice clear enough to pass through the crack around the door, he saw the uninvited visitors off as they left the pavilion.
“Thank you. Truly.”
Their footsteps paused, as though they’d heard him. Then they quickly faded away.

chapters.title: Chapter 982
paragraphs: I’m a selfish bastard.
As long as the people around me and I can be happy, I don’t much care what happens elsewhere.
But every now and then, I notice that somewhere along the way, I’ve changed.
Like when I put on a ridiculous little show because I couldn’t stop worrying about someone who was beating himself up and crying.
“Sometimes, when I look at you, Captain, I think...”
It had been a while since I’d fled the pavilion, practically running away from Jin Mukyung.
We were walking in silence when Hyuk Mujin spoke up. I cut him off.
“Don’t think. No, just don’t talk.”
“Why not?”
“Because I don’t want to hear it.”
“It’s not because you’re embarrassed, is it?”
He was right.
That was why I’d been trying so hard to ignore the way Hyuk Mujin kept staring at me.
“It’s just...”
“Just?”
“I somehow felt concerned, so I stuck my nose in where it didn’t belong. That’s all.”
The words I’d said to Jin Mukyung through the door were also the conclusion I’d reached after a long time thinking about it.
I didn’t know if it was the right answer. If it could comfort him even a little right now, that was enough.
In the end, time and experience solved most problems.
An answer wasn’t something someone else could hand you. You had to find it yourself.
*For him, this is only the first step.*
He was an unparalleled genius born of the Jin Family of Taiyuan, and in this world, at least, he was my older brother. But Jin Mukyung was only in his mid-twenties.
He’d spent his life honing his martial arts. He could count his experiences in real combat on one hand, and he wasn’t used to the loss that came with them.
If a few embarrassing words could bring him even a little comfort, I’d say them dozens or hundreds of times.
Jin Mukyung’s heart and his feet were pointed toward the righteous path, without a hair’s breadth of deviation.
The more he grew, the more livable the world would become.
*Walk. Don’t sit down. Keep walking, and walking, and walking.*
At the end of that road was an answer.
There was light.
I believed that.
With all my heart.
“But, Captain. Can I tell you something?”
“What?”
“This is the wrong way. If we keep going, we’ll hit a dead end.”
I was silent for a moment, then looked at Hyuk Mujin in disbelief.
“Wait... Why are you only telling me now, you bastard?”
“Well, you suddenly got this intense look in your eyes and started making a cool face.”
I wanted to hit him.
I really did.
Too much had happened over the past three days for me to tell Jin Mukyung everything.
A great battle, with tens of thousands of allies and enemies tangled together.
Three days had already passed since the people of Shanxi won their great victory, but the battle had left a staggering mess behind.
When uninvited guests show up and leave a place filthy and wrecked, the cleanup falls to the homeowner.
From the day of our victory, Jin Wikyung had more work than ten people could handle. Before he’d even recovered from the battle, he had to begin dealing with its aftermath.
Of course, the people around him weren’t going to stand by and let him do that.
“I’m going to give the Lesser Family Head three choices. Hear them all before you pick one.”
The first to step in was the Medicine King Hall Master.

At a glance, he looked like a stubborn old man. But with a menacing gleam in his eyes that didn’t match his calm tone, he glanced back and forth between the long needle in his hand and Jin Wikyung, then said:

“You can keep ignoring my orders and working until you ruin your health and die. Or you can get treated now, take it easy, and live a long life. Or, if you’d rather not drag it out, you can die by my hand. Which will it be?”
Only then did Jin Wikyung begin to get some proper rest. Everyone who’d witnessed the exchange fiercely debated what they’d seen behind his back.
Had his face gone as pale as a corpse’s from exhaustion, or from the Medicine King Hall Master’s long needle?
Hyuk Mujin put it plainly.
“The needle. No question. Didn’t you see that old man’s eyes? If he hadn’t studied medicine, he’d have a position in Dark Heaven by now.”
What mattered was that Jin Wikyung had relented. Others had helped make that possible, too.
“That quack who calls himself the Medicine King Hall Master is absolutely right. You focus on recovering. The others will take care of what’s left.”
We’d won the battle on the Double Ninth Festival, but we still couldn’t be sure every threat was gone.
Even so, the presence of a giant like the Fire King, Jeok Cheongang, was enough to wash away the slightest worry.
So was the Bow Saint, who had finally appeared before people again after decades.
“I’ll go to Hebei.”
The Bow Saint left as soon as the battle ended, with only those few words.

Peng Cheolyeong—the Thunderbolt Saber King’s son, the current Family Head of the Hebei Peng Family, and the Iron Blood Saber—had no choice but to take the family members fit to travel and return to Hebei with her.
It was only natural.
The North Heaven Demon Lord—no, Murong Baek—hadn’t betrayed us alone.
That meant the entire Murong Family had joined Dark Heaven. Two days later, a messenger eagle arrived at the Jin Family of Taiyuan with news confirming part of what we’d suspected.
“As we expected, there was trouble in Hebei.”
Several people had forced Jin Wikyung to rest, but getting the paperwork out of his hands was nearly impossible.
The instant the messenger eagle arrived at the Jin Family of Taiyuan, Jin Wikyung received the news. He immediately called me in and told me what had happened in Hebei.

“It seems the Murong Family targeted both Shanxi and Hebei from the start. They used their offer to support us as a pretext to cross Hebei, leaving some of their forces behind to ambush the Peng Family.”
The bloodshed on the Double Ninth Festival hadn’t been confined to Shanxi Province.

The Hebei Peng Family had been caught completely off guard by the Murong Family’s betrayal. With the Thunderbolt Saber King and many of their strongest masters away, they’d suffered heavy losses and had barely managed to defend their family home, fighting to the death.
“But even that would only have bought them time. If everything had been delayed by two days, something irreversible would have happened.”
But just as the family stood on the brink of ruin, Peng Cheolyeong, its Family Head, finally arrived.

Peng Cheolyeong announced himself with a roar. Behind him came some five hundred family members who’d returned from Shanxi at his side, along with hundreds of martial artists from the Jinzhou Yan Family, who were effectively vassals of the Hebei Peng Family.
If that had been all, the battle would have been a hard one for the Hebei Peng Family.
The surprise attack had already devastated the Hebei Peng Family, and the thousand troops Peng Cheolyeong had assembled in haste were exhausted.
But at their head stood a giant whom even Peng Cheolyeong, Family Head of the Hebei Peng Family, would not dare step ahead of.
“Once Senior Bow Saint made up her mind, the outcome was as good as decided.”
It was another victory for us—and a terrible defeat for the Murong Family.
The kind of defeat they could never recover from.
And so the Murong Family was annihilated.
Several dozen enemies, including its Lesser Family Head, Murong Yeonghwi, barely escaped the battlefield and vanished. But who knew?
“Unless they have a Moving Formation hidden somewhere, they’ll be caught soon enough. We have eyes everywhere.”
Jin Wikyung wasn’t boasting.
Even if the dark clouds cast by Dark Heaven eventually covered everyone’s heads, for now, the orthodox Murim factions still ruled the land.
The Murong Family had made an enemy of the world.
They couldn’t flee into the vast Central Plains without breaking through the Jin Family of Taiyuan and the Hebei Peng Family. To the east, the Great Nation’s warships guarded the open sea.
And the Great Steppe—their roots and little more than the final destination for outlaws—was already practically under the Jin Family of Taiyuan’s control.
“Send your tribespeople after them. Hunt them to the ends of the earth if you have to.”
It wasn’t a request.
As Shanxi’s Alliance Leader, the victor of the great battle, and the master who had brought a defeated hunting dog to heel, Jin Wikyung gave his first order.
“You don’t want to leave yourself trouble later, either. Do you, Temur?”
“I... will obey.”
The young chieftain who had once dreamed of uniting the vast steppe as its Great Khan submitted helplessly.
Of course he did.
He was a commander defeated in battle, and a coward who had betrayed his brothers and tribespeople for fear of death.

For his defeat, he’d been given a pretext: Jamukha and the North Heaven Demon Lord had drawn him into their schemes. He’d also been given the false absolution of having prevented greater losses by submitting to the Jin Family of Taiyuan. His betrayal was another matter.
If the whole truth came out, Temur would die.
Not at our hands or Dark Heaven’s. At the hands of his own tribespeople.
That was the leash Jin Wikyung held tight. The hunting dog couldn’t even think of betraying him.
From the moment Temur accepted Jin Wikyung’s offer and joined the attack on the Murong Family, every other choice had effectively disappeared.
*It’s disgusting, but now that we’re holding his leash, we need him on our side.*
How many lives had Temur’s petty cowardice and instinct for survival cost?
“Go. Just looking at you pisses me off.”
Temur lowered his head at my contemptuous words and left. I called over the man who could deal with the remaining problem once and for all.
“You called?”
His brilliant golden armor drew every eye wherever he went.
His expression and manner of speaking were as stiff as the helmet tucked under his arm.
I deliberately frowned at Jeong Hogun, Thousand Captain of the Embroidered Uniform Guard.
“What’s with you? Why do you look so fine?”
“Because I fought well.”
“Or did you just show up at the end and take all the credit?”
“Is that what you say to a Benefactor who traveled thousands of li to help you?”
“Hey, remember who helped you first. What would you have done at the Imperial Palace without me?”
“What would I have done? The Bow Saint would have helped.”
“...Huh. Now that I think about it, you’re right.”
“...I didn’t expect you to admit that.”
Silence settled between us for a moment. Then, as if on cue, we both chuckled.

He was grateful to me, and I felt the same way about him.

“A favor?”
“Yeah. It might be a little difficult. No, very difficult.”
“Someone might die.”

“Ah.”
His tone was as sharp as a blade.

What an interesting guy.

“Jeong Hogun, Thousand Captain of the Embroidered Uniform Guard.”
As though our conversation had never happened, Jeong Hogun respectfully bowed his head.
“Give your order.”
“Lead the Embroidered Uniform Guard under your command to Liaoning.”
Liaoning Province.
The Murong Family’s stronghold, and the last threat left to deal with.
At my order, Jeong Hogun struck his armor.
“I obey the Marquis of Shangshan’s command.”

sentences.text: I’m a selfish bastard.
As long as the people around me and I can be happy, I don’t much care what happens elsewhere.
But every now and then, I notice that somewhere along the way, I’ve changed.
Like when I put on a ridiculous little show because I couldn’t stop worrying about someone who was beating himself up and crying.
“Sometimes, when I look at you, Captain, I think...”
It had been a while since I’d fled the pavilion, practically running away from Jin Mukyung.
We were walking in silence when Hyuk Mujin spoke up.
I cut him off.
“Don’t think.
No, just don’t talk.”
“Why not?”
“Because I don’t want to hear it.”
“It’s not because you’re embarrassed, is it?”
He was right.
That was why I’d been trying so hard to ignore the way Hyuk Mujin kept staring at me.
“It’s just...”
“Just?”
“I somehow felt concerned, so I stuck my nose in where it didn’t belong.
That’s all.”
The words I’d said to Jin Mukyung through the door were also the conclusion I’d reached after a long time thinking about it.
I didn’t know if it was the right answer.
If it could comfort him even a little right now, that was enough.
In the end, time and experience solved most problems.
An answer wasn’t something someone else could hand you.
You had to find it yourself.
*For him, this is only the first step.*
He was an unparalleled genius born of the Jin Family of Taiyuan, and in this world, at least, he was my older brother.
But Jin Mukyung was only in his mid-twenties.
He’d spent his life honing his martial arts.
He could count his experiences in real combat on one hand, and he wasn’t used to the loss that came with them.
If a few embarrassing words could bring him even a little comfort, I’d say them dozens or hundreds of times.
Jin Mukyung’s heart and his feet were pointed toward the righteous path, without a hair’s breadth of deviation.
The more he grew, the more livable the world would become.
*Walk.
Don’t sit down.
Keep walking, and walking, and walking.*
At the end of that road was an answer.
There was light.
I believed that.
With all my heart.
“But, Captain.
Can I tell you something?”
“What?”
“This is the wrong way.
If we keep going, we’ll hit a dead end.”
I was silent for a moment, then looked at Hyuk Mujin in disbelief.
“Wait...
Why are you only telling me now, you bastard?”
“Well, you suddenly got this intense look in your eyes and started making a cool face.”
I wanted to hit him.
I really did.
Too much had happened over the past three days for me to tell Jin Mukyung everything.
A great battle, with tens of thousands of allies and enemies tangled together.
Three days had already passed since the people of Shanxi won their great victory, but the battle had left a staggering mess behind.
When uninvited guests show up and leave a place filthy and wrecked, the cleanup falls to the homeowner.
From the day of our victory, Jin Wikyung had more work than ten people could handle.
Before he’d even recovered from the battle, he had to begin dealing with its aftermath.
Of course, the people around him weren’t going to stand by and let him do that.
“I’m going to give the Lesser Family Head three choices.
Hear them all before you pick one.”
The first to step in was the Medicine King Hall Master.
At a glance, he looked like a stubborn old man.
But with a menacing gleam in his eyes that didn’t match his calm tone, he glanced back and forth between the long needle in his hand and Jin Wikyung, then said:
“You can keep ignoring my orders and working until you ruin your health and die.
Or you can get treated now, take it easy, and live a long life.
Or, if you’d rather not drag it out, you can die by my hand.
Which will it be?”
Only then did Jin Wikyung begin to get some proper rest.
Everyone who’d witnessed the exchange fiercely debated what they’d seen behind his back.
Had his face gone as pale as a corpse’s from exhaustion, or from the Medicine King Hall Master’s long needle?
Hyuk Mujin put it plainly.
“The needle.
No question.
Didn’t you see that old man’s eyes?
If he hadn’t studied medicine, he’d have a position in Dark Heaven by now.”
What mattered was that Jin Wikyung had relented.
Others had helped make that possible, too.
“That quack who calls himself the Medicine King Hall Master is absolutely right.
You focus on recovering.
The others will take care of what’s left.”
We’d won the battle on the Double Ninth Festival, but we still couldn’t be sure every threat was gone.
Even so, the presence of a giant like the Fire King, Jeok Cheongang, was enough to wash away the slightest worry.
So was the Bow Saint, who had finally appeared before people again after decades.
“I’ll go to Hebei.”
The Bow Saint left as soon as the battle ended, with only those few words.

Peng Cheolyeong—the Thunderbolt Saber King’s son, the current Family Head of the Hebei Peng Family, and the Iron Blood Saber—had no choice but to take the family members fit to travel and return to Hebei with her.
It was only natural.
The North Heaven Demon Lord—no, Murong Baek—hadn’t betrayed us alone.
That meant the entire Murong Family had joined Dark Heaven.
Two days later, a messenger eagle arrived at the Jin Family of Taiyuan with news confirming part of what we’d suspected.
“As we expected, there was trouble in Hebei.”
Several people had forced Jin Wikyung to rest, but getting the paperwork out of his hands was nearly impossible.
The instant the messenger eagle arrived at the Jin Family of Taiyuan, Jin Wikyung received the news.
He immediately called me in and told me what had happened in Hebei.
“It seems the Murong Family targeted both Shanxi and Hebei from the start.
They used their offer to support us as a pretext to cross Hebei, leaving some of their forces behind to ambush the Peng Family.”
The bloodshed on the Double Ninth Festival hadn’t been confined to Shanxi Province.
The Hebei Peng Family had been caught completely off guard by the Murong Family’s betrayal.
With the Thunderbolt Saber King and many of their strongest masters away, they’d suffered heavy losses and had barely managed to defend their family home, fighting to the death.
“But even that would only have bought them time.
If everything had been delayed by two days, something irreversible would have happened.”
But just as the family stood on the brink of ruin, Peng Cheolyeong, its Family Head, finally arrived.
Peng Cheolyeong announced himself with a roar.

chapters.title: Chapter 983
paragraphs: By the time the thousand Embroidered Uniform Guards led by Jeong Hogun crossed Hebei and reached Liaoning Province, everyone in the region knew the truth. Not just the martial artists—even the common people.
The nomads’ invasion. The Murong Family’s betrayal.
And, finally, Dark Heaven lurking behind it all.
Not even the most hot-blooded martial artist dared stand in the Embroidered Uniform Guard’s way. There were two main reasons.
First was the force and authority of the Embroidered Uniform Guard, among the Great Nation’s finest troops. Second was the banner flying beside the imperial flag.
The Murim Alliance.

Even a renowned veteran of the martial world who had loudly insisted that martial artists should handle Murim affairs themselves would have had no choice but to accept it quietly before the Murim Alliance’s towering banner.
The two great powers guiding the world had joined forces. All that remained was to punish the Murong Family.
Before long, everyone’s attention turned to one place.
Shenyang, Liaoning Province.
The Murong Family’s ancestral estate. They had once thundered across the continent with a charging spear and a composite bow and founded a nation.
Now they faced ruin.
“Surround it.”
Thud-thud-thud-thud!
Jeong Hogun’s terse command shook the earth.
There was no need for all thousand Embroidered Uniform Guards to take action.

The authority of the Marquis of Shangshan, personally appointed by the Son of Heaven not long ago, was vast enough to encompass the entire northern frontier. And when the Embroidered Uniform Guard—the force said to knock birds from the sky—arrived, Liaoning Province’s City Lord had rushed out to greet them and immediately surrendered all the military authority at his disposal.
Thud. Thud. Thud.
The first thousand cavalrymen galloped out to surround the Murong Family estate. Heavily armored infantry filled every gap with shields, spears, and swords.
Finally, the archers took their positions. Everything was ready.
Like any Murim family on the frontier, the Murong Family estate was a fortress made by nature itself. And now it was sealed off without a single gap.
Grrrrrr.
With a heavy grinding sound, the iron gate slowly began to open.
A man dressed in white as snow appeared beyond it. Jeong Hogun spoke.
“Loose.”
There was not a moment’s hesitation in the order.
The archers were already in formation, ready to fire.
Fwoosh!
For an instant, part of the sky turned black. Hundreds of arrows tore through the air toward the man in white, and he hastily swung his sword.
Clang-clang-clang!
Steel struck steel, scattering sparks.
When the rain of arrows had swept past the gate, the man stood there looking shaken. From behind him came anguished cries.
“Young Master!”
“You mustn’t! Please, come back!”
“What are you doing? Bring the Young Master back—!”
Instead of answering, the man waved them back. He bit his lip, fixed his gaze on Jeong Hogun in the distance, and took a heavy step forward.
Step.
Jeong Hogun watched him in silence, then spoke again.
“Loose.”
Another rain of arrows fell. The sword flashed.
This time, blood spattered the ground.
Drip. Drip.
The shoulder pierced by an arrow twitched, but the man kept walking. He did not stop even when arrows from the third volley drove into him in several places.
Thwack!
At last, his knees buckled. His once-white clothes had long since turned red.
The family retainers could bear it no longer and rushed out through the gate. Yet there was not a trace of pain in his shout.
“Stop! Have you all forgotten my orders?”
“B-but—!”
“Don’t come any closer! Whatever happens, you must not act rashly!”
The family members who had started to run through the gate clenched their teeth and stopped.
The man gave a small nod, then leaned on his sword and staggered to his feet.
At last, he faced Jeong Hogun, who was riding slowly toward him.
“We finally meet. It seems risking my life was worth it.”
Jeong Hogun looked down at him quietly from the saddle.
Up close, he could see that the man was barely twenty.
“Are you of the Murong bloodline?”
“I am. My father committed an unforgivable wrong.”
They said blood could not lie.
Looking at the young man’s distinctly foreign features, Jeong Hogun suddenly recalled a face he had seen while collecting the dead, just after the fierce battle around Eight Spring Gorge had ended.
“Then you’re Murong Baek’s...?”
“His seventh son, born in his old age. The son of a father burdened with sin.”
The young man answered calmly and cupped his hands in greeting.
“I am Murong Su, the Murong Family’s Seventh Young Master. I greet you, Thousand Captain Jeong.”
“You know me.”
“I have eyes and ears. I’d heard you were coming.”
“Then why did you stay?”
“If I fled like my elder brothers, I would be admitting that I was a traitor and an enemy of Murim.”
“Staying changes nothing. But let’s hear your second reason.”
The young man, Murong Su, lowered his hands and lifted his head.
His gaze at Jeong Hogun was clear, and his voice was calm.
“Someone has to take responsibility, don’t they?”
“...Responsibility.”
“I’m the only direct descendant left at the estate. Everyone involved has either died or fled.”
Jeong Hogun studied him in silence beneath the brim of his helmet, then looked past his shoulder.
“Then who are those people who stayed with you?”
“I don’t know if you’ll believe me, but they, too, were betrayed by my father. And they aren’t people who could really be called members of the Murong bloodline.”
Jeong Hogun could guess who they were.

People so isolated within the family that they could never have learned the truth. Distant branches of distant branches, perhaps, or people who had never fit in. There would also be former guests who had become part of the Murong Family without sharing a drop of its blood.
All but one.
“Did you not know about your father’s crimes, either?”
“I can’t say I knew. Nor can I say I didn’t. I had only a vague feeling that something was wrong.”
“And?”
“I simply watched from a distance.”
“Was it your affection for your own blood?”
“I don’t know when I was ever considered part of the Murong Family. My mother was a barbarian, my birth lowly, and my martial talent nothing worth speaking of...”
Murong Su smiled bitterly.
“But one thing I do know. Saving those who remain is the best I can do.”
“So in the end, you’re the only one left. Murong Su, Murong Baek’s son. A traitor’s blood.”
“That’s right. So, the others—”
“Execute them on the spot.”
At Jeong Hogun’s firm interruption, all color drained from Murong Su’s face.
“What do you—”

“The Murong Family Head, Murong Baek, and his family colluded with foreign enemies, disrupted the order of the Great Nation, and caused immense harm throughout the northern frontier. This was clearly an act of treason. Not the slightest mercy can be shown in punishing it.”
“Thousand Captain!”
Blood mingled with the cry he forced out.
Crack. Murong Su snapped the arrows lodged in his body, his face contorted with anguish.
“I told you! They—they...!”
He coughed up blood and fell to his knees before he could finish.
The retainers, who had watched it all from a distance, could bear no more. They rushed out through the iron gate.
“Young Master!”
“No! The Young Master has done nothing wrong!”
As they ran toward him, crying out in desperation, Jeong Hogun slowly raised a hand.
In Murong Su’s wide eyes, hundreds of archers drew their bowstrings taut.
There was no choice left.
One small gesture. Or one short command.
That would end it. Everything.
“N-no! Please, stop!”
Murong Su’s desperate plea burst out with a spray of dark red blood.
And then, a hoarse old voice spoke from behind Jeong Hogun.
“People only show their true hearts when their lives are in danger. Don’t you agree, Thousand Captain of the Embroidered Uniform Guard?”
The speaker was a small old man with dark skin and distinctive features unlike those of a Han man.
But what made him truly unusual was his mount. He rode neither a horse nor a mule, but a person.
A huge man who might have rivaled a bear.
“Taishan can’t understand what you’re saying. Has Namho gone senile?”
“Damn you. Not again.”
The old man, Namho, was unfazed.
As if he had been waiting for the moment, he pulled out a chunk of jerky and stuffed it into Taishan’s mouth. Then he nodded toward Jeong Hogun.
“Anyway. In this old man’s opinion, this is probably enough for now. What do you think?”
Jeong Hogun thought for a moment, then lowered his hand.
As his fingers slowly relaxed, hundreds of taut bowstrings lowered in silence.
“We’ll take them into custody and bring them to the government office first. Their fate will be decided after a thorough interrogation.”
“Do that. An old man like me couldn’t stop you from going that far. They should be grateful for even that much.”
Namho shrugged and patted the top of Taishan’s head.
The huge man crouched, bringing Namho roughly eye to eye with Murong Su. The young man could only blink, still unable to make sense of what was happening.
“You said your name was Murong Su?”
“Y-yes. But who are you, sir?”
“No need to know an old man’s name. Just know that I belong to the Murim Alliance.”
“The Murim Alliance...!”
“Oh, one more thing. Right now, I also represent the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon—no, the Marquis of Shangshan.”
Namho smiled bitterly at Murong Su’s face, which had gone stiff as stone.
“Don’t look so surprised. I’m only offering you a chance.”
“A chance...?”
“Yes. A chance for those who haven’t strayed from the orthodox path.”
Namho knew.
No—Jin Taekyung knew.
There was light even in deep darkness, and darkness even in the brightest light.
That was why Jin Taekyung had sent Namho here.
There was more than one way to eliminate a future threat. If what remained was not diseased plants but strong, green shoots, there was no reason to pull them up by the roots.
*If we’re the orthodox faction, shouldn’t we at least live up to the name?*
Remembering what Jin Taekyung had said before leaving the Jin Family of Taiyuan, Namho smiled faintly.
Then he addressed Murong Su and all the others who had come running, though barely a hundred of them remained.
“From this moment on, the Murong Family no longer exists.”
“Those who abandoned benevolence and righteousness and strayed from the orthodox path can no longer belong to the Murim Alliance’s orthodox factions, nor can they be a great family.”
His voice carried a force that seemed impossible for someone so small. Though he had put not a trace of internal energy into it, every word reached their ears clearly.
“But if any among you still walk the right path, the Murim Alliance will not cast you aside. That is the right thing to do.”
Namho looked straight at Murong Su.
“As I said, the Murong Family no longer exists. The Murong household, however, is another matter.”
This was not his decision alone. Every sect in the north and the Murim Alliance had agreed to it.
“If your innocence is proven in the future, the Murong family will have another chance to prove itself under a new Family Head.”
At that moment, the hundred or so members of the family trembled.

They had thought everything was over. Now they had one last chance to clear their names and prove themselves—all because of the sacrifice and courage of the one man who had not abandoned them to the very end.
“Young Master!”
No longer retainers of the Murong Family but of the Murong household, they surrounded Murong Su with fervent voices and shining eyes.
The man they would soon call Family Head.
As Namho watched the scene with a calm gaze, he suddenly remembered something he had forgotten and smiled faintly.
The Five Great Families.
Together with the Nine Sects and One Gang, they were the fifteen pillars holding up the vast world of the Nine Provinces.
He already knew who would fill the vacant fifth seat left by the fall of the Murong name.
No—in fact, all the martial world knew.

Yet there was not a trace of pain in his shout.
“Stop!
Have you all forgotten my orders?”
“B-but—!”
“Don’t come any closer!
Whatever happens, you must not act rashly!”
The family members who had started to run through the gate clenched their teeth and stopped.
The man gave a small nod, then leaned on his sword and staggered to his feet.
At last, he faced Jeong Hogun, who was riding slowly toward him.
“We finally meet.
It seems risking my life was worth it.”
Jeong Hogun looked down at him quietly from the saddle.
Up close, he could see that the man was barely twenty.
“Are you of the Murong bloodline?”
“I am.
My father committed an unforgivable wrong.”
They said blood could not lie.
Looking at the young man’s distinctly foreign features, Jeong Hogun suddenly recalled a face he had seen while collecting the dead, just after the fierce battle around Eight Spring Gorge had ended.
“Then you’re Murong Baek’s...?”
“His seventh son, born in his old age.
The son of a father burdened with sin.”
The young man answered calmly and cupped his hands in greeting.
“I am Murong Su, the Murong Family’s Seventh Young Master.
I greet you, Thousand Captain Jeong.”
“You know me.”
“I have eyes and ears.
I’d heard you were coming.”
“Then why did you stay?”
“If I fled like my elder brothers, I would be admitting that I was a traitor and an enemy of Murim.”
“Staying changes nothing.
But let’s hear your second reason.”
The young man, Murong Su, lowered his hands and lifted his head.
His gaze at Jeong Hogun was clear, and his voice was calm.
“Someone has to take responsibility, don’t they?”
“...Responsibility.”
“I’m the only direct descendant left at the estate.
Everyone involved has either died or fled.”
Jeong Hogun studied him in silence beneath the brim of his helmet, then looked past his shoulder.
“Then who are those people who stayed with you?”
“I don’t know if you’ll believe me, but they, too, were betrayed by my father.
And they aren’t people who could really be called members of the Murong bloodline.”
Jeong Hogun could guess who they were.
People so isolated within the family that they could never have learned the truth.
Distant branches of distant branches, perhaps, or people who had never fit in.
There would also be former guests who had become part of the Murong Family without sharing a drop of its blood.
All but one.
“Did you not know about your father’s crimes, either?”
“I can’t say I knew.
Nor can I say I didn’t.
I had only a vague feeling that something was wrong.”
“And?”
“I simply watched from a distance.”
“Was it your affection for your own blood?”
“I don’t know when I was ever considered part of the Murong Family.
My mother was a barbarian, my birth lowly, and my martial talent nothing worth speaking of...”
Murong Su smiled bitterly.
“But one thing I do know.
Saving those who remain is the best I can do.”
“So in the end, you’re the only one left.
Murong Su, Murong Baek’s son.
A traitor’s blood.”
“That’s right.
So, the others—”
“Execute them on the spot.”
At Jeong Hogun’s firm interruption, all color drained from Murong Su’s face.
“What do you—”
“The Murong Family Head, Murong Baek, and his family colluded with foreign enemies, disrupted the order of the Great Nation, and caused immense harm throughout the northern frontier.
This was clearly an act of treason.
Not the slightest mercy can be shown in punishing it.”
“Thousand Captain!”
Blood mingled with the cry he forced out.
Crack.
Murong Su snapped the arrows lodged in his body, his face contorted with anguish.
“I told you!
They—they...!”
He coughed up blood and fell to his knees before he could finish.
The retainers, who had watched it all from a distance, could bear no more.
They rushed out through the iron gate.
“Young Master!”
“No!
The Young Master has done nothing wrong!”
As they ran toward him, crying out in desperation, Jeong Hogun slowly raised a hand.
In Murong Su’s wide eyes, hundreds of archers drew their bowstrings taut.
There was no choice left.
One small gesture.
Or one short command.
That would end it.
Everything.
“N-no!
Please, stop!”
Murong Su’s desperate plea burst out with a spray of dark red blood.
And then, a hoarse old voice spoke from behind Jeong Hogun.
“People only show their true hearts when their lives are in danger.
Don’t you agree, Thousand Captain of the Embroidered Uniform Guard?”
The speaker was a small old man with dark skin and distinctive features unlike those of a Han man.
But what made him truly unusual was his mount.
He rode neither a horse nor a mule, but a person.
A huge man who might have rivaled a bear.
“Taishan can’t understand what you’re saying.
Has Namho gone senile?”
“Damn you.
Not again.”
The old man, Namho, was unfazed.
As if he had been waiting for the moment, he pulled out a chunk of jerky and stuffed it into Taishan’s mouth.
Then he nodded toward Jeong Hogun.
“Anyway.
In this old man’s opinion, this is probably enough for now.
What do you think?”
Jeong Hogun thought for a moment, then lowered his hand.
As his fingers slowly relaxed, hundreds of taut bowstrings lowered in silence.
“We’ll take them into custody and bring them to the government office first.
Their fate will be decided after a thorough interrogation.”
“Do that.
An old man like me couldn’t stop you from going that far.
They should be grateful for even that much.”
Namho shrugged and patted the top of Taishan’s head.
The huge man crouched, bringing Namho roughly eye to eye with Murong Su.
The young man could only blink, still unable to make sense of what was happening.
“You said your name was Murong Su?”
“Y-yes.
But who are you, sir?”
“No need to know an old man’s name.
Just know that I belong to the Murim Alliance.”
“The Murim Alliance...!”
“Oh, one more thing.
Right now, I also represent the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon—no, the Marquis of Shangshan.”
Namho smiled bitterly at Murong Su’s face, which had gone stiff as stone.
“Don’t look so surprised.
I’m only offering you a chance.”
“A chance...?”
“Yes.
A chance for those who haven’t strayed from the orthodox path.”
Namho knew.
No—Jin Taekyung knew.
There was light even in deep darkness, and darkness even in the brightest light.
That was why Jin Taekyung had sent Namho here.
There was more than one way to eliminate a future threat.
If what remained was not diseased plants but strong, green shoots, there was no reason to pull them up by the roots.
*If we’re the orthodox faction, shouldn’t we at least live up to the name?*
Remembering what Jin Taekyung had said before leaving the Jin Family of Taiyuan, Namho smiled faintly.
Then he addressed Murong Su and all the others who had come running, though barely a hundred of them remained.
“From this moment on, the Murong Family no longer exists.”
“Those who abandoned benevolence and righteousness and strayed from the orthodox path can no longer belong to the Murim Alliance’s orthodox factions, nor can they be a great family.”
His voice carried a force that seemed impossible for someone so small.
Though he had put not a trace of internal energy into it, every word reached their ears clearly.
“But if any among you still walk the right path, the Murim Alliance will not cast you aside.
That is the right thing to do.”
Namho looked straight at Murong Su.
“As I said, the Murong Family no longer exists.
The Murong household, however, is another matter.”
This was not his decision alone.
Every sect in the north and the Murim Alliance had agreed to it.
“If your innocence is proven in the future, the Murong family will have another chance to prove itself under a new Family Head.”
At that moment, the hundred or so members of the family trembled.
They had thought everything was over.
Now they had one last chance to clear their names and prove themselves—all because of the sacrifice and courage of the one man who had not abandoned them to the very end.
“Young Master!”
No longer retainers of the Murong Family but of the Murong household, they surrounded Murong Su with fervent voices and shining eyes.
The man they would soon call Family Head.
As Namho watched the scene with a calm gaze, he suddenly remembered something he had forgotten and smiled faintly.
The Five Great Families.
Together with the Nine Sects and One Gang, they were the fifteen pillars holding up the vast world of the Nine Provinces.
He already knew who would fill the vacant fifth seat left by the fall of the Murong name.
No—in fact, all the martial world knew.

chapters.title: Chapter 984
paragraphs: The saying that words without feet can travel a thousand *ri* was wrong. They could travel ten thousand—or even farther—in the blink of an eye.
The chain of events in the north spread with astonishing speed, and without end.
From person to person, on the beating wings of messenger eagles, and on the pounding hooves of horses driven by messengers’ hurried whips.
Before long, the fallout from the truth that had come to light was enough to shake the entire Central Plains.
“How could the Murong Family...!”
“That’s impossible. It can’t be true!”
Disbelief was the first reaction of the martial artists who heard the news.
Of course it was.

The traitors exposed before the whole world weren’t groups rooted in demonic, heterodox arts, like the Yangtze River Channel League or the Green Forest Alliance. They were none other than the Murong Family.
One of the Five Great Families.
Though based at the very edge of the north, it was a great family in the truest sense, renowned from the vast lands of Liaoning all the way to the Central Plains.
And yet that very Murong Family had supposedly joined forces with Dark Heaven.
Worse, it wasn’t the work of a handful of rogue members. Most of the family, including its Family Head, Murong Baek, had been involved.
The shock this unbelievable news dealt to those who heard it was beyond words.
“The Family Head, the Divine Spear of the Imugi, distinguished himself in the Great Faction War. Why would he—or the Murong Family—do such a thing...?”
But their disbelief lasted only a moment.
The Beggars’ Sect, the Lower District Sect, Huashan, and the Hebei Peng Family—
and the Murim Alliance, the heart of the martial world—
all officially confirmed that every word of it was true, without the slightest falsehood.
Even the giant beyond the martial world—who existed, yet might as well not have—confirmed it.
“Clear the way!”
Groups of government soldiers, some numbering dozens and others hundreds, swept through the land.

For so long, they had spent their days leaning against their spears, their faces slack with the ease of a lasting peace. Now, fully armed, they carried out their orders with sharp eyes beneath their helmets, watching every direction.
“Hey, what’s going on?”
“How should I know? But with things this tense, I’d guess it has something to do with whatever happened in the Imperial Capital recently.”
“Oh, I heard about that too. You mean those bastards called Dark Heaven? I heard from a martial artist I know that they went on another rampage...”
This wasn’t happening in just one place.
Seeing the soldiers’ sudden change in demeanor, people gathered, both bewildered and on edge.
Before long, they read the proclamations the soldiers had posted all around before leaving.
Let it be known to all under Heaven, to all the people:

That was how the proclamation began. Men of letters in every province had written it in a single flowing hand. Pressed forward under the crowd’s gaze, the scholars reading it aloud found their voices trembling more and more as the recitation went on.
“...Th-therefore, I shall join forces with the martial men outside government service to make an example of the traitorous band known as Dark Heaven. This is my will and Heaven’s decree.”
Even after the lengthy recitation ended, the gathering remained silent as the grave.
Those who understood the sudden proclamation stared wide-eyed, like the scholars reading it. The country folk who didn’t understand glanced about and whispered under their breath.
“What in the world does that mean?”
“I don’t rightly know. Seems like ‘martial men who don’t belong to the government’ means martial artists, though... Couldn’t they just say it plain? Why’d they have to write it so fancy?”
They lived from day to day, earning only enough to eat.

They had been born with little chance to learn anything but hard work and how to use their bodies. Their pockets were always light, while their shoulders bore the weight of a thousand *geun*. How could they be expected to read a line of writing?
But there were always people who couldn’t stand silence or ignorance.

“It is an imperial decree personally issued by His Majesty. He has declared Dark Heaven a band of traitors and announced to all his people that he will join forces with the martial artists of the world to punish them.”
Only then did people look down.
Beneath the tiny letters was a clear imprint of a seal.
It was the mark of the imperial seal, reserved for only one person in all the vast Nine Provinces—one that countless people had never even seen.
Even those who couldn’t read could tell at a glance that it was no ordinary seal.
“This is more serious than I expected. They’re even borrowing the martial world’s swords and spears.”
At the young scholar’s sudden remark, someone else murmured with a sigh.
“I’ve heard all the rumors about Dark Heaven, but... I never thought it was this bad.”
The first to hear news from every corner of the world were martial artists and merchants.
People outside those circles rarely had their ear to the ground unless they had special connections. And even when something happened, they generally saw no reason to worry.
The Great Nation stood on a firm foundation.
The countless purges and provincial warlord rebellions that had followed its founding were long over.

With the passage of time, the world had settled into peace. Even during the calamity some fifty years ago that martial artists called the Great Faction War, the common people had suffered almost no harm.
Why?
It was simple.
Even the fanatics from far to the west, who bore the chilling name of the Demonic Cult, had feared the Great Nation joining the war.
They had wanted it to be seen as nothing more than a struggle between martial-world factions.
But...
“This time will be different. Different from any other.”

When Shaolin Temple’s Abbot, once likened to a living Buddha, entered nirvana and the grounds where only the peaceful sound of wooden fish had once echoed ran red with blood, no one there had felt anything beyond sorrow.

It was the same when they heard that the Daoists of Qingcheng and Emei, who seemed like immortals, had fallen, and that the Sichuan Tang Clan—whose people had a reputation for being a fearsome bunch even among ordinary folk—had suffered terrible losses.
That was the Murim everyone knew.
In that cruel forest, where spears and swords ran wild in place of green trees, even venerable monks and Daoists could die at any moment.
No, there was another reason they had watched it all without much concern.
*Whatever happens, surely nothing will happen to us.*
They lived in different worlds, behind different walls.
The people had entrusted their safety to the Great Nation’s walls. All they had done was watch the martial artists fight their fierce battles in their own domain.
Now and then, they pitied the unlucky common folk caught up in Murim affairs and killed. But that was all.
A fire blazing hundreds of *li* away couldn’t warm everyone.
The people’s feelings and interest burned hot for a moment, then quickly cooled.
Compared to the whole, the victims were only a handful. The rest could wake up tomorrow just fine.
They had the Great Nation, a great and sturdy wall.
But that unshakable faith was crumbling at that very moment.
“W-wait, sirs. Then what you’re saying is...”
Gulp.
The village elder couldn’t finish. He only swallowed dryly, and the old scholar spoke in his place.
He spoke the truth no one wanted to believe or even hear.
The truth they had no choice but to face.
“That’s right. It’s exactly what you think.”
He let out a quiet sigh.
The old scholar looked down at his wrinkled hands, etched with the marks of time.
He remembered when they had been white and smooth.
He remembered his younger self, with so many possibilities before him, unable to go any farther because an age of chaos refused to end. He remembered those turbulent years.
Slowly, he continued.
“The war has already begun.”
Some clenched their teeth and fists. Others squeezed their eyes shut.
Soundless shock surged through the crowd like a wave.
The word *war* spread in every direction, carried in wide-open eyes and slackened lips.
Along broad avenues, through narrow, dark alleys, and with the hurried footsteps of those rushing to carry the unbelievable news onward.
War.
The flames of a great war that would burn everything.
At that moment, the old scholar saw it.
The darkness that had slumbered for so many years had finally awoken, painting everyone’s faces with despair.
And suddenly, he repeated in his mind an unfamiliar name from the proclamation bearing the Son of Heaven’s command.
Jin Taekyung of the Jin Family of Taiyuan.
No—the Marquis of Shangshan, Jin Taekyung.
The foremost contributor to stopping this rebellion, a martial artist still so young, yet raised to the rank of marquis.
*I don’t know much about the affairs of the martial world... but one thing is certain.*

The old scholar had once served in government. He could guess well enough what future awaited that young martial artist, who had achieved something without precedent—and something that would never happen again.
*I don’t know who you are, but please, give it everything you have and keep moving forward. Not only for the Murim you’ve always known, but for this country as well.*
Though his words would never reach him, the old scholar bowed toward the proclamation.
First, to the Son of Heaven, who watched over all things from the distant Imperial Capital.
Second, to the countless heroic souls who would shed their blood and fall to protect this world.
And lastly, to the new marquis who stood at the heart of the martial world by virtue of the solemn imperial decree.
The old scholar continued to bow.
In full view of the crowd, he did so silently, offering all the respect and sincerity he could.
And thousands of *li* away, in a narrow gorge, bright yellow chrysanthemums colored the landscape in every direction.
I’d heard of the Double Ninth Festival a few times in passing, but that was about all I knew.

As a Korean born and raised, I’d always observed the big holidays like Lunar New Year and Chuseok. But I didn’t have so much time on my hands that I could take an interest in the customs of those guys on the continent.
Today, though, I followed the customs of the Double Ninth Festival too.
I held more bright yellow chrysanthemums than my arms could contain, and awkwardly wore a pouch of cornelian berries at my side.
It was a way to honor those who had passed before they could celebrate the Double Ninth Festival themselves.
And we had to keep moving forward, leaving their sacrifice behind us.
*Whoosh.*
Wind from far away stirred the chrysanthemums in my arms.
It came out of nowhere and tugged insistently at them, as if taking them by the hand. Several petals, large and small, gave in and went along with it.
Before long, they fluttered through the air like a rain of flowers.
Riding the wind, they swam through the twists and turns of the Eight Spring Gorge, as those who had lived on this land long ago had named it.
*Ah.*
I swallowed the exclamation that almost escaped me.
It was beautiful and, at the same time, unbearably sad.
I wasn’t the only one who felt it. Tens of thousands of people filled the Eight Spring Gorge, and I knew they felt it too.

Watching the yellow petals fall, I found myself wondering: Even now, as they drifted farther and farther away with the wind, were they only petals? Or were they the souls of those who had willingly thrown away their lives to protect what they cherished?
There was no single right answer.
There was no need to find one.
We could believe whatever we wanted to believe. Someday, we would return here and remember them.
Each in our own way.
With laughter. With chrysanthemums and cornelian berries.
Or...
With tears.
Drip. Drip, drip.
Senses far beyond human limits sometimes told me things I didn’t want to know.
Like the tears wetting the leather shoes of a man whose head was bowed and whose body was trembling slightly.
No. Raindrops.
*Yeah. That’s how it is.*
I quietly looked up at the sky.
I couldn’t bring myself to look at Jin Wikyung like that, or at Lee Seowol silently mourning the death of her uncle, who had been her strongest support, or at the countless others in tears.
*Whoosh.*
The wind blew again.
The rain of flowers rose high, then fell around everyone as if to comfort them.
Yet beneath a sky clearer than ever, countless raindrops kept falling.
The Double Ninth Festival had passed, but the chrysanthemums hadn’t withered.
I knew that those who had left and those who remained were all here together.
And I knew that because of them, the road ahead had grown wider and brighter.
*Ding.*
A clear chime rang through the sky, mingling with the rain of flowers.

I held more bright yellow chrysanthemums than my arms could contain, and awkwardly wore a pouch of cornelian berries at my side.
It was a way to honor those who had passed before they could celebrate the Double Ninth Festival themselves.
And we had to keep moving forward, leaving their sacrifice behind us.
*Whoosh.*
Wind from far away stirred the chrysanthemums in my arms.
It came out of nowhere and tugged insistently at them, as if taking them by the hand.
Several petals, large and small, gave in and went along with it.
Before long, they fluttered through the air like a rain of flowers.
Riding the wind, they swam through the twists and turns of the Eight Spring Gorge, as those who had lived on this land long ago had named it.
*Ah.*
I swallowed the exclamation that almost escaped me.
It was beautiful and, at the same time, unbearably sad.
I wasn’t the only one who felt it.
Tens of thousands of people filled the Eight Spring Gorge, and I knew they felt it too.
Watching the yellow petals fall, I found myself wondering: Even now, as they drifted farther and farther away with the wind, were they only petals?
Or were they the souls of those who had willingly thrown away their lives to protect what they cherished?
There was no single right answer.
There was no need to find one.
We could believe whatever we wanted to believe.
Someday, we would return here and remember them.
Each in our own way.
With laughter.
With chrysanthemums and cornelian berries.
Or...
With tears.
Drip.
Drip, drip.
Senses far beyond human limits sometimes told me things I didn’t want to know.
Like the tears wetting the leather shoes of a man whose head was bowed and whose body was trembling slightly.
No.
Raindrops.
*Yeah.
That’s how it is.*
I quietly looked up at the sky.
I couldn’t bring myself to look at Jin Wikyung like that, or at Lee Seowol silently mourning the death of her uncle, who had been her strongest support, or at the countless others in tears.
*Whoosh.*
The wind blew again.
The rain of flowers rose high, then fell around everyone as if to comfort them.
Yet beneath a sky clearer than ever, countless raindrops kept falling.
The Double Ninth Festival had passed, but the chrysanthemums hadn’t withered.
I knew that those who had left and those who remained were all here together.
And I knew that because of them, the road ahead had grown wider and brighter.
*Ding.*
A clear chime rang through the sky, mingling with the rain of flowers.

chapters.title: Chapter 985
paragraphs: Leaving behind countless tears and a ceaseless rain of petals, tens of thousands of people—martial artists and ordinary folk alike—departed Eight Spring Gorge and returned to their places.
The memorial for the departed, and the belated Double Ninth Festival, had come to an end. But those who remained had to keep moving forward, toward tomorrow and the day after.
And when we returned to the Jin Family of Taiyuan, more than the few family members left behind in case of an emergency were waiting for us.
“My name is Huang. I serve, though inadequately, as a Hall Master of the Murim Alliance. I’ve come to deliver a message from the Alliance Leader.”
The Murim Alliance’s envoy introduced himself with impeccable courtesy, and everyone’s gaze turned toward the three of us brothers.
More precisely, toward Jin Wikyung.
“I see.”
His voice was calm, though the corners of his eyes were still red.
As if welcoming a guest he had long expected, Jin Wikyung calmly led the envoy inside.
“Before we talk, please come in and rest after your journey.”
“I’m deeply grateful for your consideration, Great Hero Jin.”
In that moment, an unmistakable emotion passed over the faces of the Jin Family of Taiyuan’s senior members and the Sect Leaders under its protection.
It wasn’t only because the envoy bowed so deeply, with genuine respect and reverence.
*Great Hero.*
Just two words, but they carried a special weight.

This wasn’t some nobody, one of those self-important fools forever puffing each other up. A renowned master of the martial world, entrusted with the important position of Hall Master in the Murim Alliance, had come as an envoy and addressed him that way.
*Everything is changing.*
I, too, felt the weight of it all over again.
Jin Wikyung was no longer the Lesser Family Head who had led a fading family in place of a father whose whereabouts were unknown. Nor was he merely a young martial artist.
He was the ruler of Shanxi Province, another Alliance Leader recognized by everyone in this land.
No, now he was...
“What are you thinking about so hard?”
At Hyuk Mujin’s sudden question in my ear, I shook my head.
“Nothing.”
“Doesn’t look like nothing.”
“Mujin.”
“Yes?”
“Want me to make your life a living hell?”
“...No. I was just going to tell you to hurry up and follow them. You were standing there by yourself.”
Hyuk Mujin was right.
Behind Jin Wikyung, who strode forward with confidence, came the Murim Alliance’s envoy, the family’s senior members, and the Sect Leaders under the Jin Family of Taiyuan, including Lee Seowol.
Their faces held a mixture of grief that had not yet faded and joy over something soon to become reality.
I watched them walk away in silence, then turned and headed in another direction.
“Huh? Where are you going?”
“No idea. Wherever I feel like.”
“What do you mean? Maybe someone else could miss it, but you of all people shouldn’t, Captain.”
“Doesn’t matter. I more or less know what they’re going to say anyway.”
“What?”
Hyuk Mujin tilted his head in confusion, then hurried after me. Hearing his footsteps behind me, I laughed softly.
At the same time, a memory came to me.
Eight Spring Gorge.
The narrow gorge that had swallowed so many lives, and the clear chime that rang out amid the rain of petals.
The holographic window that had announced yet another change.
*Ding. Ding-ding.*

**System** Since the world first began, nothing beneath the heavens has been eternal. The vast land and sea, the countless lives that dwell within them, and even the mighty power held by the rarest few are no exception. No flower stays red for ten days (*花無十日紅*), and no matter how great one’s power, it does not last ten years (*權不十年*). But when a tree’s roots run deep, its branches grow thick (*根深枝茂*). When a spring runs deep, its waters flow far (*源遠流長*). At last, it will become another world where many can dwell and find rest.
As the System had told me, the Jin Family of Taiyuan, once rotting like an ancient tree, had now become a forest.
It bore fruit at the ends of countless branches and created a lake as vast as the sea.
Though they might lack strength, the people I had seen and known among them had always been just and righteous.
Unlike those who had chosen the wrong path, seized by anger and greed.

**System** The Murong Family has fallen. They are no longer one of the Five Great Families. At long last, the fame of the Jin Family of Taiyuan resounds throughout the world! The fame and power of the Jin Family of Taiyuan have risen to that of a member of the Five Great Families!
The Nine Sects and One Gang. The Five Great Families.
Fifteen pillars that had upheld the martial world for hundreds of years.
And now, the Jin Family of Taiyuan had become one of those mighty pillars.
It wasn’t simply because the Murim Alliance had appointed them, or because renowned masters from across the martial world had strongly urged it.
The whole world had accepted it. They had recognized the Jin Family’s courage in standing against an army of tens of thousands.
They had recognized its resolve to protect not just Murim, but this land and its people.
And so, the provincial martial family that had once been slowly fading, its glory behind it, had come together and grown stronger than ever.

**System** The Title Scion of a Prestigious Family has been removed! You have acquired a new Title: Direct Descendant of a Prestigious Family! As your family’s standing has risen, you have gained a tremendous amount of Fame! Hidden Quest Might As Well Go All the Way to the Five Great Families successfully completed! You have earned the very rare Achievement Dad, Where Are You? Glory and blessings to the three Jin Family brothers, who overcame countless hardships and trials through their own efforts! Jin Wikyung and Jin Mukyung have been granted the effects of Amazing Natural Healing and various bonus buffs. It goes without saying that these effects will not be displayed to the individuals in question. You have acquired 10 bonus stat points as an Achievement reward! You have gained a tremendous amount of EXP! Level Up! You have gained a tremendous amount of Fame! Your name and reputation have now reached beyond Murim and across the world. You are a feudal lord appointed by the Son of Heaven, a successor of the Fire King Jeok Cheongang, and a great martial artist in your own right. Your footsteps have been inscribed in history. Martial artists have begun to speak cautiously of the glorious Title granted to only ten martial artists beneath the vast sky and its three stars. They speak of the birth of a new young king. Nothing has been decided yet. Just as the small flap of a butterfly’s wings can bring a typhoon from afar, each of your choices, big or small, will gradually change this world. But remember: time keeps moving. May you have good fortune in Murim.
The System window had been far longer than usual. It had made the changes all the more palpable, but as always, it ended with a wish for good fortune in Murim.
For the first time in a long while, there was no follow-up Quest.
And yet that was the one thing that left me uneasy, even in the peace that had finally arrived.
*What is this? I was sure something else would happen.*
It had been a long time since I’d cared about getting stronger just for the sake of it.
In the Quests that came one after another, someone’s death had been so inevitable that it might as well have been written into the bargain. And the burden I carried had grown just as heavy.
On top of that, a greater crisis than ever hung over all of Murim.
*They’re not the type to back off just because this plan failed.*
It had always been like that.

Dark Heaven had carried out numerous schemes across Murim. Since murdering the Dharma King Hong Dao and stealing Shaolin Temple’s divine artifact, the Green Jade Buddha Staff, they hadn’t made a move anyone could call a success.
And yet, in Sichuan. In Hubei.
Then Nanman, the Imperial Palace, and now even here in Shanxi Province, they had brought one blood-soaked disaster after another.
*The Murong Family’s betrayal and the nomads’ invasion were certainly huge events. But the forces Dark Heaven has revealed in the process are still far below what I expected.*
Apart from the four Demon Lords and Demon Empress who were certainly key figures within Dark Heaven, more than half the enemies we had fought so far had been traitors and underlings.
In other words, it was as if they’d recruited their forces locally.
*And they still haven’t shown themselves. Why? And why keep up this string of costly battles that lead only to failure?*
My steps had carried me onward without my noticing, but I stopped and frowned.
Then another memory came to me: part of a conversation with Murong Baek, Family Head of the Murong Family, who had met his end as the North Heaven Demon Lord.
“If that’s what you all believe, fine. There’s nothing wrong with continuing to hope.”
“What?”

“Now that I’m in this situation, I find myself wondering why the Western Heaven Demon Lord, the Southern Heaven Demon Empress, and the Eastern Heaven Demon Lord failed. How did a plan prepared so carefully for so long fall apart in an instant?”
We never found out what those incomprehensible words meant.
The North Heaven Demon Lord died without explaining them.
But even after I drove the spearhead into his heart, and even now, days after all the fighting had ended, I remembered every detail of that moment clearly.
His utterly calm voice and expression.
The North Heaven Demon Lord had been ready to die. He’d proved it moments later by drawing on even his innate qi.
*He wasn’t just saying it to shake my composure.*
I know how honest a person can become when facing certain death.
At the end of a life they’ve chosen for themselves, people don’t tell lies.
*Then why? Why say that at all?*
Of course, the North Heaven Demon Lord’s tone and manner had given me some idea.
I just hadn’t thought much about it because the possibility seemed so utterly unrealistic.
*It was as if he thought this situation had been fated from the beginning—or as if he, too, had been used...*
No matter how I looked at it, it made no sense.
After the fierce battle ended, I’d shared my thoughts with Jeok Cheongang. He’d answered more firmly than ever.
“Fate, my ass. And as much as those bastards deserve to die, you think masters that powerful grow on trees?”
“Yeah. Something does seem off, doesn’t it?”

“Lord of Heaven. No matter how powerful that bastard is, he can’t use people like them as disposable pawns. Not unless they’ve had their heads cracked open a couple of times by my Flame-Extinguishing Divine Fist.”
He was right.
There wasn’t a madman anywhere in the world who would use Supreme Peak masters as pawns.
The Bow Saint hadn’t agreed or disagreed. She’d only made an inscrutable face, but whatever she might have said probably wouldn’t have differed much from Jeok Cheongang’s answer.
*No. Then why say it at all? And what’s with this suspiciously quiet stretch of time?*
I screwed up my face and thought it over.
Had he just spouted bullshit before he died? Or had his words carried some other meaning none of us, myself included, could guess?
As I clung to that endless chain of thoughts, a familiar voice suddenly broke in.
“No wonder you never came, even after I waited all that time. So this is where you were.”
Jeok Cheongang.
His expression was heavier than ever. His voice was low and subdued as he continued.
“Come with me. There’s someone who wants to see you.”
