“I heard they lost more than thirty elite agents.
After their first and last messenger eagle, all contact was lost.”
“Damn it.
Then there’s no room for doubt.
How many enemies are we looking at?”
“That...”
Even I couldn’t bring myself to answer right away.
Namho groaned at the look on my face.
“I see.
The Hundred Thousand Demonic Disciples all over again.”
“Maybe more than that.
At least, that’s what the information I received suggests.”
More important, these enemies would be far stronger and more terrifying than the Demonic Cult’s followers had been fifty years ago.
The desert no longer belonged to the Demonic Cult.
It belonged to Dark Heaven.
They weren’t merely the successors of the Demonic Cult under a different name.
They were a new group of followers, ruled by a power incomparably stronger and more dangerous.
*Could that be why Logout was suddenly blocked?*
The thought crossed my mind, but I shook my head.
No.
That wasn’t it.
The Quest hadn’t appeared yet, because I hadn’t made my choice.
Now was the moment to make it.
“From this moment on, we’re heading west.”
Ding.
An alert sounded, announcing a new Quest.

chapters.title: Chapter 996
paragraphs: Sometimes, I wonder.
Maybe the real benefit of circulating your qi isn’t growing stronger by accumulating internal energy. Maybe it’s calming your mind.
Kwoooosh.
I had no idea how much time had passed.
I simply let myself be carried by the swift, powerful current.
At last, the wave of internal energy swept through the Eight Extraordinary Meridians and hundreds of acupoints. The moment I gathered it in, I opened my eyes to a breathless silence.
Ding.
A clear chime rang out right on cue.
As the alert confirmed that I’d successfully finished circulating my qi, I calmly examined the energy within me.
*The very best.*
The words came to mind without hesitation, and there wasn’t a shred of exaggeration in them.
That’s right.
I’m stronger now than I’ve ever been.
I’d fully absorbed the Heavenly Power Demon’s energy, which had remained inside me for quite some time without being completely assimilated, and the Thunderbolt Saber King’s as well.
*Four jiazi.*
An incredible amount of internal energy—especially considering my age and how long I’d been practicing martial arts.

A greenhorn just starting out in Murim might wonder why I’d gained only one jiazi after receiving Transmitting Internal Energy Across the Body from two old masters. But martial artists who’d reached a certain realm knew better.
Martial arts weren’t as simple as one plus one.
No matter how much internal energy you possessed, if its essence was impure, you couldn’t draw out even half of it. You couldn’t control it properly, either.
In that sense, the four jiazi of internal energy reborn through complete fusion was pure power I could control entirely.
*If the Heavenly Power Demon and the Thunderbolt Saber King had been in their usual condition when they transferred their energy, I might’ve grown even stronger, but...*
Wanting more would be greedy.
Even I, with the mysterious divine strength known as the System, had risked my life twice while undergoing Transmitting Internal Energy Across the Body.
And yet I couldn’t help feeling a little disappointed. The reason was the reality I’d faced the moment I finished circulating my qi.

**System Quest** Desert Mirage You have learned of troubling signs in Xinjiang, at the far western edge of your world. A cursed land, long separated from the Central Plains. A group is crossing the scorching desert, where nothing exists but hot sand and the blazing sun, and heading toward the center of the world. But their true nature remains hidden behind a dense mirage. Please remember. Never forget. The world—and the heavens—are changing. Nothing is set in stone. The countless enemies drawing near from far away, even now, may prove to be no more than a momentary spark. Or they may become a hellfire that brings the world to ruin. **Grade:** Supreme Peak **Restriction:** Jin Taekyung **Mission:** Head west (Incomplete) **Reward:** A large amount of EXP and Fame Follow-up Quests depending on your choice **Failure:** ???
I’d read the Quest window dozens of times already, ever since sending the Fire Dragon Pavilion members away to prepare for the perilous journey ahead.
I gestured it away from the corner of my vision and remembered the conversation I’d had with Jin Wikyung two hours earlier.
“If Dark Heaven crosses Xinjiang and cuts through the desert, as the information from the Hidden Shadow Pavilion suggests, where would it focus its attack?”

“The Murim Alliance is considering three possibilities at once. They might advance through Tibet, which could be considered part of the Outer Lands. They might target Gansu Province, where the Kongtong Sect and Black Dragon Demon Gate are holding their ground. But the most dangerous place is probably...”
“Qinghai. The Kunlun Sect, then.”

“That’s right. Kunlun Mountain is a natural fortress, but for Dark Heaven, which has its sights on the Central Plains, it’s also the first obstacle they must overcome. They won’t leave Qinghai alone.”
Shanxi Province was a remote backwater, but it was nothing compared to Qinghai, at the westernmost edge of the Central Plains.

Its highlands included terrain so rugged it was downright forbidding, making it difficult to produce abundant supplies. Commerce and industry hadn’t developed much, either, thanks to the Demonic Cult’s long hold over the desert.
Merchants would risk their lives for profit, but even they couldn’t cross a desert knowing death awaited them.
But even setting all that aside, Qinghai was an indispensable strategic stronghold from a military standpoint.
One side had to defend it. The other had to trample it underfoot to get past.
*Dark Heaven has the strength to do it. Besides, Qinghai has been overrun before.*
Over fifty years ago, the hundred thousand demonic soldiers led by the Heavenly Demon defeated the Kunlun Sect and took Qinghai. That was the beginning of the Great Faction War.
And now, that brutal history of bloodshed was about to repeat itself after all these years.
*Qinghai. Qinghai Province...*
I stared out the window, my gaze heavy.
Beyond the latticed frame, hundreds of torches swayed in the darkness that had settled without my noticing.
Night had fallen, but everyone in the Jin Family of Taiyuan was still awake.
No, it wouldn’t be just the Jin Family.
I could picture the whole of Murim in the Central Plains—including the Nine Sects and One Gang and the Five Great Families—boiling like a cauldron over hot coals.
*It’s coming. The all-out war we can’t avoid.*
The drums of war had been pounding across the land for a long time. But the countless enemies even now crossing the desert toward somewhere in the west weighed on my heart more heavily than ever.
Those who meant to defend, and those who meant to take.
A battle unlike anything we’d faced so far awaited us all in the west. Each side would stake its fate on it.
*The fate of this world might be decided by a single battle, soon to come.*
Maybe that was why the System had suddenly malfunctioned. Why this absolute law, which had never strayed from its set path no matter what happened, had begun to waver.
Then what had caught me by the ankle when I tried to leave this place for a little while—just a little while?
The System? Or...
*Dark Heaven. No—the Lord of Heaven, to be precise.*
I couldn’t be sure yet, but I could guess one thing.
Far away in the west, somewhere hidden in that pitch-black darkness, an answer to this mystery was waiting.
Or perhaps death.
*Damn it.*
Nothing ever goes smoothly.
I gave a bitter smile to myself, then spoke to someone waiting beyond the firmly shut door.
“We leave in exactly fifteen minutes.”
“As you command.”
I heard Hyuk Mujin’s footsteps receding after his unusually forceful reply. As I stood, I suddenly sensed something strange and turned around.
Tap. Tap-tap.
Something damp and white drifted into the room on the wind.
I looked at the unwelcome visitor that had arrived months ahead of schedule—the snowflakes slowly piling up—and remembered a line from the Quest window.
*The world—and the heavens—are being turned upside down.*
I prayed silently that those words, at least, weren’t an error.
Because the world as I felt it now—and the sky spilling those white snowflakes—seemed to have finished changing already.
The light in the room was dim.
It was already pitch-black outside, and the wind seeping through the crack in the door made the candle flame flicker precariously.

Yet the man reading the letter in his hand didn’t so much as twitch an eyebrow. Years of grueling training since childhood had honed his eyesight enough to distinguish its tiny writing even by a flame that looked ready to go out.
He stared at the letter he’d already read several times. In his eyes, the wavering candlelight reflected part of its message.
**Return immediately.**
The handwriting was sharp as a blade, and beside it was a familiar official seal.
Guessing who had sent the letter, he muttered softly.
“You haven’t changed, have you?”
His voice echoed hollowly, low and subdued.
The letter wasn’t a request or a favor. It was an order.
It had always been this way. Everyone took it for granted, but he had never grown used to it.
The person who’d written that dry, impersonal command, as though ordering a servant, was his own flesh and blood.
More precisely, the person who had given him that blood.
“...Father.”
The word came after a brief hesitation.
It still felt unfamiliar. As he murmured it, he remembered a rigid, cold childhood with no room for dreams, only purpose—and the stern pair of eyes that had watched him through it.
Creepy as it was, those eyes still seemed to be watching everything he did.
Perhaps that was why he failed to notice someone approaching outside the door.
Thump.
“Ugh!”
A sudden noise overlapped with a cry of pain. Then a sharp shout rang out, breaking the silence.
“You idiot! Height! I told you to mind your height!”
“Taishan not stupid. Namho stupid. You saw it. Why didn’t you dodge?”
“You little punk! Is this because I didn’t give you any sweets?”
The familiar voices reached his ears. Guessing the intruders’ identities, he tossed the letter in his hand into the lamp.
Fwoosh. Crackle.
The paper was less than half the size of his palm and had been treated with oil to keep it dry. It went up in flames at once.
At that moment, the firmly shut door flew open.
Or rather, it was smashed to pieces.
“My lord! Are you ready?”
*Bam!*
The booming shout came with a shower of splinters. But the man—Sama Pyo—didn’t look the least bit startled. He picked up the travel bag beside him and stood.
“Of course. What about you, Taishan?”
“Taishan ready! Perfect!”
Namho, perched on Taishan’s shoulders, spat out a few pieces of wood.
“Of course it’s perfect. Bring just the jerky he packed back to life and you’d have five cows.”
“That sounds like a reasonable amount to me. Not excessive.”
“...It’s a wonder the Black Dragon Demon Gate hasn’t gone bankrupt. He’s a gluttonous demon through and through.”
Sama Pyo gave a short laugh. He already knew that the old Hidden Shadow Pavilion agent, who hadn’t seemed all that pleasant at first, had a warm heart and a fair amount of affection for others.
“More importantly, what were you doing in here alone?”
“I stopped by for a moment. There was something I needed to take care of before we left.”
“Is that so?”
Namho glanced over Sama Pyo’s shoulder, but the letter, soaked through with oil, had already burned away without a trace.
“Then put that fire out before you come out. The weather’s shitty enough without you burning down someone else’s thatched cottage.”
“Oh, I almost forgot.”
Sama Pyo answered mildly and waved a hand, snuffing out the candle. Then, as though nothing had happened, he headed for the doorway.
“Let’s go. Everyone must be waiting.”
Namho watched Sama Pyo’s back with a curious look.
But only for a moment.
Thump.
“Ugh!”
Namho struck his forehead on the eaves again. With a cry, he grabbed Taishan by the hair and yanked.

chapters.title: Chapter 997
paragraphs: Fifteen minutes.
Too short to properly savor even a cup of tea, but plenty of time for the Fire Dragon Pavilion members, myself included, to finish our preparations.
And to prepare a send-off no one else had expected.
Whoooosh. Fwoosh.
Countless torches swayed.
Neither the early darkness nor the snowstorm now whipping fiercely through the air could put out that vast blaze.
Crunch.
Footprints marked the snow-covered ground.
Leaving behind hundreds of people standing like iron towers, each holding a torch in one hand, Jin Wikyung stepped forward alone. Then he suddenly spoke.
“The prodigal son finally came home, only to leave again.”
His voice was stern, as if he were passing judgment on a criminal, but *prodigal son* drew quiet laughter from here and there.
By now, everyone in the Jin Family of Taiyuan knew it. Not just them, but all of Shanxi Province—or rather, the whole world.
Jin Taekyung was no longer the Shame of the Family or a dissolute rogue.
Ever since the day, more than a year ago, when I defeated the traitors—including the Head Elder—and restored peace, I had been their pride and their symbol.
“I never wanted to send you away again.”
I shrugged at Jin Wikyung, who muttered the words with a bitter expression.
“What can I do? Guess it’s fate.”
“What came from the Murim Alliance was information, not an order. If you change your mind, even now, you can stay with the family and leave with everyone else.”
“That sounds nice. But I’ll go ahead and wait for you. I hate being late.”
Jin Wikyung let out a small groan at my polite refusal.

He was practically the Family Head of the Jin Family of Taiyuan, so he couldn’t simply leave. He had to keep not only the family members but countless martial artists from Shanxi under control as they moved—and the nomads they had subdued, too.
It was much the same for the Bow Saint and the Embroidered Uniform Guard, who still hadn’t returned after rooting out the Murong Family’s threat.
A massive army and a small advance unit.
It was obvious which would be slower and which would be faster. And that considerable gap in timing might become the flap of a butterfly’s wings somewhere far away and change a great many things.
Of course, knowing that did nothing to ease his worry for his own flesh and blood.
“It will be dangerous. More than ever before.”
At the sight of Jin Wikyung’s worried expression, my journey so far flashed before my eyes.
Dangerous, huh?
Yeah, of course it would be.
But...
“It always has been. Not once has it been any different, and it won’t be from here on out.”
Looking back, there had never been a time when I wasn’t in danger.
There had never been an easy moment, either.
When I first opened my eyes, I was a tadpole. I struggled to survive and became a frog.
I leaped and leaped with all my might until I escaped the well. Beyond it waited a world incomparably wider and more treacherous than the one I’d left behind.
And at every fork in the road that blocked my way, I had always made a choice.
“It’s the road I chose. I don’t know when I’ll be able to stop, but... I have to keep running. All the way to the end.”
Jin Wikyung was silent for a moment at my matter-of-fact answer. Then he let out a quiet laugh.
“You’ve grown up. Before I knew it, you’d grown so much I hardly recognized you.”
Looking at Jin Wikyung, whose imposing build was enough to make me wonder if he had Hebei Peng blood, I smiled back.
“I’m still not as big as you, hyung.”
“Hyung. That sounds especially good today. Maybe because it’s been so long since you called me that.”
It wasn’t just because I’d spent so long away. I’d simply needed a little more time to truly accept the new family I’d found in this unfamiliar world.
Even if this body’s true owner wasn’t me.
*Right. The real owner—the Jin Family’s Third Young Master—is someone else.*
The thought weighed on me, but the familiar face that appeared beside Jin Wikyung a moment later washed it away.
“Oh, would you look at that. Isn’t that our family’s second son?”
At my exaggeratedly wide-eyed look, Jin Mukyung shook his head.
“Here we go again.”
“What? Did I say anything wrong? You are the second son.”
“You conveniently left out the ‘hyung’ that’s supposed to come after it.”
“I’ll add it if you want. Beat me first.”
“...You shameless bastard.”
“What, you don’t think you can?”
Jin Mukyung stared at me in disbelief, then gave a short laugh.
“Of course I can. Just wait. I’ll catch up soon.”
“Confidence is good, but don’t expect it to be easy.”
“I know. But you’d better remember one thing, too.”
“What?”
“Until I catch up, don’t let anyone else take you down. Ever.”
For a moment, I couldn’t speak. Seeing me blink at him in silence, Jin Mukyung seemed to regret what he’d said. He hesitated, then suddenly extended his fist.
Tap.
His slow but solid punch landed against my chest.
Even with the snowstorm raging all around us, warmth spread through the spot where his fist had touched before drawing away.
“Go ahead. This time, I won’t be late. I promise.”
Maybe he was embarrassed to have shown a side of himself he usually kept hidden. Or maybe some emotion had welled up in him.
Whatever the reason, Jin Mukyung turned away after those words. In the direction he headed, more familiar faces were waiting for me.
Wipeng, who had come to see me off despite his grievous injuries.
Lee Seowol, forcing a smile despite the death of her uncle, Cheol Mubaek—the Tiger of Mount Heng—who had been her staunchest guardian and almost another father to her.
The Jin Family of Taiyuan’s senior members, who had served Jin Wikyung with unwavering loyalty and helped him raise the once-declining family into one of the Five Great Families.

The scouts who had once crossed life and death alongside me. The young brother and sister who had grown so much while I was away from the Jin Family of Taiyuan. And countless family retainers whose faces were more familiar than their names.
Every one of them was looking at me.
As I met each person’s eyes, they smiled brightly, nodded quietly, and stamped their feet with such overwhelming emotion that their hearts seemed ready to burst.
Hard and strong. Without anyone having to lead, they stamped the ground, now blanketed in white, and drew their weapons like lightning.
Clang-clang-clang-clang!
Amid hundreds of swaying torches, a dazzling wave of steel lit up everything around us, brighter than the snowstorm pouring down overhead. An aura like wildfire rose and heated the air.
Thud. Thud. Thoom!
The ground shook beneath their vigorous footfalls. My heart, which had gradually settled into a steady rhythm to match them, began to pound. Just then, Jin Wikyung’s quiet voice slipped into my ear.
“Do you see it?”
I didn’t answer.
No—I couldn’t.
I could only listen to Jin Wikyung’s voice echoing around me, my chest trembling deep inside.
“You are our pride.”
“Go. Down the road you chose.”
Go forward without hesitation, with all your might.
Hearing the rest of his words swallowed by the fierce snowstorm, I finally moved my feet.
Crunch.
Beneath a roof of countless crossed blades, new footprints began to mark the white snow.
The untimely snowstorm wasn’t confined to Shanxi Province.
The young man had remained silent for a long time, even after his expected guest arrived. Watching the snow whip past the window, he suddenly spoke.
“Long ago—very long ago—someone said something like that to me.”
Across the rough table, the guest sat with perfect composure despite a full shichen—about two hours—of silence.
“You’ve made me curious already. Who was it?”
To anyone who didn’t know them, it would have seemed a strange sight.
The room’s owner was a young man, while his guest looked to be about eighty.
Yet the scar visible beneath the older man’s graying hair spoke of a life spent in secrecy. The same was true of the young man opposite him.
“You know the person, too. I can tell you now, if you want.”
The casual way he addressed the older man came as naturally as breathing.
The Thousand-Faced Fox, Song Ho, lightly declined the Sword Saint Mae Jonghak’s offer.
“I’ll try to guess after I hear what was said. I prefer figuring things out for myself to being given the answer.”
“Wouldn’t most people choose the former?”
“As Chief of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion, shouldn’t I be able to manage at least that much?”
“That’s a fair point.”
“So, what did this person say to you, Alliance Leader?”
Still gazing out the window, Mae Jonghak answered.
“He told me to protect it. The place where I stood, the convictions I held in my heart, and the world.”
“I was told to remain here, unchanged, even if that person disappeared one day. Of course, at the time, it sounded like a passing remark, so I didn’t think much of it. That’s all.”
The Thousand-Faced Fox let out a breath he’d been holding.
“I think I know who it was.”
“You do?”
“Yes. As it happens, I believe I heard something similar myself.”
“That person would be pleased to know it. You didn’t take those words lightly. You’ve kept the Hidden Shadow Pavilion’s intelligence network going all this time.”
The Thousand-Faced Fox nodded without a word.
He certainly would have been pleased. Maybe he would even have clapped his hands and burst out laughing.
In Song Ho’s memories, the Martial God seemed to carry every worry in the world, yet at times he could be as innocent as a child.
“There’s something I’d like to ask you.”
“Go ahead, Alliance Leader.”
The Thousand-Faced Fox tensed without meaning to.

But Mae Jonghak’s next words swept that fear away at once.
“When this war is over, what are you going to do?”
“Pardon?”
“No, I just started worrying about you. You hardly get paid for all the work you do. Should I give you a raise now? How about doubling your salary?”
“Hmm. Or tripling it? Then you wouldn’t have to worry about retirement.”
The Thousand-Faced Fox stared blankly at Mae Jonghak, frozen like a statue. Then he suddenly burst into a hearty laugh.

“Don’t worry about my retirement. If I need to, I can always siphon some money off to the side.”

“Of course.”
“But let’s keep this between the two of us. If our friends outside that door find out, we might get some dirty looks. Don’t you think?”
Mae Jonghak stood without waiting for an answer.
A gust of qi swept through the air and threw open the firmly shut door. Beyond it, dozens of people sat around a massive table.

At the first playful remark from a middle-aged man, Mae Jonghak nodded with satisfaction.

“You’re too kind.”
“Now then, did you complete your mission safely, Family Head Zhuge?”
The middle-aged man, Zhuge Feng—the Crouching Dragon Guest—waved his tattered feather fan.
“Can you see it?”
“Quite clearly.”
“These are the marks of my suffering. I thought I was going to die.”
“Which means...”
“The Zhuge Clan has completed every task assigned to it.”
Exclamations rose from around the room. Everyone present knew what Zhuge Feng had been assigned to do, and how important it was.
And it meant one thing.
All preparations were complete. A new phase was beginning.

The opening act of an all-out war had begun.

sentences.text: Fifteen minutes.
Too short to properly savor even a cup of tea, but plenty of time for the Fire Dragon Pavilion members, myself included, to finish our preparations.
And to prepare a send-off no one else had expected.
Whoooosh.
Fwoosh.
Countless torches swayed.
Neither the early darkness nor the snowstorm now whipping fiercely through the air could put out that vast blaze.
Crunch.
Footprints marked the snow-covered ground.
Leaving behind hundreds of people standing like iron towers, each holding a torch in one hand, Jin Wikyung stepped forward alone.
Then he suddenly spoke.
“The prodigal son finally came home, only to leave again.”
His voice was stern, as if he were passing judgment on a criminal, but *prodigal son* drew quiet laughter from here and there.
By now, everyone in the Jin Family of Taiyuan knew it.
Not just them, but all of Shanxi Province—or rather, the whole world.
Jin Taekyung was no longer the Shame of the Family or a dissolute rogue.
Ever since the day, more than a year ago, when I defeated the traitors—including the Head Elder—and restored peace, I had been their pride and their symbol.
“I never wanted to send you away again.”
I shrugged at Jin Wikyung, who muttered the words with a bitter expression.
“What can I do?
Guess it’s fate.”
“What came from the Murim Alliance was information, not an order.
If you change your mind, even now, you can stay with the family and leave with everyone else.”
“That sounds nice.
But I’ll go ahead and wait for you.
I hate being late.”
Jin Wikyung let out a small groan at my polite refusal.
He was practically the Family Head of the Jin Family of Taiyuan, so he couldn’t simply leave.
He had to keep not only the family members but countless martial artists from Shanxi under control as they moved—and the nomads they had subdued, too.
It was much the same for the Bow Saint and the Embroidered Uniform Guard, who still hadn’t returned after rooting out the Murong Family’s threat.
A massive army and a small advance unit.
It was obvious which would be slower and which would be faster.
And that considerable gap in timing might become the flap of a butterfly’s wings somewhere far away and change a great many things.
Of course, knowing that did nothing to ease his worry for his own flesh and blood.
“It will be dangerous.
More than ever before.”
At the sight of Jin Wikyung’s worried expression, my journey so far flashed before my eyes.
Dangerous, huh?
Yeah, of course it would be.
But...
“It always has been.
Not once has it been any different, and it won’t be from here on out.”
Looking back, there had never been a time when I wasn’t in danger.
There had never been an easy moment, either.
When I first opened my eyes, I was a tadpole.
I struggled to survive and became a frog.
I leaped and leaped with all my might until I escaped the well.
Beyond it waited a world incomparably wider and more treacherous than the one I’d left behind.
And at every fork in the road that blocked my way, I had always made a choice.
“It’s the road I chose.
I don’t know when I’ll be able to stop, but...
I have to keep running.
All the way to the end.”
Jin Wikyung was silent for a moment at my matter-of-fact answer.
Then he let out a quiet laugh.
“You’ve grown up.
Before I knew it, you’d grown so much I hardly recognized you.”
Looking at Jin Wikyung, whose imposing build was enough to make me wonder if he had Hebei Peng blood, I smiled back.
“I’m still not as big as you, hyung.”
“Hyung.
That sounds especially good today.
Maybe because it’s been so long since you called me that.”
It wasn’t just because I’d spent so long away.
I’d simply needed a little more time to truly accept the new family I’d found in this unfamiliar world.
Even if this body’s true owner wasn’t me.
*Right.
The real owner—the Jin Family’s Third Young Master—is someone else.*
The thought weighed on me, but the familiar face that appeared beside Jin Wikyung a moment later washed it away.
“Oh, would you look at that.
Isn’t that our family’s second son?”
At my exaggeratedly wide-eyed look, Jin Mukyung shook his head.
“Here we go again.”
“What?
Did I say anything wrong?
You are the second son.”
“You conveniently left out the ‘hyung’ that’s supposed to come after it.”
“I’ll add it if you want.
Beat me first.”
“...You shameless bastard.”
“What, you don’t think you can?”
Jin Mukyung stared at me in disbelief, then gave a short laugh.
“Of course I can.
Just wait.
I’ll catch up soon.”
“Confidence is good, but don’t expect it to be easy.”
“I know.
But you’d better remember one thing, too.”
“What?”
“Until I catch up, don’t let anyone else take you down.
Ever.”
For a moment, I couldn’t speak.
Seeing me blink at him in silence, Jin Mukyung seemed to regret what he’d said.
He hesitated, then suddenly extended his fist.
Tap.
His slow but solid punch landed against my chest.
Even with the snowstorm raging all around us, warmth spread through the spot where his fist had touched before drawing away.
“Go ahead.
This time, I won’t be late.
I promise.”
Maybe he was embarrassed to have shown a side of himself he usually kept hidden.
Or maybe some emotion had welled up in him.
Whatever the reason, Jin Mukyung turned away after those words.
In the direction he headed, more familiar faces were waiting for me.
Wipeng, who had come to see me off despite his grievous injuries.
Lee Seowol, forcing a smile despite the death of her uncle, Cheol Mubaek—the Tiger of Mount Heng—who had been her staunchest guardian and almost another father to her.
The Jin Family of Taiyuan’s senior members, who had served Jin Wikyung with unwavering loyalty and helped him raise the once-declining family into one of the Five Great Families.
The scouts who had once crossed life and death alongside me.
The young brother and sister who had grown so much while I was away from the Jin Family of Taiyuan.
And countless family retainers whose faces were more familiar than their names.
Every one of them was looking at me.
As I met each person’s eyes, they smiled brightly, nodded quietly, and stamped their feet with such overwhelming emotion that their hearts seemed ready to burst.
Hard and strong.
Without anyone having to lead, they stamped the ground, now blanketed in white, and drew their weapons like lightning.
Clang-clang-clang-clang!
Amid hundreds of swaying torches, a dazzling wave of steel lit up everything around us, brighter than the snowstorm pouring down overhead.

chapters.title: Chapter 998
paragraphs: As Jin Wikyung had already said, the most likely place for a major battle with Dark Heaven was Qinghai, where the Kunlun Sect was located.
It was a strategic foothold the enemy would have to take before advancing into the Central Plains—and one the orthodox Murim would have to defend with their lives.
That was exactly why I could answer Hyuk Mujin’s question about how we would get to Qinghai without hesitation.
“We run. Fucking hard.”
“I know that much. What I wanted to ask was...”
“Running fucking hard is fine, but how long do we keep it up?”
“Ah, Captain. You know exactly what I’m thinking.”
“Keep going.”
“...Excuse me?”
“Keep going. All the way.”
“Wait, all the way to Qinghai?”
I asked without easing the reins of my galloping horse.
“Otherwise?”

“I think taking the water route would be better. We can travel overland as you said, then take a tributary of the Yangtze from Shaanxi straight to Qinghai. It’d save us about half a day and take a lot less effort.”
On the face of it, the suggestion made sense.
Half a day wasn’t much, but we’d arrive sooner and conserve our Stamina before an important battle.

Besides, even the Yangtze River Channel League—the river’s gangsters, notorious across the country for generations—was part of the Murim Alliance. If we were lucky, we might be able to hijack a swift ship... No, borrow one.
Or at the very least, a Great Nation military vessel.
But I shook my head at once.
“The land route is better.”
“Why? Do you get seasick?”
“Even if you do, try to bear with it. I’ll pat your back.”
Was this bastard looking down on a Supreme Peak master?
And I wasn’t some newly minted Supreme Peak master, either. I’d reached the pinnacle of martial arts and completed Bone Transformation. I was a superhuman among superhumans.
I could ride a Wolmido Disco Pang Pang and feel perfectly steady. Seasickness?
I stared at Hyuk Mujin in disbelief, momentarily at a loss for words. Just then, a fierce gust of wind swept toward the back of his head.
Whoosh—smack!
“Gah!”
It was the sort of impact that felt satisfying just to hear. Jeok Cheongang, who had expertly smacked the back of Hyuk Mujin’s head, clicked his tongue.
He’d found the saddle uncomfortable, so he was traveling by stepping from branch to branch along the trees lining the road.
“You stupid fool. Why do you talk so much? If your superior tells you to do something, you do it.”
If anyone but me had smacked Hyuk Mujin on the back of the head, he’d have been glaring daggers. But when that someone was the Fire King, Jeok Cheongang, it was a different story.
Unable to talk back, Hyuk Mujin rubbed his aching head and glanced around before speaking.
“I was just offering a better suggestion. Why are you doing this to me?”
“A better suggestion? Do you really think so?”
“Wasn’t it...?”
“I’ll admit it sounded plausible. But you overlooked the most important thing.”
Before Hyuk Mujin could answer, Jeok Cheongang’s low voice carried through the wind.
“Dark Heaven. Whether those devious bastards are truly targeting Qinghai.”
“We know nothing for certain yet. No one knows where Dark Heaven’s army, said to be marching beyond the desert, is headed. Qinghai isn’t the only route into the Central Plains.”
I nodded. Jeok Cheongang had the situation exactly right.
There wasn’t just one route. There were three, maybe more.
Qinghai, Gansu, and even Tibet, beyond the borderlands and counted among the Outer Lands.
Qinghai was the likeliest main target because of its strategic importance, but an invasion through Gansu or Tibet was entirely possible too.
And besides...
*They have a Warp Gate—or rather, a Moving Formation.*
The Moving Formation gave the enemy more options, while serving as a painfully sharp dagger aimed at our backs.
They could send as many as a thousand people—at least, that was the number we’d confirmed so far—to somewhere in the Central Plains through a Moving Formation. How could we take that lightly?
Of course, there was a way to deal with it.

The Zhuge Clan, renowned as the finest in the world at mechanisms and formations, possessed a formation called the Demon-Sealing Formation. As its name suggested, it could suppress and seal magical power.

When a “rift” had opened at Dongting Lake, the Zhuge Clan had managed to contain it with the Demon-Sealing Formation, led by their Family Head, Zhuge Feng. That was why the incident had been brought to an end without even greater losses.
*If they can stop a rift, they should be able to neutralize a Moving Formation, too. I’ve seen the Demon-Sealing Formation myself, so I know it works. The problem is time and manpower.*
The world was vast.
And no one knew how many Moving Formations Dark Heaven had built somewhere in that boundless sea of sand.

We’d found a way to deal with them well over half a year ago, yet several sects near Shanxi Province had still hesitated to send reinforcements, even for a short while. That alone showed how serious the risk was.
Even if just one Moving Formation remained, it would be like a sharp shard of glass, digging deep into the sole of someone walking carelessly across the sand.
*That’s why we have to travel overland.*
Qinghai had been a battlefield whenever foreign invaders came over the centuries. The Murim Alliance would have prepared the best defenses it could.
Those defenses wouldn’t be so flimsy that half a day—or even a full day—would make the difference between holding and falling.
*Tibet should be reasonably safe, too. Even if the Potala Palace has joined hands with Dark Heaven, the forces stationed in Sichuan should be able to hold out.*
The Sichuan Tang Clan, which the Western Heaven Demon Lord had targeted personally, had suffered tremendous losses. But Qingcheng and Emei were still intact.
And some unexpected guests were staying in Sichuan as well.
*The Nanman Beast Palace.*
Though we’d left in a hurry with a long road ahead, I’d heard news of them from time to time.
The warriors of the tropics had finally left their jungle in an unprecedented mass migration. They’d readily accepted the Murim Alliance’s request and were now defending Sichuan.
“The western front will have made preparations to some extent. Except in one place.”
I wasn’t speaking to Hyuk Mujin alone.
After finishing my train of thought, I suddenly spoke. I looked around at the Fire Dragon Pavilion members riding alongside me, then added quietly,
“Gansu.”
“If Dark Heaven goes against everyone’s expectations and targets Gansu, that’s where the biggest battle of this war will be fought.”
That was no exaggeration.
Dark Heaven had always found ways to catch us off guard.

Thanks to the efforts of countless people, myself included, who’d practically shit ourselves trying to stop them, their schemes had been thwarted time and again. But that didn’t mean the Murim Alliance had gained the upper hand in this war.
No. It would be more accurate to say Dark Heaven had been toying with us.
*Shutting the stable door after the horse has bolted.*
If we’d caught the arsonist before he set fire to the stable, that would have been a victory.
But the stable had burned every time, and countless people had been slaughtered like livestock.
As the person who’d repeatedly run around dousing the stables wherever I went, I was sick and tired of all of it.
So...
*This time, we have to stop them. No matter what.*
Before another fire started. Before there were more terrible losses.
We had to be cautious, then cautious again. Test the stone bridge before crossing it. I needed to see the situation in Gansu with my own eyes before moving on to Qinghai.
That was the biggest reason I’d chosen the land route over the slightly faster, more comfortable water route.
*And this choice should be a lot more reassuring for him, too.*
I glanced at one man.
Half a day had passed since we left the Jin Family of Taiyuan, and Sama Pyo still hadn’t said a word. He simply held his reins in silence.
He’d always been taciturn, but lately it had grown more pronounced.
*No wonder. If Dark Heaven’s army is crossing the deserts of Xinjiang right now, his family could be in danger.*
Along with the Kongtong Sect, one of the Nine Sects and One Gang, the Black Dragon Demon Gate was one of the two powers that divided Gansu Province between them.
As the Black Dragon Demon Gate’s Young Sect Leader, Sama Pyo was bound to have a lot on his mind. All the more so after hearing what Jeok Cheongang and I had just said.
But I didn’t try to console him.
Comfort was a luxury in a situation like this. When our eyes met, Sama Pyo gave me a slight, silent nod. I looked away and tightened my grip on the reins.
“Hyah!”
Thud-thud-thud-thud!
The grassland horses, said to surpass even sweat-blood horses in endurance, galloped on without a trace of fatigue.
Night and day passed once more, and the moon and sun crossed paths overhead.
Three days swept by like the wind. We left Shanxi Province and reached the border between Shaanxi and Gansu.
“Stop. We’ll rest here for half a shichen.”
The man who suddenly spoke, bringing everyone to a halt, appeared to be around sixty. He was slender, with strikingly narrow eyes.
Of course, the several hundred people following him knew appearances didn’t tell the whole story.
Just as what they saw with their eyes wasn’t all there was, the old man had lived far longer than he looked. Only his formidable martial prowess could account for it.
Great age and formidable skill.
Of everyone present, only one person could refuse an order from a man who possessed both.
“A rest, out of nowhere? What on earth do you mean, Eldest Senior Brother?”
A half-white-haired Daoist in a clean robe hurried over, looking confused. The old man answered without a care.
“This old body of mine is giving me trouble. I can’t go any farther, so I thought we’d rest for half a shichen. Is there a problem?”
“Eldest Senior Brother!”
“Lower your voice, Junior Brother Sect Leader. How can you be so rude to Eldest Senior Brother?”
Someone else had cut in. The graying Daoist turned toward the reproachful voice and sighed.
“Why are you doing this too, Senior Brother? It’s been two days since we left the main sect, and we still haven’t reached Gansu. You both know that...”
“Enough.”
The man he’d called Senior Brother—an old Daoist with a luxuriant white beard that made him look like an immortal—raised a hand to cut him off.
“What can we do? Our bodies have grown weak. There’s a limit to how far we can travel. Eldest Senior Brother and I are disappointed in you, Junior Brother Sect Leader.”
“What do you mean?”
“After spending so long recuperating, your two Senior Brothers have only just become able to get around again. Why must you rush us?”
The graying Daoist’s lips moved as if he wanted to say something, but no words came. He turned away.
Even if he had spoken his mind, the outcome would probably have been much the same.
At that very moment, pounding hooves rang through the deserted forest.
Thud-thud-thud-thud!
Several grassland horses burst through the rising cloud of dust. They spotted the group halted in the middle of the forest path and began to slow.
More precisely, they slowed when they saw the flag rising above the group.
**The Great Zhongnan Sect.**
From atop his panting grassland horse, the young man riding in front read the characters embroidered in a single flowing stroke and muttered under his breath,
“I think there’s a typo...”

“Wasn’t it...?”
“I’ll admit it sounded plausible.
But you overlooked the most important thing.”
Before Hyuk Mujin could answer, Jeok Cheongang’s low voice carried through the wind.
“Dark Heaven.
Whether those devious bastards are truly targeting Qinghai.”
“We know nothing for certain yet.
No one knows where Dark Heaven’s army, said to be marching beyond the desert, is headed.
Qinghai isn’t the only route into the Central Plains.”
I nodded.
Jeok Cheongang had the situation exactly right.
There wasn’t just one route.
There were three, maybe more.
Qinghai, Gansu, and even Tibet, beyond the borderlands and counted among the Outer Lands.
Qinghai was the likeliest main target because of its strategic importance, but an invasion through Gansu or Tibet was entirely possible too.
And besides...
*They have a Warp Gate—or rather, a Moving Formation.*
The Moving Formation gave the enemy more options, while serving as a painfully sharp dagger aimed at our backs.
They could send as many as a thousand people—at least, that was the number we’d confirmed so far—to somewhere in the Central Plains through a Moving Formation.
How could we take that lightly?
Of course, there was a way to deal with it.
The Zhuge Clan, renowned as the finest in the world at mechanisms and formations, possessed a formation called the Demon-Sealing Formation.
As its name suggested, it could suppress and seal magical power.
When a “rift” had opened at Dongting Lake, the Zhuge Clan had managed to contain it with the Demon-Sealing Formation, led by their Family Head, Zhuge Feng.
That was why the incident had been brought to an end without even greater losses.
*If they can stop a rift, they should be able to neutralize a Moving Formation, too.
I’ve seen the Demon-Sealing Formation myself, so I know it works.
The problem is time and manpower.*
The world was vast.
And no one knew how many Moving Formations Dark Heaven had built somewhere in that boundless sea of sand.
We’d found a way to deal with them well over half a year ago, yet several sects near Shanxi Province had still hesitated to send reinforcements, even for a short while.
That alone showed how serious the risk was.
Even if just one Moving Formation remained, it would be like a sharp shard of glass, digging deep into the sole of someone walking carelessly across the sand.
*That’s why we have to travel overland.*
Qinghai had been a battlefield whenever foreign invaders came over the centuries.
The Murim Alliance would have prepared the best defenses it could.
Those defenses wouldn’t be so flimsy that half a day—or even a full day—would make the difference between holding and falling.
*Tibet should be reasonably safe, too.
Even if the Potala Palace has joined hands with Dark Heaven, the forces stationed in Sichuan should be able to hold out.*
The Sichuan Tang Clan, which the Western Heaven Demon Lord had targeted personally, had suffered tremendous losses.
But Qingcheng and Emei were still intact.
And some unexpected guests were staying in Sichuan as well.
*The Nanman Beast Palace.*
Though we’d left in a hurry with a long road ahead, I’d heard news of them from time to time.
The warriors of the tropics had finally left their jungle in an unprecedented mass migration.
They’d readily accepted the Murim Alliance’s request and were now defending Sichuan.
“The western front will have made preparations to some extent.
Except in one place.”
I wasn’t speaking to Hyuk Mujin alone.
After finishing my train of thought, I suddenly spoke.
I looked around at the Fire Dragon Pavilion members riding alongside me, then added quietly,
“Gansu.”
“If Dark Heaven goes against everyone’s expectations and targets Gansu, that’s where the biggest battle of this war will be fought.”
That was no exaggeration.
Dark Heaven had always found ways to catch us off guard.
Thanks to the efforts of countless people, myself included, who’d practically shit ourselves trying to stop them, their schemes had been thwarted time and again.
But that didn’t mean the Murim Alliance had gained the upper hand in this war.
No.
It would be more accurate to say Dark Heaven had been toying with us.
*Shutting the stable door after the horse has bolted.*
If we’d caught the arsonist before he set fire to the stable, that would have been a victory.
But the stable had burned every time, and countless people had been slaughtered like livestock.
As the person who’d repeatedly run around dousing the stables wherever I went, I was sick and tired of all of it.
So...
*This time, we have to stop them.
No matter what.*
Before another fire started.
Before there were more terrible losses.
We had to be cautious, then cautious again.
Test the stone bridge before crossing it.
I needed to see the situation in Gansu with my own eyes before moving on to Qinghai.
That was the biggest reason I’d chosen the land route over the slightly faster, more comfortable water route.
*And this choice should be a lot more reassuring for him, too.*
I glanced at one man.
Half a day had passed since we left the Jin Family of Taiyuan, and Sama Pyo still hadn’t said a word.
He simply held his reins in silence.
He’d always been taciturn, but lately it had grown more pronounced.
*No wonder.
If Dark Heaven’s army is crossing the deserts of Xinjiang right now, his family could be in danger.*
Along with the Kongtong Sect, one of the Nine Sects and One Gang, the Black Dragon Demon Gate was one of the two powers that divided Gansu Province between them.
As the Black Dragon Demon Gate’s Young Sect Leader, Sama Pyo was bound to have a lot on his mind.
All the more so after hearing what Jeok Cheongang and I had just said.
But I didn’t try to console him.
Comfort was a luxury in a situation like this.
When our eyes met, Sama Pyo gave me a slight, silent nod.
I looked away and tightened my grip on the reins.
“Hyah!”
Thud-thud-thud-thud!
The grassland horses, said to surpass even sweat-blood horses in endurance, galloped on without a trace of fatigue.
Night and day passed once more, and the moon and sun crossed paths overhead.
Three days swept by like the wind.
We left Shanxi Province and reached the border between Shaanxi and Gansu.
“Stop.
We’ll rest here for half a shichen.”
The man who suddenly spoke, bringing everyone to a halt, appeared to be around sixty.
He was slender, with strikingly narrow eyes.
Of course, the several hundred people following him knew appearances didn’t tell the whole story.
Just as what they saw with their eyes wasn’t all there was, the old man had lived far longer than he looked.
Only his formidable martial prowess could account for it.
Great age and formidable skill.
Of everyone present, only one person could refuse an order from a man who possessed both.
“A rest, out of nowhere?
What on earth do you mean, Eldest Senior Brother?”
A half-white-haired Daoist in a clean robe hurried over, looking confused.
The old man answered without a care.
“This old body of mine is giving me trouble.
I can’t go any farther, so I thought we’d rest for half a shichen.
Is there a problem?”
“Eldest Senior Brother!”
“Lower your voice, Junior Brother Sect Leader.
How can you be so rude to Eldest Senior Brother?”
Someone else had cut in.
The graying Daoist turned toward the reproachful voice and sighed.
“Why are you doing this too, Senior Brother?
It’s been two days since we left the main sect, and we still haven’t reached Gansu.
You both know that...”
“Enough.”
The man he’d called Senior Brother—an old Daoist with a luxuriant white beard that made him look like an immortal—raised a hand to cut him off.
“What can we do?
Our bodies have grown weak.
There’s a limit to how far we can travel.
Eldest Senior Brother and I are disappointed in you, Junior Brother Sect Leader.”
“What do you mean?”
“After spending so long recuperating, your two Senior Brothers have only just become able to get around again.
Why must you rush us?”
The graying Daoist’s lips moved as if he wanted to say something, but no words came.
He turned away.
Even if he had spoken his mind, the outcome would probably have been much the same.
At that very moment, pounding hooves rang through the deserted forest.
Thud-thud-thud-thud!
Several grassland horses burst through the rising cloud of dust.
They spotted the group halted in the middle of the forest path and began to slow.
More precisely, they slowed when they saw the flag rising above the group.
**The Great Zhongnan Sect.**
From atop his panting grassland horse, the young man riding in front read the characters embroidered in a single flowing stroke and muttered under his breath,
“I think there’s a typo...”

chapters.title: Chapter 999
paragraphs: When I first started working as a Hunter, the veterans had a saying they repeated all the time: you never knew when or where you might cross paths with someone again. So you had to be careful and flexible about making or breaking ties, or you’d have trouble later.
Looking back, I can’t think of a more useful piece of advice.
There was just one problem. Advice like that didn’t mean a damn thing to a guy like me.
“I think there’s a typo...”
**The Great Zhongnan Sect.**
The words slipped out the moment I read the four characters embroidered on the ornate silk. The nearest Daoist frowned.
“Daoist friend, what did you just say?”
“Oh, nothing. Talking to myself.”
“Talking to yourself?”
“Yeah.”
“That’s rather familiar of you.”
“Yeah, sir.”
The middle-aged Daoist stared at me, momentarily dumbfounded. He drew a breath before he managed to speak.
“What are you playing at?”
“You called me a friend, so I talked to you like one. Besides, you started speaking casually to me first.”
“You look to be a fellow martial artist, but you’re much younger than I am. You have quite a mouth on you.”
“I can get away with it. I’m young, but in martial seniority I’m an old man.”
“What... did you say?”

At that point, it was only natural for him to sense something was amiss. My answer had thrown him off, and an uneasy murmur spread among the Zhongnan Sect disciples watching me and the Fire Dragon Pavilion members who’d appeared so suddenly.
“It’s true.”
At the sound of a low voice, the crowd parted to either side. I smiled warmly at the familiar faces beyond them.
“It’s been a while. Both of you.”
Neither returned my greeting. The two old Daoists had stopped abruptly three jang away.
“May your health be... uh... what comes after that?”
Hyuk Mujin answered without hesitation.
“Split in two.”
“May your health be split in two. That sounds a little off. Are you sure?”
“No. I don’t really know either. I just said the first thing that came to mind.”
“Are you insane? Now I’m even more confused.”
“I’m sorry.”
“Whatever. Anybody know it?”
Ju Hwaran shot up a hand.
“May you be healthy in every way. May your health be sound in every respect.”
“Oh. As expected of Young Lady Ju. Ten points to the Griffin Yongbong Escort Bureau.”
“Hehe.”
She smiled bashfully, though she had no idea what I meant. I gave her a thumbs-up, then respectfully clasped my hands toward the two old Daoists.
“Anyway. Have you both been split in two?”
The mood turned as cold as if someone had dumped a bucket of water over us.
I belatedly realized I’d said it wrong and let out a deep sigh. Depending on how they took it, they might misunderstand, but it really was a slip of the tongue.
“Damn it, I got mixed up. Hyuk Mujin.”
“Yes?”
“Get down and put your head on the ground.”
“Ah, yes.”
As Hyuk Mujin performed the remarkable feat of putting his head down while seated in the saddle, one of the old Daoists finally spoke.
“You haven’t changed. Still as brazen as ever.”

He was the first of the two to speak, an old Daoist with a thick snow-white beard. It hung down to his navel, making him look like an immortal who’d descended to the mortal world. But I already knew better.
Hwangbo Eom, the Taeeul Merciless Sword, was about as far from an immortal as a man could get.
*Not even close. If he were half as good inside as he looked, he never would’ve pulled a stunt that shameless.*
It might be unfortunate for him and the Zhongnan Sect, but I didn’t have the memory of a goldfish.

They’d entrusted Ju Hwaran’s Yongbong Escort Bureau with transporting their priceless Thousand-Year Snow Ginseng, then secretly stolen it back and demanded compensation. It was an insurance scam meant to swallow the Bureau whole. I’d remember it for the rest of my life.
Of course, the old man beside Hwangbo Eom, darting his eyes this way and that, had a colorful record of his own.
“Looking for someone?”
“...What?”
“I asked if you were looking for someone, Great Hero Song Il.”
The Roaring Fury Swordsman’s eyebrows twitched at the amusement in my voice.

A year and several months ago, Song Il had tried to overturn the Jin Family of Taiyuan’s banquet, backed by his Supreme Peak martial prowess and his illustrious position as a Zhongnan Sect Elder. He’d nearly ended up the guest of honor at a funeral instead.

Now he was anxiously scanning our group, searching for one person: a man who, Zhongnan Sect or not, wouldn’t think twice about slapping someone across the face and kicking them in the shins for good measure if the mood took him.
I spoke gently.
“You can relax. The person you’re looking for isn’t here.”
“Oh, did I get it wrong? Were you looking for someone else?”
Song Il glared at me in silence before squeezing out his answer.
“You dare—”
“Dare to what?”
That wasn’t me.
Jeok Cheongang dropped out of empty air, and Song Il’s eyes went wide.
“H-How can you be here?”
“What? ‘You’?”
“N-No, that’s not what I meant.”
Song Il stammered and backed away.

A bristly crop of red hair had grown over Jeok Cheongang’s once-smooth scalp, and his face now looked middle-aged. Word that he’d broken through to another great realm and regained his youth had spread far and wide. The Zhongnan Sect was no exception.
“F-Fire King Jeok Cheongang...!”

Someone blurted out the name, and shock swept through the crowd. They were seeing the Fire King himself for the first time—and realizing that the young upstart who’d appeared out of nowhere was the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon, Jin Taekyung.
Song Il looked between Jeok Cheongang and me as though he couldn’t believe his eyes. I spread my arms wide.
“Ta-da! I lied!”
“What do you think? Surprised?”
We hadn’t seen each other in ages. A little surprise was only fair.
From the way he sucked in a breath and started trembling, I’d definitely surprised him. He looked less startled than on the verge of a fit, though.
Fortunately for Song Il, someone intervened before he keeled over.
“This humble Gong of the Zhongnan Sect pays his respects to Great Hero Jeok.”

A graying Daoist with a goatee of awkward, in-between length clasped his hands respectfully despite his haste. At the sight of the Zhongnan Sect Leader, Jeok Cheongang clicked his tongue, disappointed that he couldn’t keep tormenting Song Il.
“Well, it’s been a while. What was your name again? Gong Piljung?”
“Not Piljung. Iljung. I’m Gong Iljung, Great Hero Jeok.”
“Ah, yes. I remember now. Wind-and-Cloud War God Gong Iljung.”
“...Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord.”
“Good grief. I keep getting my words mixed up today. Sorry about that, Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord Gong Piljung.”
The Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord looked at me, all the fight gone out of him. His half-resigned eyes held a question he desperately wanted answered.
*Is he doing this to mess with me on purpose?*
Eyes can be an excellent way to communicate. I answered with mine.
*No. He’s just like that.*
That wasn’t empty reassurance. Honestly, neither Jeok Cheongang nor I had any particular grudge against Gong Iljung.

We had plenty against his Senior Brothers, Song Il and Hwangbo Eom. But we’d only crossed paths with Gong Iljung a couple of times, at the Star-Array Grand Banquet and the founding of the Murim Alliance. We had no reason to hold anything against him.
Jeok Cheongang looked ready to punch Song Il, yet he was still addressing Gong Iljung with a measure of courtesy. That said enough.
*Besides, people don’t have much bad to say about the Zhongnan Sect Leader.*
Feeling a little sorry that he’d caught some of the insult unintentionally, I shook my head. Gong Iljung seemed to relax.
“I’m surprised. I didn’t expect to see you here again.”
“Likewise.”
Jeok Cheongang answered without hesitation, then looked over the Zhongnan Sect Disciples filling the forest path and added,
“I thought you’d be in Gansu or Qinghai by now.”
“Shaanxi’s right next door. Why are you sprawled out resting here?”
Now that was a direct hit. Gong Iljung flushed.
“W-Well...”
He couldn’t bring himself to finish, but his eyes shifted toward the answer.
Song Il and Hwangbo Eom watched us with grim faces. I could piece together most of what had happened.
*They’d dug in their heels and dared anyone to do something about it.*
For some reason, those old bastards seemed to have held the whole Zhongnan Sect back. I was almost certain of it, especially since something similar had happened recently.
*Come to think of it, those two were the only ones who didn’t show up.*

When the bloodshed erupted in Shanxi Province, the Hebei Peng Family, Huashan, and even Murim Alliance Headquarters sent reinforcements. Their timely arrival helped us bring the fighting to a complete end.
The Zhongnan Sect?
Strictly speaking, they came.
A day after the battle was over.
Of course, sending reinforcements meant taking some risk, and I was grateful for that much. But it still left a bad taste in my mouth.
*They said they’d sent a thousand troops. Three hundred reached Shanxi Province, more than half of them useless nobodies. And even that lot was late.*
Put all three together, and the feeling of *this is fucking bullshit* was bound to rise from deep in my gut. Add the sight of two faces I never wanted to see again, and my mouth moved on its own.
“Well, it happens. Making the journey at all in your condition is a fine display of righteous spirit.”
Song Il and Hwangbo Eom frowned as the remark found its marks.
“You brat! I told you to stop running your mouth!”
Jeok Cheongang’s stern rebuke was directed at me. He went on without pause.

“Just making it this far while pissing blood all the way here makes you heroes! These great seniors of the Murim are only now beginning to act their age after all this time. How can you speak to them so rudely?”

“What have they done that’s so wrong? Did they throw their weight around to force a weaker sect to close its doors? Or steal a Thousand-Year Snow Ginseng and try to swallow an innocent Escort Bureau whole?”
Each word from the merciless Tongue King cut to the bone. Gong Iljung struggled to get his voice out.
“G-Great Hero Jeok. Please, for my sake and my Master’s...”
“All right. I’ll stop here.”
“Thank you.”
“No need to thank me, Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord Gong Piljung.”
Vicious. Absolutely vicious.

chapters.title: Chapter 1000
paragraphs: If the Roaring Fury Swordsman and the Taeeul Merciless Sword had shown even a hint of displeasure at that moment—or if they’d been unable to keep their itching hands still and started fiddling with their sword hilts—something serious might have happened.
Me aside, Jeok Cheongang was not the sort of man to stand by and let that happen.
And the Zhongnan Sect Leader, the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord Gong Pil—no, Gong Iljung—shared that concern.
—Tell me, Friend Jin. Are you just going to watch?
A low voice reached my ear through Sound Transmission.
Jeok Cheongang’s brow twitched as he sensed the sound waves. At that very moment, someone spoke.
“What must we do... to earn your forgiveness?”
Everyone’s eyes widened, mine included.
Why?
Simple.
Someone we never expected had said something we never expected to hear.
The Roaring Fury Swordsman, Song Il.
That old Daoist, whose pride bordered on arrogance, had opened his tightly sealed lips and asked for forgiveness.
And the “we” he’d used included someone else.
“I’ve thought about it countless times over the past few months. About the wrongs I committed, and what came of them.”
The Taeeul Merciless Sword, Hwangbo Eom.
He and the Roaring Fury Swordsman were the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord’s only two Senior Brothers and the most senior members of the Zhongnan Sect. Hwangbo Eom looked at me as he continued.
“It was my fault. I can’t deny that.”
His gaze sank. His voice trembled.
I watched him in silence, then suddenly spoke.
“Did you mean what you just said?”
“Do you doubt my sincerity?”
“Of course not.”
I swallowed hard and added, “I believe you. At the same time, I’ll put the unpleasant memories of the past behind me. I can’t say I was blameless in the trouble that happened that day, either.”
Everyone’s eyes widened at my calm reply. Those who knew me well were probably the most surprised.
Even to me, the voice coming out of my mouth sounded like someone else’s.
But another voice slipped out at the same time, and that one was different.
It was what I truly thought, but couldn’t say aloud in front of everyone.
—I don’t believe you. No, I *won’t* believe you.
—If Great Hero Hwangbo truly regretted what he did, I can’t explain what we saw just a moment ago. I think you both know what I mean.
I sent the Sound Transmission and looked calmly at the Roaring Fury Swordsman and the Taeeul Merciless Sword.
Only moments had passed since they’d clenched their teeth and trembled with their fists balled tight. That wasn’t long enough to forget.
And yet it must have been a long, painful road for them to stand here on their own two feet.
*There’s still resentment. Of course there is.*
I wasn’t asking them to erase it completely.
People don’t change easily.
Not me. Not them.
But now was the time to set aside the bad blood between us and move forward. Everyone knew that.
—What answer do you want from us?
—The truth. What you genuinely think—not something meant to be shown or said for someone else’s benefit.
—You don’t have to understand each other. But you have to acknowledge your own feelings and accept the distance between you before you can join hands. I think you both know that already.
A silence that lasted too long would invite suspicion.
In the brief hush, the two old Daoists looked at each other, then clasped their hands toward us.
“I, Song Il, bow my head and apologize for the disrespect I showed the Jin Family of Taiyuan.”
“Please forgive me for forgetting my duty as a Daoist and putting the Yongbong Escort Bureau in danger. I promise to apologize again and do everything I can to compensate you.”
The Roaring Fury Swordsman bowed to me. The Taeeul Merciless Sword bowed to Ju Hwaran.
The Zhongnan Sect Disciples who witnessed it reacted in all sorts of ways.
Some bit their lips in frustration. Some wore faint smiles. Others couldn’t bear to watch their elders apologize to outsiders, so they closed their eyes as if they hadn’t seen it or looked away.
But most of them probably didn’t notice that those stiff bows, made by men who had gone so long without bending to anyone, hid the slight movement of their lips.
—Yes, you’re right. Bad blood doesn’t disappear so easily once it’s there. And I know that you, who say so, aren’t much different from us.
—But now is the time to gather our strength and face our great enemy. That is why we, as members of the great Zhongnan Sect and respected masters of the Murim, will fight for the world. Nothing more.
Their Sound Transmissions reached both my ears at once.
If those were their genuine feelings, I had no reason to refuse.
Step.
For the first time since we’d encountered the Zhongnan Sect, I dismounted. Ju Hwaran followed my cue and set her feet on the ground.
Then?
We clasped our hands toward the two old Daoists, so respectfully that no one could have found fault with it.
Jeok Cheongang watched me in silence with a curious smile, then shrugged at the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord.
“Better to keep things friendly. Right, Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord Gong Iljung?”
The Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord had looked like he’d just aged ten years. Now, as the situation came to a gentle close, he let out a sigh.
“Piljung. I’ve told you several times already, it’s Gong Piljung...”
“Gong Piljung? Wasn’t it Gong Iljung?”
“Ah.”
“What’s the problem?”
Only then did the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord realize something was off. He shook his head as if he’d been bewitched.
The tense atmosphere had lasted only a little while at the start.
Once things had settled, the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord—briefly confused by Jeok Cheongang’s dazzling name-changing technique—was the first to speak.
“May I ask where you’re headed?”
Jeok Cheongang answered flatly.
“Of course not.”
“Pardon?”
“Ask someone else. I’m only here as a guest. Someone else is in the presiding chair.”
Who was Jeok Cheongang? The Fire King himself.
He was also the head of the Five Kings Hall, newly established alongside the Murim Alliance. The idea that he was merely a guest was ridiculous.
But the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord nodded without argument and came over to me.
If Jeok Cheongang said so, then that was how it was. If he said otherwise, then it wasn’t.
As the leader of a great sect like the Zhongnan Sect, he took Jeok Cheongang’s answer to mean that his Master wanted to give his Disciple the authority to speak.
I saw it differently, of course.
“Great Hero Jeok cares for you a great deal.”
“He must have found you pretty annoying.”
“He doesn’t like it when people he isn’t close to keep talking to him. Give him some space for the next half day or so.”
“I’m telling you so you don’t misunderstand. I’m not joking.”
The Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord looked back and forth between me and Jeok Cheongang as if he couldn’t believe what he was hearing. He gave an awkward reply.
“Thank you for the kind advice.”
“Don’t mention it.”
“And as Sect Leader, I can’t say this in public, but I’m grateful to you for the other matter, too.”
The other matter.
It was vague, but I had no trouble understanding him.
He was thanking me, in his own way, for settling things peacefully with his two Senior Brothers.
“You don’t have to thank me. Honestly... they were the ones who brought it up, and that helped resolve things.”
What would have happened if even the slightest killing intent had slipped from the Roaring Fury Swordsman or the Taeeul Merciless Sword?
Given the situation, it probably wouldn’t have turned into a massive bloodbath. But neither Jeok Cheongang nor I would have stood by and done nothing.
No matter how close Dark Heaven’s blade was to our throats, we couldn’t ignore a dagger coming at us from behind.
“Well, thanks to them, things are more or less settled for now. That’s a relief.”
“Mm. It surprised me, too. Though I doubt my Senior Brothers have entirely let go of their feelings.”
I looked at him in surprise. The Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord gave a faint, wry laugh.
“What, did you think I wouldn’t know?”
“No. I just...”

“I joined Zhongnan when I was twelve. We served the same Master, and we’ve spent well over fifty years together. I know my Senior Brothers better than anyone. But as their Junior Brother and as Sect Leader, I should say no more.”
From the sound of it, he’d cleaned up the messes his Senior Brothers made more than once.
I decided this was the time to ask him directly.
“Is that why the reinforcements never really came?”
“...That’s a sharp question.”
“I just want to know what happened. I’m not accusing you.”
The Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord let out a faint sigh under my unwavering gaze.
“It wasn’t any one person’s fault. Even I couldn’t bring myself to send a large portion of our sect’s main force.”
“Meaning?”
“I made that decision out of concern for Zhongnan’s safety. If it upset you and the Jin Family of Taiyuan, there was nothing to be done.”
Sometimes a direct, plain answer is the right one.
Like now.
I thought for a moment, then quietly nodded.
“What does that mean?”
“I mean I understand. Completely.”
“Then...”
“It would be ridiculous to tell people who are helping us exactly how they should help. We had enough reinforcements without Zhongnan. I only wanted to know why.”
“I see. Then is that enough?”
“Of course.”
I didn’t bother adding *for now*.
Nor did I bring up the bad blood between the Zhongnan Sect and the Nanman Beast Palace from the Great Faction War.
For the moment, this was the best we could do.
Now was the time to look at the forest, not the branches. There was nothing to gain from falling out with the Zhongnan Sect.
*We need Zhongnan’s strength to face Dark Heaven’s army threatening the west.*
There were three Supreme Peak masters here alone.
And even at a glance, the Zhongnan Sect Disciples they led were the elite of the main sect.
That meant they, too, intended to give their all in the great battle to come.
Remembering the bad blood of the past without dwelling on it was the right choice.
I hoped that choice would lead everyone in a better direction.
That was the only way we could send the Fire Dragon Pavilion members back home in one piece after a short rest—one they were getting up from now, after days of marching without respite.
*Actually, two of them are already on their way home.*
I was lost in thought, looking at Sama Pyo and Taishan, when the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord spoke.
“So, where are you headed? Qinghai, like Huashan, who passed us earlier? Or...”
“Gansu. We’re going to Gansu.”
I’d been about to ask where the Zhongnan Sect was headed, but realized I didn’t need to.
The Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord’s face had brightened considerably. That told me they were going the same way we were.
